WHERE DO THE NEW YEARS COME FROM? Two bright heads in the corner, Deep in the easy chair; One with a crown Of yellow gold, And one like the silver fair; One with the morning's rosy flush, And one with the twilight's tender hush. "Where do the New Years come from r Asks Goldlocks in her glee; "Do they sail in a pearly shallop Across a wonderful ses— A sea whose waters, with rainbows spanned, Touch all the borders of fairly-land? "Do all the birds in that country Beep singing by night and by day, Singing among the blossoms That never wither away? Will they let yoa feel, as they hold them near, Their warm hearts beating, but not with fear? " And the happy little children, Do they wander as they will, To gather the sweet wild roses, And the strawberries on the hill— White wings, like butterflies all afloat, And a purple cloud for a fairy boat? "There sure is such a country; I've seen it many a night; Though I never, never could find it, Awake in the morning light; And that is the country over the sea, Where the beauttful New Years waitfor me." "Where do the New Years come from?" Says Grandpa, looking away Though the frosty rime on the window To the distant hills so gray; "They come from the country of Youth, I know, And they pass to.the land of the Long-Ago. "'And which is the fairest country?' • Dear heart, I never can tell— Where the New Years wait their dawning, Or the beautiful Old Years dwell; But the sweetest summers that ever shone To the land of the Long-Ago have flown. "The New Years wait for you, darling, And the Old Years wait for me; They have carried my dearest treasures To the country over the sea— The eyes that were brightest, the lips that sung The gladdest carols when life was young. • "But I know of abetter country, Where the Old Years all are new; I shall find its shining pathway Sooner, sweet heart, than you; And I'll send you a message of love and cheer With every dawn of a glad New Year." The eyes of the dear old pilgrim Are looking across the snows, While closer nestles the merry face. With its flush like a kind wild rose; • Dreaming together. the young and old— Locks of silver and crown of gold. • EMILY HUNTINGTON' MILLER. —Leeds Mercury Weekly.

Probably in no part of the United Kingdom was super- stition more rife, up to so recently as half a ceatury ago, than in the districts enclosed by the estuaries of More- cambe Bay—Lonsdale North, portions of Westmoreland, and Cumberland. It is more than probable that the intercourse with Scotland might have much to do with this. Ghosts and supernatural warnings as ere firmly believed in. There was no railway communication with the outer world, and the inhabitants led a very primitive life. Few newspapers penetrated into the towns and villages, so that news of a fortnight old was considered "late news" in those days. Gas was unknown even in the towns, and the faint oil lamps but served, in many instances, to make the darkness the greatel• outsid& the reach of their rays. This eerie state of the streets at night but added to the fears of the superstitious, and there were many " haunted " places in the neighbourhood, past which none but the boldest would go on a dark night, and they, no doubt, did so with much quaking and perturbation. When a child was born, at the first house it entered after the christening, it must be presented with an egg, a match, a piece of bread, a pinch of salt, and a piece of money. If this were not done its future career would be unlucky. If an engaged couple' stood sponsors for the child, it was a certainty that the engaged pair would , never marry. If crickets were heard chirping about the hearthstone, or the small insect known as the " death- watch " was heard in some old woodwork during the stillness of the night, they were sure forerunners of the death of a relative or of a member of the house. A bright spark in a tallow candle wick meant a letter in the morning—letters were not so frequent then as now. If' the family cat, in washing itself, got its paw over both ears with the same stroke, a stranger would shortly arrive. If you were unlucky enough to tread upon and and kill a black snail, rain would shortly follow, and as the district rainfall was and is very high, this, at certain periods of the year, was looked upon as a misfortune. No one ever saw a magpie cross the road in front of him without stopping to expectorate and make the, sign of the cross. So strong was the belief that this presaged ill-luck that many, starting upon a day's journey, would return hom3, and delay the journey until another day. On the other hand, if two magpies crossed your path, the wayfarer went on with a light heart:— One a sign of sorrow, Two a sign of mirth; Three a sign of a wedding. Four a sign of death. That certain persons possessed the gift of "taking, fire out" is believed up to this day. It was a gift handed down from father to son, and the charm lay in repeating certain lines from the Scriptures. The secret must only be divulged on the death-bed of the possessor. Should. he recover, both he and the person to whom it had been divulged lost the power. Thus, whenever a person was burnt or scalded, a messenger was despatched, or the injured person was taken, to some one having this "virtue." and so soon as the incantation was said—not aloud, the fire departed from the burn or scald, and the 'pain left the injured person. The present writer can remember a child was scalded, being in great agony. A messenger was despatched to a farmer. who lived a mile and a half away, who was said to be able to "take fire out." She kept asking how long-it would take the messenger to get there. At length she was told that the time hadharrived. and such was the force of imagination even on the mind of a dhild that her sobs ceased on being informed that the words had been uttered, that the fire was out; and she sank into a quiet sleep. Perhaps the most dreaded superstition was that having reference to the "toad in the pot." It was firmly believed that cer- tain persons had the power to devote an enemy to a lingering death. The mode of procedure was to capture a live toad, to put this into an earthenware pot, to utter over it certain lines, repeated backward, frora the Bible, and then to seal up the pot with its living occupant, and as the toad lingered and died, so would the person cursed live a future of pain and decay, and die at the same time as the toad. The writer also knew of a well-authenticated case of the foree of imagination. A young and healthy-looking married woman had a serious quarrel with a neighbour much her senior. Amongst other threats, the old woman averred that she had the secret of the cause of the toad in the pot, and would indict it upon her neighbour. A few days after, toe latter was told that the spell had been worked, and the toad buried. From that day the younger woman began to decline in health, and a doctor was called. He could find no tangible trace of disease, and; despite the reason- ing of the doctor, of her husband, and friends, so strongly was she imbued with the belief of tho reality of the curse that she lingered on and died. The neighbours were afraid to openly make their dislike known of the elder woman, fearing a like fate. Probably she had never anticipated the sad result that followed, and had merely threatened in the heat of passion. She became so unpopular and shunned that she deemed it best to leave the neighbourhood. Resurrectionists and kid-nap- ping had a strong hold on the minds of the people. At one time, this would probably be when the deeds of Burke and Hare filled the country, the graves of rela- tives were carefully examined day by day, and few per- sons cared to stir abroad by night for tear of a black patch over the mouth, and being consigned to a sack for transportation to the dissecting-room. Such was the state of feeling in the district when it became rumoured that a certain farmhouse and the wood adjoining were haunted. Lights had been seen flitting about in the wood at uncanny hours of the night, attended by hideous groaning and the clanking of chains. He was a bold man who passed through that wood after nightfall. Several of the braver spirits obtained permis- sion to sleep in the farmhouse. They told horrible tales of how they had been awakened by the awful groans of the ghost and the clanking of chains in their bedroom, yet nothing was visible, and none cared to repeat the experiment. He was, indeed, a sceptical man who doubted the existence of the "Aide Ho Debby." The tenant threatened to leave, but as no other tenant could be found, each threat drew forth a reduction of rent. At lentils matters were brought to a climax, and the ghost was most unexpectedly laid, never to re-appear. A stilwart young farm servant had been to a Christmas party, and had taken such an inward supply of spirits as to be indifferent to one outward spirit or ghost. His nearest way home lay through the haunted wood. He whistled as he went to keep up his courage. Suddenly a light shone before him, and flitted curiously in and out amongst the thick growth of trees. The most harrowing groans were heard, accompanied by the clank- ing of chains. Stalwart as he was, arid primed as he was with Christmas cheer, the young fellow stood still; his knees had a friendliness for each other, and the sweat ran down his face. Shortly he recovered himself, and thus he reasoned. "Well, I always thought thou had a bit of pluck in thee, Tom. Thou has never yet been frightened of a man, and thou has never done aught to be frightened of the devil. I'll have a shy at that ghost." He had a pliant ash sapling in his hand, such as is used by farm servants amongst cattle. He started to follow the light. In and out amongst, the trees it flitted; now up the wood, now down. It wa- evident the ghost was well acquainted with its intri- cacies. Tom received many a bump in his pursuit from the hanging branches, but he plodded sturdily on. After a chase of some duration. the ghost swidenly disappeared—light, chains, groaning, ghost, and all— disappeared apparently as thoroughly as if the earth had opened and swallowed them up. This was a poser for Tom, and again he reasoned the matter out. A ghost might fly away, but lie had never heard of one taking a light and chains away with it in its flight. So thinking', he groped his way to We place where he had last seen the light. Nothing was to be seen, and the "beating of his own heart was the only sound he heard." He was thoroughly puzzled, so lie deemed it best to endeavour to make his way hack to the top of the wood along which ran the footpath he had to traverse on his way home. Ile lad taken but a few steps in that direction when his foot suddenly sank into a hole. There was a crash, and an audible exclamation of pain in a very human-like voice. Tom recovered his footing, went down upon his knees, reached down into the hole, and dragged up—a man, who began to beg for mercy. The voice was that of (the tenant of the farm. A broken lantern was fixed above his head, and he had a plentiful supply of old rusty chains. Tom vigorously applied his ashplant ; the ghost roared and danced, and the chains clanked more vigorously than ever. The entertainment went on, until the young fellow was obliged to cease from sheer exhaus- tion. Next day the farmer was reported to be ill, and before long the farm was vacant. The secret was

One of the most delicate ways of taking revenge on a neighbour is to make his boy a present of a drum. "What is an affair dst emir, papa?" said the small boy who had been endeavouring to read the daily paper. That must be a new name for a dog fight," said the old gentleman as he reached for the paper. An Irish girl heard an account read from a newspaper of the death of a woman at the age of 107 years. "Do you believe that, Nora ?" she was asked. "Belave it ?" she said. "An' why sleu'dn't I belave? How do I know that I'm not a hoondhred and sivin years old mesilf ? Faith, I may well be that, for all I know, for shore I can't remember the time whin I wasn't alive !" During an equestrian performance. a number of ladies in the front stood up, thus obstructing the view of those persons who were seated.. In vain were they collec- tively requested to sit down, till at last a happy thought occurred to one of the sufferers. He called out in measured tones, "Will the pretty lady in front kindly sit down?" whereupon about fifty old women briskly seated themselves. A correspondent who lived close to the residence of the late Tom Moore tells the following anecdote:—" Once driving home to Chippenham from Devizes, I gave an old lady a lift in the trap, and in conversation I asked her if she saw much of Tom Moore in her village when he was alive. 'Tom Moore, sir? Tom Moore?' said she; oh, you mean Mr. Moore. Mrs. Moore was a very kind lady, but Mr. Moore used to write all sorts of verses about the moon, and such like things. He were of no account'" The following is from Professor Longfellow's prrvate journal, under date of January 5,1853 :—Lowell gave a supper to Thackeray. The other guests were Felton, Clough, Dana, Dr. Parson's (Dante's translator), Fields, Edmund Quincy, Estes, and myself. We sat down at ten, and did not leave the table till one. Very gay, with stories and jokes. "Will you take some port?" said 'Lowell to Thackeray. "I dare drink anything that be- comes a man." "It will be a long time before Oat becomes a man." "Oh no," cried Felton; "it is .fast turning into one." As we were going away Thackeraie said', "We have staid too long." "I should say," replied: the host, "one long and two short—a dactylic supper."— Harper'e -Magazine. A negro man went into Mr. E—'s office for the pur- pose of instituting a divorce suit against his wife. Mr. E— proceeded to question him as to his grounds for complaint. Noticing that the man's voice failed him, Mr. E— looked up from his papers, and saw that big tears were running down over the cheeks of the appli- cant for divorce. "Why," said the lawyer, "you seem to care a great deal foe your wife. Did you love her?" "Love her. air? I jest analysed her!" This was more than professional dignity could withstand, and Mr. E____: laughed until the negro, offended, carried his case else- where. SWALLOWING LIVING MACILINERT.—We sit -down to dinner and swallow our oysters, without any idea of how they came to be raised, and without realising-. perhaps without knowing, that they are complex organised crea- tures, instinct with life and motion. Motion? Yes, motion. As I write there lies before me, tastefully dis- posed on its natural dish, an oyster in the form in which it giads the sight of hungry mortals when grace has been said, and they have taken their seats at table. With fine scissors I snip off a delicate slice of the so-called" beard," which constitute the oyster's gills; and this slice I place on a glass silo, covering it with a thin glass disc, and then transfer Ping it to the stage of my microscope. Would that you could see, my friend, the trembling, quivering, glancing life that is thus disclosed. The field of the tuicroecepe is occupied by the yellowish translucent material of which the gill is constructed. Across it run a number of closely-set parallel bars, and here and there i between the bars s an elongated slit. Each slit is the 1' centre of a little living whirlpool; for the edges of the bar that bound it carry a vast number of delicate micro- Scopic translucent hairs, which are waving to and fro in ceaseless motion. The waves travel in one direction down one side of the slit, and in the opposite direction up the other side of the slit. Hence the appearance of an elon- gated living whirlpool. In the eight or ten square inches of gill-surface there must be tens of thousands of these trembling life-whirlpools, all of which, my friend, you suddenly engulf, with a gentle. smothered smack of the lips. "I suppose," says Professor Huxley, "that when the sapid and slippery hnorsel—which is and is gone, like a flash of gustatory summer lightning—glides along the palate, few people imagine that they are swallowing a piece of machinery (and going machinery, tool greatly more complicated than a watch."—Murray's Maeaeine. OE' WINDMILLS.-9 man must be born in the North duly to love the South. lam not now speaking of that ceaseless beat of sunshine that leads the denizens of the snows to the land of the palm and olive,: and has been the cause of every human inundation that has spread Beneath Gibraltar to the Libyan sands • I refer only to the kind of deligfit- that inhabitants of Scotland, or the northern counties of England, experi- ence when they see what Mr. Stevenson depicts as "The warm habitable age of towns and hamlets; the green, settled ancient look of the country; the lash hedgerows. • stiles, and privy pathways in the fields: the sluggish, brimming rivers, chalk and smock-frocks; chimes of bells, and the rapid pertly sounding English speech the list of atteaction.s does not pretend to completeness, and might be indefinitely prolonged. The keenness of enjoyment that the North countrymen derives from ' these things cannot be measured by Southern minds. It is, moreover, easily reconcilable with a warm affection for his native district. It ig not to be false to Cumber- land to revel in the beauties of Warwickshire. One phrase in Mr. Stevenson's paper, "The Foreigher at Etomer appeals to me as little of the same class in literature appeals. He rhapsodises over the revolutions at the end of airy vistas of windmill sails. Neither Alps uor Pyramids will greatly surpass the pleasure of the viaion. "There are, indeed," he continues, "few merrier spectacles than that of many windmills bickering together in a fresh breeze over a woody country; their halting alacrity of movement; their pleasant business, making bread all day with uncouth gesticulations; their air, gigantically human, as of a creature half alive, put a spirit of romance into the tamest landscape. When the Scotch child sees them first he falls immediately in love, and from that time forward windmills keep turning in his drean s." This is literally and scrupulously true. To my boyhood life hi a windmill seemed to offer some of the temptations of life in a ship. To this day my ad- miration for them, using the term admiration in its true sense, remains, and the only thing I miss from Mr. Stevenson's description is a sense of the mystery, the eeirdness. the unconsciousness that attends their beauty. ltleman's Magazine. STRAITS. A MIGRATION OF THE WOODCOCK. By Rolm PEERS. At the bottom of Llandudno Bay—very pleasant as long as the weather keeps good. But there are possibilities of change ; and the proverbial "weather eye" must be kept open to notethe first indications of their approach, and this fine bay, to us who must return as we came, by its mouth, has siren-like qualities of which its crowds of. landsmen visitors little dream. For, though the sea, still gently heav- ing from some passion past, lies sleeping in seeming innocence, placid as a slumbering babe, what little Causes serve to break this rest, and rouse to direst anger the loud-voiced child! And then how' soon from innocent impotence. this babe , would spring full armed, gigantic, arbiter of death. Let but the rude awakening come, by loud-voiced diction of the winds, shrilly shrieking in the sleeper's ear and. Oceanus rises in his might, and sends his serried ranks to thunder on this rocky coast! When Boreas, from his ic‘V caves released, i)ortrs his impetuous mit-rents on this shore, and fills the rocky mouth of Tudno's Bay with leaping, roaring, curly crested waves em- ulous of the cliffs high to,—ill-starred the beat if thus embayed, and thrice unhappy her belated crew! Oh! then Tor a' hundred miles of good open sea, free from the appalling horrors of a dead lee shore! Within this man-trap perilously engulfed they seek by many weary tacks from shore to shore to win the open freedom of the sea. Vain are re- grets. But bitter in their breasts must .be the thought of little warnings sleepily overlooked. The first faint mutterings of the coming breeze, the playful catspaw on the glassy bay, the incipient symptoms of the coming storm, are friendly warn- ings the wary mariner would heed, to seek the safety of some sheltering shore. These are the pos- sibilities the future may have in store. How very different the actualities of the. hour I No thundering surges shake the rocky shore or wake the echoes of the lime-stone caves! The sea still calm and Zephyrs all asleep. In slumberous, amiable, pleasing moods, it cradles the weary boat- man on its heaving bcsom by soothing rhythm of its rise and fall, or strives to ad4l new beauty to the scene by mirrored semblance of the enclosing cliffs, or later still when placid eve to star-lit night gives place, each scintillating star a twinkling brother sees reflected on its face:— To emulate the starlit vault aspire-A 'And adds a liquid lustre to its fires. Returnirig daylight found us reposing peacefully .but watchfully upon the smooth bosom and between the vel- vet-seeming paws of this sleeping tiger, so beautiful in repose and yet replete with the latent potency to rend to death! Leaving this beautiful but uneasy anchorage about two o'clock on Thursday morning, we rowed round the majestic head. The sea being so very calm, we could creep close round the base of the wall-like cliff, and market leisure the sculpturing handiwork of thei sea. And tradition says that one dark night 'a wave- tossed wind-belaboured ship ran stem upon :this huge unyeilding cliff and bore to death its shrieking crew„ merged in the seething waters at its feet. All,eave one, whose duty being to stow the !outer jib, had sought the swaying, quivering, far-outstretching spar and clinging there was lodged by the shock upon a projecting cornice of the cliff, till daylight and sweet succour came. Oh! for the use, for one good hour, of a good wholesailful cut from the middle of that death-dealing gale! FrOni that, or from the next of nature's too unequal gifts of wave compelling winds, who pours from her full lip these unneeded redundancies with lavish hand and leaves herself, like a spendthrift, bare to ease the hunger of the needy hour! Still the planished surface of the sleeping sea is guiltless of a ripple. Its oily undulations are un- noticed and unseen until they reach the tangLliting foot- ing of the cliff, there to spend, with scavce a murmur, the feeble remnant of their lives; their self-sung re- quiem but a gentle wash. Not a breath to still the idle flapping of the sail, whose flaccid breadths are swaying to and fro responsive to the indolent motion of the lol- ling hulL Row! brothers, row! for the harbour is past -And the red light of Trwyn-Du flickers its last, The Orme's Head is sinking and Puffin is by, The Levens are showing, Beaumaris is nigh. Row! brothers, row! till the white wake boil! For rest and sweet sleep is the fruit of your ten, You're nodding and blinking, your oars as yo ti dip, ' The " pommel's " oft idle and the "blades "often slip`! Row! brothers„row ! "them woods you must work," Though sleepy and tired and longing to "shirk." Though sleep o'er your eyelids, insidious, steal, With "those sticks at the water" continue "te Row! brothers, row! though progress is slow. And "whistling for wind" you find is "no go," And hands may be blistezed and mutiny rife,' You must "pull" as though pulling you pulled for your life.

Oh! for the glorious sense of freedom and of life, when favouring gales impel the willing boat that bends so gayly to the freshening breeze, and dances merrily to the tune it sings! How bravely she breasts the back- ward-beating surge, as, with a proud disdain, she shakes th' encumbering water from her sides! Thrice happy he whose privilege it is to guide this all but sentient pro- duct of man's skill, o'er the glad waters of the deep green sea. Who feels a sympathetic thrill prevade his frame when, mounting some hissing wave's high top, she rests a moment on its curling crest, trembling as in doubt, the wavering plunge might be her last! See! down the smooth watery slope ef this she glides, but to mount superior to the neat! "She stoops but to conquer," and rides triumphant o'er these moving hills. A noble sport, "to snatch,a fearful joy," and cull the flower Recreation from thebeds grim Neptune guards! And, crown and glory of the sport, it leaves no mangled victims in its train. No half-shot bird left to lament the blundering shooter's " prentiee hand," and t wear its weary life away in solitude and pain! Ignoble joy, emasculated sport! where all the risk is on the victim's side! Where Creation's self-styled lord, armed with the latest form of lethal tube, murders right and left the un- resisting, uncomplaining game, and boasts the bigness of his bag; the solid certificate of his being but the incom- pul:sory butcher of the birds. This is sport-the coward dares to join ; and craven hearts undetected mix withthe sterner metal of to throng, and wage one-sided war on unretaliative grouse. Not so the yachtsman, he who dares the grim god's liquid realm with one frail inch of timber twixt life and death. With him d spice of danger gives ; thezest to sport, which, wanting that, falls flat and tame and tasteless in his mouth. Slowly the sleepy oars win leaxle,n progress from the sluggish boat. slowly and monotonously dip the oars in like accompaniment of the idle Tapping of the loose reef-points that strike at each return the swaying sail. Slowly the rounded form of Puffin Island is past, and then the Sound, and then the long sought haven—Beaumaris—reached at last. Then o'er that slumbrous crew peace and con- tentment like a mantle fell; and soon from beneath • its ample folds strange sounds were heard. For the salt- laden air, unusual toil, and the weary watching of the night, left no work for sleeping thoughts tp do. "Now blessings ori the man who first invented sleep," said honest Sanclao, arid go said we. (To be contimeed.)

To THIS DEAF.—..t person who was cured of deafness of 23 years' standing by a simple remeay will send a description of it free to any person who applies to Nicholson, 16, Camden Parlc-road , London, , Callan and Harkins, the two men charged with being in possession of large quantities of dynamite or an un- lawful purpose, were brought up on Wednesday at the Central Criminal court, and pleaded not giiilty. The trial was postponed until the next sessions. At the Central Criminal Court, on Thursday, a young man named Ernest Albert Vickery, who was chasged with the murder of Robert Maxwell, his brother-in-law, at Deptford, during a drunken brawl, was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to five years' penal servi- tude.

TELE SNOWSTORMS ON THR CONTINENT.—The recent snowstorms in Austria and Hungary have caused the death of a great number of persons. Most of the victims are women. In the Croatian comity of Fiume 14 women have already been dugout of the snow, but many more still lie buried under it. A Mtmincayr Oak-T.—Sir Dinshaw Petit has made a gift to the Indian Government of a block of build- ings valued at £30,000 for a technical institute in Bombay. The same donor ha a contributed £12,500 towards a hospital for women. Both gifts have been received by the Executiyo with warm expressions of thanks.

ALLEGED MCIRDBR OF A UrAMIIKBHPER.—The magis- trates at Pontefract were engaged on Wednesday in hear- ing the charges against David Pilmore, a young collier, of murdering an under gamekeeper named Copley and attempting to murder William Illlngworth, head game- keeper. at Raiisworth, last April. Illingworth described the encounter of himself and his assistant with the pri- soner and his companion (Roberts), and stated that be- fore the fray in which the deceased man was killed the prisoner had threatened to shoot them if they continued to follow. Asked why he so persistently followed the poachers, the witness said he did so because it was his duty to watch the game. The prisoner's written "con- fession" was put in evidence. In this document—which spoke only of Roberts as being "now dead"—Pihnore said he." pleaded not guilty,'. and the corporal who took down the statement further deposed that the pri- soner added in the course of,a conversation that his gun went off in the struggle and shot the keeper. The pri- soner was committed for trial. Public Analysts have submitted Ckniniti's COCOA to close teats, and the result has always proved its great value as a sustaining and nourishing beverage. OUTWITTING A MASHER. Br SIGEL, , in Nature formed Gerty Trevor,' she must have been in one of her happiest moods, for she succeeded in turning out as exquisite a piece of workmanship as ever the covetous eye of man looked upon. Gertie was not what is generally understood as a fine girl. In height she was not more than five feet three, but she was so built and proportioned that when she was talking or walking, or in whatever way else she 'was engaged, she seemed to be the very personification of poetic motion. She had very dark 'hair, and large dark eyes that seemed to look into one's very soul. She was vivacious and sympathetic, and when engaged in conversation, she was all animation, and her eyes scintillated so brightly that one was liable to forget what she was saying in the admiration of her beauty and manner. Gerty was about twenty when this little story opens, and, as may be expected, had a great many admirers. Amongst them were two for whom she had a greater liking than the rest. But Gerty was like a good many girls of her age, she did not know her mind. One of the two young fellows for whom Gerty Trevor showed a preference was Frank Wilders, a young man who was just about finishing an apprenticeship to a trade for which he was peculiarly adapted. Frank was undoubtedly a fine young fellow. He was honourable in his conduct, and upright in his dealings, and he was looked upon as a very promising young man. . The other, and as it seemed the greater fakourite of Gerty's, was Bill Farrel, as he was generally. called amongst his acquaintances. He was a clerk at an office in the town. Now, Farrel was considered by most young men of his acquaintance to be up to snuff. He was twenty-six years of age, had a good appearance, knew all the fast young ladies of the town, dressed well, and, taken altogether, was a very dangerous rival to homely Frank Wilders. Both the young men had made Gerty's acquaintance at a Wlnt-Tueeday afternoon picnic, and both were smitten with her. Now, after the introduction at the picnic, it had been a struggle with the two young men as to which should be with Miss Trevor oftenest. So far Farrel had •out- manceuvAal Wilders, consequently Wilders was having anything but a happy time. He toyed Gerty with all the ardour of a first love, and, young as he was, he felt that his future happiness depended upon his winning her. He had been in Gerty's presence when Farrel was there, and in comparison with him hefelt that he wasn't in the race. Farrel had all the confidence of a known successful masher. When Wilders happened to chime in, during a conversation that Gerty might be having with Farrel in his presence, Farrel would sometimes im- pertinently fix his eyeglass, and wither him with a look. Now, though Frank felt and knew that this was•imper- tinence, his feelings were so mixed, and he was se diffident •in Miss Trevor'a • presenceo that, try as he might to conquer the weakness, he always' blushed more or less. This, of course, pleased Farrel, and he would repeat the operation with a tact that was almost fiendish. And then, to 'make things worse, Gerty's big, lustrous eyes were sure to be`bent upon Frank when he was being tortured thus by his rittal. • It is necessary that I should inform my readers that both young men were members of a political club in the town, and that they had both made the acquaintance ce., Tom Mitters, another meniber of the same club: Mitterg was considerably older than either of them, but singular as it may possibly seem, he had been made a confident of by both -if them with regard to their prospects with Miss Trevor. Farrel had bragged to Mitters of his con.' quest of Miss Trevor's affections, and in his language had pronounced her a "spiffier." Frank had told his trouble to Mitters, and he had cheered Frank and had encouraged him to trope that Gerty' e preference for Farrel was only a girlish flirtation, and that in the, end, if she was a sensible girl, she would see the emptyness of his character, and would eventually give :him up. Mitters, besides being good-hearted, was a bit of a wag, and he had made up his mind that in s'oriae way he would, as he had expressed himself to Frank, "upset Farrel's apple cart." He had not yet arranged how this l'was to be done, but he had decided that in one way or another he would do it. Fate decided for him. Mitters was reading the evening paper one Thursday evening, about half-past seven, in the billiard-room of his club, when who should walk in as smart as a newly-painted barber's pole but Bill Farrel. He was got up in his best style, and he sported a flower in his button-hole, and he had a spare spray which he carried loose in his hat. Seeing Mitters, he went and sat down beside him. • "By jove, Bill," said Mitters, "I think there's some- thing in the wind to-night. What' to do that you're dressed up and gone out in that superb style?" " Oh, I've got to meet my best mash under the market clack at half-past eight to-night. I'm taking her to the theatre." "And who do you call your best mash ?' "Why, the little girl I told you about; the one that Frank Wilders is so spoony on—little Gerty Trevor." "You're taking her to the theatre late, aren't you ?" " Well, sfie cannot get out any sooner," said Farrel, commencing to take off one of his shoes, which had burst out at the side. Calling to a boy (the billiard marker), he said, "Here, Ben, take this boot down to Henderson's, the shoemaker's, and tell him to mend it first thing, as I want it by a quarter past ' eight at latest. I'll mark for you till you come back.' • Ben vent, and in two or three minutes he came back and mill, "Mr. Henderson wants to know will id do i' t' mornin', as idal tek him till twenty minutes kast eight, un he wants to g 3 hooam at eight o'clock; he's a child poorly." "No; go back, and tell him that I must have it done." , when Ben came back he said, "All right; he says he'll do id. He'll send id up when he's finished id." "Oh, that'll do," said Farrel. Mitters resumed the interrupted conversation about Miss Trevor, and Farrel talked in such a way about her that he came to the conclusion that the sooner the con- nection between the two was severed the better it would be for Miss Trevor's peace of mind. About five minutes to eight an idea struck him, and it seemed to so tickle his fancx,that he could not refrain from smiling to him- self. But he did not let Farrel see that he VMS .in any way amused. Remarking that he had some letters to post before eight, he got up and went out. When he got to the bottom of the steps he.laughed aloud, and, slapping his knee, he uttered the inonosyllable, Grand!" Making his way down to Henderson's, the shoemaker, he dropped in kind of casually, and said to Henderson, "I've just come from the club, and Bill Farrel told me to call and tell you that you don't need to do that boot ' tonight; it'll do in the morning." " Oh, aw'm varra fain," said Henderson, putting the shoe on one side and untying his apron. " Avr want to gooa hooam badly." Mitters said "Good night," and went out of the shop. When he got outside, he increased his pace to a run, and kept it up till he got to the shop where Wilders worlted. Frank was busy putting up the shutters, so Mitters had the opportunity of speaking to him at once, Be said, "Frank, get yourself dressed and washed at once. Gerty Trevor will come under the Market clock, at half-past eight. Watch her till you see her going away, then go up and speak to her, and after you have had a few words with her, tell .ner, that you are going to the theatre, and ask her to go with you. Now, don't ask antqUestions, but do as I tell you, and mind this—get her away from the Market clock as soon as you can. Now, make yourself look smart, and put your best foot foremost. Good night." "Good night," said Frank, as he watched the de- partirek form of Mitters in a dazed sort of a way.- nut knowing Mitters teas to be trusted, he resumed his work_ with alacrity. Meanwhile, Mitters proceeded leisurely, back to the club to see the fun. Farrel was busy watching a game of billiards when he got back. Mitters again took up his paper and appeared to be completely absorbed in it. About a quarter-past eight Farrel began to look anxious, and when it got to twenty Minutes past he had grown so very restless that he was standing at the top of the stairs, waiting for the person's appearance who was to bring the boot. At twenty-three minutes past he said to the boy, "Ben, you must go for that boot, and quick." "It's no use goin' for id," said the boy, who was interested in the game that was being played. "He'll bring id is soon as ever it's done; he sed he wod." "Lie's going to bring it when it'll be too late. You must go for it at once,'and bring it whether it is done or not. Now, go on and be quick and bring the boot whatever you do.' Ben handed the cue rest to Farrel and went, un- willingly and grumblingly. Nor did he make any haste as requested. • It would be fully half-past eight when he returned. As soon as put his head into the room he shouted, "He's locked up and gone hooam." "Wrier?" yelled Farrel. , "Ile's shut up un gone hooam," repeated Ben. "Go back and kick at the door," said Farrel. "He'll be in the cellar. Run as fast as you can and I'll give you tuppence." Ben darted off again, but he came back without the I boot. He said, "Itas no use. O's P darkness, un he's gone hooam." Farrel now -went nearly out of his mind. He offered up an "inverted prayer on behalf of the shoemakers. And little Ben, he very nearly blistered the skin on his face with the language he used to him. The other members in the room began now to see the fun, and Mitters, whispering to one near him that Farrel should have met a girl at half-past eight, it was considered good sport to prevent his keeping his appointment., Not having another pair of shoes to send for, he had to go home about nine o'clock wearing one of the club' keeper's slippers. He offered a shilling to anyone who would lend him a boot for two hours; but no one would accommodate him till it was too late. Like all fictitious love stories, this story, though a trip one ended happily. Frank met Gerty, spoke to her; and carried her off to the theatre, where fate assisted to bring about his wishes. There was a love scene and declaration in the piece at the theatre, at the close of which Frank mustered sufficient courage to say to Gerty. "If I c9uld only speak to you like that, Miss Trevor !" "And why not?" said Miss Trevor, in her naive way. As Gerty's husband, Frank often tells the story of Tom Mitters's stratagem for outwitting a masher.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THTILSDAY NIGHT. There is nothing more remarkable in daily life at the present time than the feeling of certainty that war is impending over Mil ope. Trade is unques- tionably improved, and if the vision were concen- trated on the relations of bu,siness men and the operation of economic laws it might confidently be said.that we are upon .the .eve of an era of abound-

. • ing SU prosperity. disquisitions on trade prospects -begin with this admission, and then qualify ex- pression of hope by the condition that all.will be well if there should be no war. At the present

time the only apprehension of war rests UpAou the movements of a single man the etnbodiment of that personal authority of which Mr. Bright in his old days becomes the devotee. Last spring there really was a near prospect of war based upon reasons understanded of the peo- ple. The French were afflicted with one of their recurring fits ..of martial enthusiasm. Boulgnger

was the hero of the hour, and there was an uneasy belief that hewould feel himself bound to justify ,the expectation formed of him by committing some Mill act. Germany was alarmed and alert. Prince Bismark was growling out once more his favourite utterances about the inevitableness of war with France and the desirability of striking the 'blow be- fore French preparations were carried to the point of perfection. War was averted by what seenrad a miracle, and a great deal has hap..ened since then. The French have worked out their fit of restlessness by 'diamissing a President and once or twice chang- ing a Ministry. Boulanger has disappeared into obscurity. Germany is at ease and Prince Bismarck is tilling his occasional role of the man of peace. It is only the Czar who is viewed with apprehen- sion.. He is still sore about Bulgaria, and may in a moment of anger or suffering from indigestion plunge Europe into war. It is not, I think, pro- bable, but it is possible, and it comes with•chilling effect upon the natural expansion of trade. As Lord Salisbury's speech at Liverpool last night testified, the Government confidently look forward to a maintenance of their position. Everything depends upon the attitude of the Diasentient Liberals, and M. Bright's letter, published to-day, shows that the union of the two parties is Stronger than ever. In abandonment of his old principles, and in personal animosty towards his oldest living friend, Mr. Bright has excelled himself As long as this spirit exists, Lord Salisbury is safe for the full term of the life of the present Parliament. His majority will doubtless regularly decrease by th'e process of bye-elections; but it is so sloW against such a majority as he musters, that at the end of six years he will still be able to stand out against the national feeling. One source of strength to Lord Salisbury lies in the natural tendency of events with respect to th e Dissentient Liberals. As time goes by, they drift further afield troni their own party ; "a rash and Unthinking party," a Mr. Bright calls it, since he happens to differ from it to‘n a matter of opinion. They have crossed the Styx. To go back is impossible. They can only go forward in the direction of formal adhesion to Toryism, in which respect Mr. Goschen has anticipated the bulk of , them only bye brief space of time. Thus Lord Salisbury can afford to look on with contemptuous indifference at the angry feeling rising in the nation. And, truly, the popular majority have no right to complain. In a momentary fit of angry im- patience, they placed Lord Salisbury and his friends in power, and must take the consequences through, probably, six disastrous years, AS was the case fol- lowing the General Election of 1874. " Tie ras voulu George Dandin.l - The procession of the liberated WA members through England promises to be one of the most impressive marches on record. Beginning; with the Proposal to give Mr. Balfour's victims a hearty wel- come in London, the'suggestion has run like wild- fire all along the route to 'Holyhead, and there is not a large town on the w 4 that does not claim its right to take part in the demonstration. In truth, Mr. Sullivan, Mr. 0 Brien, and their colleagues will have to make a considerable detour if they satisfy all demands. Manchester peremptorily insists upon its claim, and as between Holyhead and London Manchester, it must be admitted, is a little out of the way. Lord Salisbury niay sneer at such an out- break of popular sentiment. and Mr. Balfour may smile; but in their hearts they must know that this is a matter of ill omen for them. It marks a revolution in public feeling altogether without pre- cedent. Two years ago Mr. T. D. Sullivan would not have been able to draw in any English town or vil- lage a decent audience to hear him make a speech, whilst Mr. O'Brien would probably have, been hoo- ted. Now, coming out of their prison house they will be treated as conquerors back from a glorious campaign.- The English people as a body, or to quote Mr. Bright again,," the credulity of a rash and unthinking party" have made up their minds at last to do justice to Ireland, and they do not stop half-way. According to reputable authority trouble is brew.- ing in high places. Strikes are familiar enough in ordinary business establishments. But it ivould be something too terrible if the Royal establishments of Balmoral, Windsor, and Osborne were to be scenes of such a vulgar experience. Yet, according to "Vanity Fair," such a condition is pending. It is stated in the pages of this journal that Her Majesty, disturbed by the extra demandS upon her privy purse, created during Jubilee week, has determined to take it out of the servants, and has caused an edict to be issued reducing their wages by one-third. This is a remarkable and not very reasonable statement, to be accepted only upon special authority; and it must be admitted, from one extreme or the other of high life (whether above stairs or below it does not matter to the public) "Vanity Fair" is generally well informed. There was much money spent in Jubilee tune, but it was not known or observed that the Queen's share was unduly large Whatever it may have been,' it was more than covered by the intrinsic value of the presents received. That, whether consequent upon Jubilee expenses or for other reasons, there has been some heart searching in royal eirCles •oh the point of domestic expenses is proved in the case of the Duke of Edinburgh, who has intimated , to the committee of the Kent and Canterbury' Hos- pital net, as he has left Eastwell Park, he will no -longer contribute his princely subscription of five guineas per annum to the funds of the institu- tion. It is strange, at this time of day, to read of "Charles Dickens in America." Yet the heading is familiar enough in the papers published on the other 'side of the Atlantic. .The son of the great novelist is over there just now, delivering a course of read- ings from his father's works. He has been received with that generous enthusiasm which America ex- tends to all Englishmen of repute, increased tenfold by cherished recollections of the memory of .Charles Dickens. Mr. Dickens is not nearer his father in genius than is common in the case of sons of great men. But in very considerable measure he shares his father's talent as a public reader. He has done so well in America that according to his latest letter home he intends to remain there till June, by wiOch time he will-have visited most of the principal cities not only in the East. but West and South. In the smoking room of a London Club to-day I saw, smoking tho cigarrette of consolation, Bright, Gladstone, and Macaulay. Penbaps to avoid misap- prehension, I should add that the two first were sons, and the last a nephew, of the men who have made these names historic. There is, by the way, a story current about Mr. W. L. Bright that I have refrained from telling before, since it involves some private relationships. But it is now all over the clubs in London, and may be regarded as public property. It is an honourable fact in connection with Mr. W. L. Bright's public life that he has suffi- dent, independence to take a line on the Home Rule question different from that his father pursues.

Mr. Bright, as all newspaper readers know, is not accustomed to mince words when-he is addressing or referring to any one who has the misfortune to differ from him on points of opinion. Such a letter, it may be presumed, Mr. W. L. Bright had received, whereupon, so the story goes, he sat down to write a reply commencing—" My Dear Father —I have re- ceived your letter. But do you really think that is the way for one statesman to write to another?" In looking over Mr. "Punch's?' Victorian Era, an illustrated chronicle of Queen Victoria's reign of fifty years, one is much struck, in coming across Mr. Tenniel's cartoons of a quarter of it century ago, with a familiar face. It appears over and oTer again through sliccessive weeks in diverse com- pany, but always the same—large featured, calm . faced, quiet eyed,.with eminently respectable Wbis- kers. There is no doubt it is Mr. W. IL Gladstone. ' till, looking at the date of the letterpress, one finds it is Mr. Gladstone himself. No one who knows the eldest son, and looks to-day upon the keen, far- rowed face of Mr. Gladstone, would iina.gine that they ever were alike. Btu if Mr. Tenniel is to be trusted, and the fidelity Of his contemporary sketches testify to his trustworthiness, Mr. Glad- stone must, shoat the period when he first became Chancellor of the Exchequer and daily, fought Dis- raeli, have been very much what we see W.H. Gladstone growing into to-day. I have an earlier portrait . in words of Mr. 'Glad- stone in a now scarce and valuable book entitled "The British Senate in 1838." It is one of those collections of personal sketches in the House of Commons which wicked people even in these days I write, and are occasionally remonstrated with: for the impropriety of the act. But out of these:few sketches of fifty years ago one gets a clearer notion of men and things than out of more pretentious tomes. Here's what it says about Mr. Gladstone at the very beginning of his political career:—" Mr. Gladstone's appearance and manners are much in his favour. He is a fine-looking man. He is about the usual height and otgood figure. His. counten- ance is mile and pleasaflt, And has a highly intellec- tual expression. His eyes are clear and quick. Ilia eyebrows are dark and rather prominent. There is not a dandy in the house but envies what Truefit would call his "fine head and jet-black hair." I is always carefully parted from the crown downwares to,his brow, where it is tastefully shaded. His features are small And regular, And his complexion , must be a very unworthy winless if lie does not possess an abundant stock of health." "Mild and pleasant " That is an admirably faithful, descrip- tion of Mr. W. H. Uladstone's face; but it would not suit the old chieftain of to-day, especially when he is discussing Lord Randolph Churchill:. ' It is curious how London aniusOments run., inl series. The Fisheries was such an unexpected suc- 6esa that it had to be followed up with three other Exhibitions till the fever abated, and the Horticul- tural Gardens are once more deserted. Buffalo Bill has gone, but the ground he, rode over stili remains, and it is not to remain idle. Already arrangements are being made for the great Italian Exhibition that will be held in the season. Two well-known artists have taken in hand the decorative part of the work. There will be sham fights and gladiatorial shows. „ Gercime'a areat picture will be sought to be realised, and medneval times will be reproduced—the far centuries taking the place of the far West in the Cowboy Exhibiticn.

div.head: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.

A meeting of this club was held at the Farmers' Stores, Cornhill, Warrington, on Wednesday even- ing, when the chair was occupied by Mr. Percival, in the absence of the chairman, Mr. W. Whitlow, who was not able to be present.—ln opening the proceedings, the CHAIRMAN said that he sincerely hoped that during the corning year the club would continue to progress. He hoped that by baeeting together they would do each other good, and help forward the cause they generally had at heart.—The SACRETARY (Mr. L. Stelfox) then read the annual statement of accounts and report. From it it app'eared that the receipts had amounted to .El 9 14s, and the expenditure £l9 lOs md. The condition of agriculture, the report cdntinues to state, was now sorrowful in the extieme. Whilst the prices for farm produce still continued to be ruinously low, no adeqaate reduction had taken place in the permanent expenditure of farms, such ,as wages, rent, taxes, and tithes. After dealing at some length with the question of the depression in agri- culture, the report stated that the farmer was made to bear a large loss, and a deadly blow was being dealt at our national prosperity by the productive wealth of the soil being diminished. There were many questions in regard to which Parliament might interfere, among them being the fraudulent sale of butterine, the promo- tion of agricultural education and railway rates. The Margarine Act recently passed would be fraught with beneficial results to farmers, and already there seemed to be a prospect, qf the Government giving assistance in extending facilities for ,the promotion of agricultural education, and the improvement of agriculture gener- 'ally. It was to be regretted that, owine to the strength a the railway interest in Parliament, nothing much had yet resulted from the labours of the commission on railway rates. The chib would do well to keep that subject before the public, and amongst other matters that would well repay attention was the fraudulent sale of foreign meat, cheese,,and other produce as home-grown pro- duce. Through this, not only did the English • farmer suffer great loss, but the consumer waS made. to pay a higher price for inferior foreign produce, unaer the belief that it was home-grown produce. The club had held five general meetings and thirteen committee meetings 'during the year. In conclusion the report recommended union amongst the farmers of the district, and expressed the hope that during, the year 1888 the club would re-; ceive a great accession of members. 'After several mem- bers had spoken in regard to the work of the club, the report was unanimously adopted.—The committee was re-elected on the proposition of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. Witmau DARRYSIIIRE, Mr. Bretherton being ap- pointed in the place of Mr. Baguley; resigned, and the name of Mr. Southorn, of Culcheth, being added to the list.—On the motion of Mr. T. DUTTON, seconded by Alfred Barber, Mr. George Percival was elected president of the club for the ensuing year.—lt was also resolved, on the proposition of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. J. Navrrox, that Mr. T. Dutton and Mr. A. Barber be elec- ted,senior and junior vice-presidents res'pectively.—Mr. Joseph Knowles was re-elected treasurer, and the retiring auditors, Messrs. William Darbyshire and William Da- vidson, were also re-appointed.—The CHAIRMAN, in eulo- gistic terms. proposed the re,-election et M. Stelfox as secretary, and the motion, having been Sectuided by Mr. Rev Davarsinae, and supported in compnmentary speeches by Messrs. T. Dutton, .Wm. Darby-shire, and., others, was unanimously agreed to.—This concluded the businpas of the meeting, a disciassion on "Some useful work for Farmers' Chubs to promote in the year 1883 " being postponed. 0

The stables belonging to the Tramcar Company at Meriden, Connecticut, have been burned down. Eight horses perished in the flames. The death is announced of Bishop Ryan, rector of Stanhope, near Darlington, who was Bishop of Mauritius from 1853 to 1868, and was subsequently, while holding the vicarage of Bradford, assistant bishop to the' Bis- hop of Ripon. THE MURDER OF A JOURINALIST.—The PrewAssociation on TueAday night received a telegram from Boulogne stating that the Procurer had received an anonymous letter accusing, by name, a man in Boulogne of the mur- der of Mr. McNeill, and an arrest is expected hourly. The doctor's official report of the autopsy has been re- ceived from Paris, and distinctly concludes that a crime has been committed. A later telegram says the man who was with Mr. McNeill at the Cafe Fowanay has been found and arrested. His name is Vermersch, not Du- bois. He professes not to speak English, but acquaint- ances contradict this. He clenies that he was with Mc- Neill, but Madame Torond, proprietress of the cafe, is quite positive that he is the man. MR. *DILLON AND LORD HARTINOTON.—On Saturday afternoon Mr. John Dillon, M.P., addressed a crowded Liberal meeting at Bacup. He said that Lord Harting- ton was mainly responsible for the power and existence of the present Government, and that if he were to turn his back upon them they could not exist for twenty-four hours. He regretted to see that in the manner and matter of his speeches Lord Hartington was beginning to tread in the steps of his Tory associates, and he was afraid that in his case the truth of the old proverb that "bad company degrades good manners" was becoming powerfully manifest. Criticising Lord Hartington's re- cent speech to his constituents at Rawtenstall, he said his inference that agrarian crime was of daily occurrence in Ireland was grossly untrue, and was totally at variance with statistics furnished to the House of Commons and which his lordship must have heard fully discussed. Those who attempted to maintain what was called the Union by such methods and on such principles as were laid down by Lord Hartington should count the cost and examine the way out before they embarked upon that road, because it meant turning their backs not only on their Irish policy but on their English policy also. Theirs was a policy which could produce no union, but which had been the curse of generations of both Englishmen arid Irishmen.—At a meeting of the Liberil Council for the Rossendalc division of Lancashire, held on Saturday at Bacup, it was resolved to invite Mr. Henry Maden of Bacup and Blackpool, to oppose Lord Hartington at neict election. It was stated that a canvass which had been made showed that there were goodsprospects for a Gladstonian candidate. KAY'S COMpOTIND.—Asthma and Bronchitis are immediately relieved by it. A SEA. CAPTAIN'S ESCAPE FROM DEATIE.

ON those who follow the sea, Nature has geaknrallY been kind enough to bestow a rugged constitntion, capable of resisting all debilitating effects of the many varieties of climate they meet, the exposure, and the terrific storms and hardships incident to their career. But those "who go down to the sea in ships" are only human, and if the elements are un- able to make the hardy mariner wince, Time, that sure harbinger of fate, will eventually find sbme weak point in his armour through which to thrust ' a lance. Tales of their life have been woven in song and story, fo'c'sle yarns have fired the heart of many .a boy, and even made the pulse of old men beat faster.. • There is, and always will be, a halo of. romance surrounding the lives of those who have kissed the sea-maiden, and have been wedded to her bosom; no lover is more true, and no knight ever battled more sturdily and bravely than the sailor in defence of his love. The following true story, vouched for by many prominent people, speaks for itself, and We commend it to our readers as being of great interest, and one which carries its own moral: "Ever since a child I have lived lon the water, rising from cabin-boy to captain. I visited eitarly every part of the globe, having no ill-health for more than twenty years, but when trouble came upon melt attacked me in the shape of sharp, acute, knife- like pains in the right side, and at thrtes so severe that I would involuntarily fall on the deck, and was,obliged to be carried below. This was accompanied with neuralgic pains, and eventually my hands became partially para.- , lysed. At last, in 1873,1 was obliged to leave my ship in Oregon, and return home to Nova Scotia.. Here I could get only temporary relief, the doctors saying I had muscular rheumatism. •I first saw one medical man, and then another, each one giving it a different name. During two years of this I was getting slowly worse, and then came to England. At this time I was suffering intensely with my urinary organs, passing blood, was muchirritated and depressed, toes stiff and painful, ankles swollen, and unable to lift my feet more than a few inched from the ground. I had an excessive thirst, and drank large quantities of water. I consulted pro- minent medical men in • Edinburgh and Glasgow, who gave me a little relief, but I soon found myself returning to my old condition, with the addition of intensemain in the back, my legs and feet more swollen than ,ever, st? that I could hot make use of them at all. At this time consulted the physicians at the Hospital, Who, c making an analysis of my water, said my case was hoi less, and they could do me no good. My life was oi great misery, and death would have been a weleol release. My oWn physician informed ray. family/ that • might last a month, but there was no hope of covert- While in this deplorable condition my attention IV called to a testimonial from a medical man who had be cuied of a serious kidney disbrder, and whose symptol were nearly the same as mine, so that I was in hopes tle. as this medicine restored him, it would at least ease in -misery. I resolved to give -it a trial, though.l was - .fined to my bed, helpless, and vuld not moverunak My son procured me a bottle of Warner's SAFE Crre, I faithfully followed the directions as to taking it, M at the end of ten days was very much better, and by month able to walk some distance. After taking it co tinuously for a few months, my health was complete restored, and to-clay'l feel better than a person of sixt; five years of age can expect to be. My stoireteh is re tored, have not a pain or ache; I eat wellandsleepwell, at I have dumbfounded all nay friends by my recovery an cure. You cannot imagine my feelings of thav4fulni when I speak of Warner SAFE Cure, and 1 15,nt whole World te know of the benefit easel such as in. can derive from the medicine. If I had paid £ a bottle it, would have been cheap, as to it I cov my life. I recommend it far and neat, and ,tal pleasure at all times in letting people know its wor virtues."
