div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

Captain Stokes, resident magistrate at Midleton, has been served with a writ at the instance of Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., for illegal arrest and false imprisonment in connection with the hearing of his appeal at Miclleton. Courthouse.

An epidemic of measles of a very severe nature is pre- veiling in Newry. The death-rate is already very large, in some instances two and three persons dying of one family. The medical officers, however, report the disease less malignant than that prevailing in the south of Ireland. •

Mr. W. J. Lane, M.P. for East Cork, was arrested at his residence on Sattirday evening, charged with deliver- ing an intimidating speech at Watergrosshill on Decem- ber 4. He was taken before a resident magistrate and remanded to the Riverstown Petty Sessioss, bail being allowed.

„ Mr. Parnell, still remains at Avondale, his resider:vie in Wicklow. He appears to have improved in health, but it is not expected that he will attend the meeting, which is to be addiessedln Dublin, by Lord Ripon, and Mr. Jno. Morley. Great excitement has been caused in Draperstown, Maghera, and the surrounding districts by the issuing of over 400 civil bill processes and ejectments against the tenants on the London Draper Company's estate in Londonderry. The latter have retaliated by serving notices on the landlords to have fair rents fixed and an extension of time, and on Saturday all the solicitors' offices in both towns were during the entire day thronged with tenant farmers preparing defences to the impending proceedings. Dr. Tanner, M.P., recently todk an active part in stop- ping bunting in Mid-Cork, and after a time gave license to the 4th Hussars, on condition that they would not permit obnoxious persons to attend their hunts. Dr. Tannersubsequently wrote to the officers a letter warn- ing them that if they did not prevent landlords attend- ing their meetings they would be stopped. The officers to this letter wrote a simple acknowledgment of its re- ceipt. The officers have now bold a meeting at Balfin- collig, at which it was resolved to break up the hunt establishment. The horses and hounds are to be adver- tised for sale in England, and there will also be a sale at the kennels. The officers express their thanks to all those who assisted them as strangers in preserving the old national pastime of fax-hunting.

div.head: LAND COMMISSIONERS' REPORT.
div.p: THE LAND COMMISSIONERS' REPORT.

... Respecting the report of the 'Land Commissioners. the Freeman's Journal says :—There is scarcely a paragraph which doe not emphasise the fact that the revision and sdhedule of'reductions were based on prices alone. It plainly shows that Judge O'Flagan's dissent was because he was in favour of further reduc- tions, and gives 'the lie to the statement in Tory papers that he considered the reductions too sweeping.

The Dublin ExnresP, says :—The'report is melancholy and commendable for its shortness. The Land Act of last year, was one which in many respects, and especially in this, can only be applied by those used to the process called self-stultification. The average reductions are admirably calculated to make everybody discontented.

• Tne Irish Peres understood, from Judge O'llagan's reasons for dissent, that he desired to take equally into account other circumstances beside 9 prices. "We now know that the schedule has the cast-iron character of an exercise in arithmetic, and must be gone through again next year."

div.head: MR. WTLFRID BLUNT -SENT TO PRISON..
div.p: MR. WTLFRID BLUNT -SENT TO PRISON..

On Saturday, Mr. T. Rice Henn, County Court Judgeof Galway, sat in the Portuinfia Courthouse, to give judg- ment in Mr. Wilfrid Blunt's.appeal from the decision of the . Woodford magistrates, sentencing him to two months' imprisonment for illegally resisting the police at a proclaimed -meeting, at 'Woodford. which the police broke up. • His Honour confirmed the decision of the Woodford magistrates. He said he had no diffiCulty 'at dealing viith the present case, notwithstanding its great importance anddlie great interest it lind excited. The Executive Government had a right to forbid, and if necessary disperse by force, all public meetings if they had reason to believethat tiiey would lead to breach of the peace. If 'Mr., Bliiiii's conduct lacked wisdom, it certainly 'did not lack cottage. Immediately 'after the Court had delivered judgment Mr. Wilfrid 'Blunt wee taken into 'custody, and he • arrived'at Galway on Saturdiit. night the half-past nine train, attended by a large police escort, About 3,000 persons crewded the platform. and cheered as the train entered the station. A carriage was in waiting, and there wastt strong force of constabulary to escort the prisoner to gaol. Cheers were given for Mn Parnell, Mr. William O'Brien.• and Mr. Gladstone, and groans for Mr. Balfour and Lord Snlisbury. The car- riage and movnted escort drove off. followed by a por- tion at . the crowd, but the pr,soner remained tsThind. This was a ruse by the police to clear oIT the ppoole, but it failed. half-an-hour later a drag was obtained, And, driveu by a policeman, conveyed the prisoner' to gaol. The police charged.tbe crowd with swords end batons. wounding several. One constable was struck on the face with a Stone and severely cut. The police con- tinued charging the crowd as the peopie proceeding to- wards the gaol shouted:9rolined, and o.loored. A young man named Sohn Cahill was seriously iiijured on the head by a blowfrom a idlicernan's baton. . ' Before the sitting of the Court on Saturday Mr. Blunt Was presented with an address from the peonle of• Portumna. In renly, he expressed the opinion that all the evidence in fils.ca.sF., both for the crown a nr; .11i6 de- fence, had gone entirely in his favour. and !,!'' Sun- ported all that lie had alleged respe.ctind the material facts,of the atfriwat Woodford. He thoughtsalso.tl wet it would confirm Sir Charles Russell and Sir Horace Davey In their opinion that his sciion was legal. In spealtlnc of general inatter4 he said betelleved that the period of coercion for Ireland was-at, an end. After the decision had been given in Mr Itlitnt's case: Mr. Shaw Lefevre, M.P., was presented with an address on behalf of the Clanricarde tenantry, and ni acknrey- ledging it he declared that Mr. Blunt, had trewht. it -constitiational battle with the highest courage and pub- lie spirit. He would be prdud to Stand•bt-; Mr. 131drn.. even then in prison. -Speaking subsequently at llihli asloe, Mr. Shaw Lefevre affirmed that the*Governmea,. were the law-breakers, and not Mr: Blunt.
THE PROSECUTION OF MR. T. HARRINGTON. M.P.

The trial of Mr. Timothy Harrington, M.P.. secretary of the National League, was commenced on Monday, at 12 o'clock, in Tralee Court-house. .defendant heing.charged before Mr. Cecil Roche and Col. Perseer, Rsal Marine, under the Crimes Act, with publishing in the Kepea Sentinel, a bi-weekly newspaper 'issued in Tralee, of which it was alleged he was one of the proprietors. ,reports of meeting a of 'Natignal 'League branches in Kerry, which had been 'proclaimed by the Lord, Lien. tenant. ! Mr. Edward Harrington, 'M.P., ,brother of the de- fendant, was examined, and depased that he is the sale proprietor of the Kerr/ Sentinel. The defendant was proprietor prior to 1879, but at that period he severed his connection with it hy deed•of assignment to witness. Since then the defendant took no part in the manage- ment of the newspaper, received no portion of the profits, and contributed none of the expenses.. .

Mr. Morphy. prosecuting solicitor, handed in as evi- dence documents from the registration office, signed by witness, and bearing the date Decensber last, describing Timothy Harrington-and 'Edward 'Harrington as joint proprietors of the Kerr?, Sentiod. The magistrates retired, mad nftera•short deliberation Mr. Roche announced the decision of the Bench. 110 said it Was proved that The 'defendant was a rev,isterrd proprietor of the Sentinel for two years, and he should be held responsible. However, before rney passed sen- tence, they were prepared to anCept Mr. flarrington's Secognisanees to enter into hail to bo-of good behaviour. —Mr. flealy,'on behalf of Mr. Harlington, declined to do so, inasmuch as it. would he an admission that his client •Was liable, which was not the ease. • Mr. Roche then. assented to the application of Mr. Healy to state a CASO for the superior Courts, and itio- posed a sentence of six weeks' imprisonment without hard labour.
ATTEMPT TO MURDER A DETECTIVE.

k desperate 'attempt to murder Inspector Lansdowne, of •Scotland-yard, was made on Saturday in the Earns- bury-road, London, by a man who' at present refuses to give his name and address, but wile states that his nee i is 30-years. It appears that on Friday night Earl Comp- ' ten arrived at St,:.,Poncras, and by some rneans his port- manteau, containing. amongst ther things, a cheque ; for OK was stolen dining the journey to his residence. On Saturday morning -Information was given at Drum- mond's sank notifying, the fact of the robbery. About ladf-past nine the mule question called at the bank, presented the cheque. and asked for cash. He was de- ! biined ;until a communication was made with the Scotland-yard authorities, and Inspector Lansdowne arrived, The man was asked to explain how he came into possession of the cheipie, and replied that he had received it from his partner, who was. a jeweller in the Rarnifioury-road. Mr. Lansdowne intimated that it would -h necessary for him to nccompany him to the address given. This the man consented to do without an apparent hesitation. On arriving there it was found that no such person as represented lived there, and the man .was told he would have to accompany Mr. Lansdowne back to the bank. A tab was hailed and the man was requested to enter. Re did 'so, and made an attempt to escape by jumping off the footboard on tilie ppnosife side. Mr. Lam downe .seized him by the cost collar, when the man pulled out a re- volver and said,' Let, me go, or you are a dead man?' A dick was hoard, and Lansdowne immediately seized the revolver and succeeded in inserting his thumb between tne hammer and the cap. The man ,made a second attempt td fire, and the hammer fell on the inspector's thumb and caused a deep cut. This prevented the re- volver from being fired, and without doubt saved the officer's life, as it was afterwards found that the revolver a six-chambered one. had only been loaded in five cham- bers, and by a miracle, as it were, the trigger was the first time pulled down on the empty chamber. A crowd assembled, but they were so alarmed Upon seeing the revolver that they ran away and left the officer and his prisoner struggling together. With the assistance of the cabman and the driver of a coal van the prisoner was secured, after a desperate resistance lasting over 10 minutes. -
WRECKS AND SERIOUS LOSS OF LIFE.

A dense fog prevailed On the Mersey on Mondav, And navigation was very dangerous. Seine-;:/ the' ferry steamers were delayed. and traffic conducted with diffi- culty. A small open boat, which left Dover with three men, on Sunday afternoon, has not since been heard of. Whilst the men were out,.a dense fog came over the Channel. The Cunard steamer Gallia, which arrived at Queens- town on Monday, brought intelligence that the British schooner Lizzie Ellen was lost, with all hands, on the 28th ult., near Cape St. Bias, Florida.

A Lloyd's telep-am announces that the steamer Ameer, from Norfolk, arrived at Liverpool, reports that en the 28th December she fell in with the steamer Maryland, of and from Bremen, for Baltimore, with petroleum. She was abandoned. The Ameer rescued the crew. •

A telegram from Lloyd's age n* at Shanghai dated ,Monclay, states that the steamer Peking, belonging Messrs. Watts. Milburn, and Co.'s Line, took fire in that port, and the probable cost of repairing the damage will be £7,000. The cargo was only slightly injured. `The tire originated in the coal bunkers. Captain Field and six of the crew of the Veracity, of London, coal laden, from Sunderland for Chatham, were landed at Shields on Sunday, their vessel having been sunk south of Flamborough Head on Saturday night through the collision with the screw steamer, Hugh Taylor, of Newcastle. The Veracity was cut down to the water's edge. The steamer, Mary C. Wadham, of Barrow, Captain Chas. Holtes, Swansea to Belfast, with a cargo of coal, was wrecked at Sheepcote, Freshwater, West Bay, Pem- broke, at seven o'clock on Sunday morning, during a fog. Tro" crew of eleven men were saved in their own boat. with the exception of one man, named Neil, of Barrow, who jumped overboard when the vessel struck, and was drowled. The vessel is now breaking up.

The steamer Shoreham, of 'Newcastle and London, was run into on Sunday morning, at five o'clock, off Kentish Knock, by the steamer Colstrup. The Shoreham sank immediately, the captain and six others going down with her. The survivors were taken on board the Colstrup, and were subsequently transferred to the Prudhoe Castle and landed at Dover. The Colstrup, which was damaged, proceeded to London. In consequence of the heavy sea and dense fog, five vessels have been driven ashore in Clovelly Roads, North Devon. They are the Boscoppa, of Padstow, the Jane and the Ann Elizabeth, of Barnstaple; and the Retches Wave and the Devon. All the vessels were laden with coals from the Welsh coast. The crews were saved with difficulty. The first three vessels are likely to become total wrecks. A dense fog prevailed on Monday in the English Channel, and steamers experienced delay and difficulty. An inquest was openedipn Monday, at Waterford, on the body of William Willey, of the American ship Alfred D. Snow, which was lost with all hands off Waterford last Wednesday. •The proceedings were, however: ad- journed, in consequence of an allegation that the master of the Dunmore East lifeboat had refused to put out to sea to assist the crew, because of the roughness of the weather, that the crew of a Manx fishing but ultimately burst open the lifeboat house and seizing the lifeboat started on the etrand of rescue. They arrived too late, however, to sive anv lives. Six more bodies from the wreck a the Altred I). Snow, off Waterford, have been washed ashore. Altogether 29 persons perished.

THIRTY-ONE DAYS ON A ,FLOATING WRECK. Two Swedish sailors were landed at Plymouth on Monday, the sole survivors of the American ship Alfred Watts, of New York, which was wrecked, with the loss of 26 lives, off the Bahama. The survivors passed a dreadful time. The ship broke up, and they remained on a part of the wreck, from the main portion of which nearly all the other hands were washed away. There was then only one chance for those on the raft, and that was to get back to the main part of the wreck. This some of theM did, but the owner's son, in his delirium, walked into the water, whilst another was drowned who jumped, in with the intention of -swimming. A Russian, who jumped into the water in his despair, was seized by sl ark;l whilst a fourth was too exhausted to prevent hire-. self from beingwashed away. The two Swedes wereso per- sistent that they finally reached the waterlogged Alfred Watts. Here they sank down exhausted and -uncoil.: scions, and on recovering found wooden tanks full of fresh water, and were So overcome with their drinking that they slept for several hours. On awakening, they found plenty of food, and thus Managed to live on tie flnating wreck for thirty one days, when the Lizzie Pen y came by and took them off. The Lizzie Perry was her- self subsequently wrecked during a gale at Barbadoes, but all hands, including the rescued Swedes, were savel by taking to the boats. They were stripped of every- thing. however, by the natives on shore, and they were landed almost penniless, with the Swedes, from the Royal %fail Steamship Company's steamer Orinoco. NINE MONTHS ON A DESERT ISLAND.

A romantic and thrilling story, of adventures upon a. desert island is related by two survivors of the schooner General Siegel, who have arrived at Honolulu. The men state that the General Siegel left Honolulu on SepList. WM for French Frigate Shoals, on a shark fishing expe- ilition. Her crew was composed of Captain Aberdine, Adolph Jorgen ,(the Mate); the two Men • already'nien- tinned, Peter Larkin, Peter Brown. Martin Neilson. And Charles 'Clemens. • On Septenther 23rd they arrived off Midway Island. On the night of Septeinber 26th• the vessel was riding at anchor off this islankthe whole of the -crew being eremped on shore.. Towards tnid night a gale of wind arose, the vessel drifted ashore and became a wreck. The 'crew thus found themselves cast upon a desolate island in mid- (clad, then° only moans of sustenance being sea birds and their eggs and fish. About 3.0- days afterwards a painful accident happened to Peter Larkin. While en- gaged in killing lish ‘vith giant powder, one of his hands was blown off. died from his injurtes in a few days. After this a fend appears to `have arisen between mate Jorgen and the Ot her survivors. William Tempe, one of the .survivors. says that while he was alone in the hut• JAvemcrept behind him' anti tried to strangle him with a rope. Tim lad naffed for help, when the mate desisted trim the attempt. . While the cantaimand Brown' were after Pegg, 4orgen murdered them. When the others ,Ireard of thi4, they taxed JM%ren with it, but ho said the two had •committed suicide. Olsen and Tempe then re- solved he leave the island. They accordingly destroyed the ship's hoat, and then sailed away, on the 28th June, in a • scow.and left, the murderous mate alone. They I,eade,t tor marshal Island, which they reached after a voyage lasting two months and abalf. •
EXECUTION OF 'tTEE CORK WIFE
POLSONP.R.-TTIE CORONER AND Tim PRESS.

Dr. Philip Cross was execnted, on Tuesday morning, in the County Gaol, fork; for the murder of his wife. - The authorities were most reticent as to the details of the execution, but it appears that the convict slept well at. night, and rose before • six o'clock; when he was visited: by the Revs. Cennelly and Day, chaplains, who remained with him. At half-past seven he partook of the sacra- ment iii the church, and a few minutes before eight o'clock walked tilhasslsted from • his cell. ,He made no attempt to resist pinioning, and walked without the. slightest- faltering to the licaffold. White there he did not. speak. When the bolt was drawn death was in- stantaneous. Berry was the executioner, and allowed a drop of six feet. Dr: Cross made TIO, confession, hut he had ceased to protest his,innocence since the decision of the .Lord T,ieutenant refusing a reprieve was made known to him on Saturday., . . Another telegram .says.' The condemned, man had been in a state of proStration. duri rig the last. few. days, but he !appeared to meet, hiC end with firm- ness• and extraordinary Coolness. Ho is stated not to have betrayed the slightest emotion. No renresentitives of the Press were admitted, and very little information was afforded by the officials as taa the circumstances attending it, but it was stated that his coat and collar were removed to allow the. rope to be properly adjusted. and that•tho neck of . the culprit ap-.. peered to have been hrolien by the shock. At the inquest, on the body of the culprit, one of the jurors insisted on the production of the executioner, as the press hail been excluded,and no reliable information could he obtained As to how the execution had been carried out. The 'Deputy Governor said that Derry had left, and the inquest was ndiourned till next day, when Berry returns. The Deputy-governor was questioned as to alleged discourtesy shown to the reporters admitted after the exeCution; and the Coroner and jury gave ex- pression to an opinion that 'representatives of the Pr:?ss should be admitted to all executions. rhe crime for which Dr. Cross suffered was one of the most deliberate and oold-bloodod that has found a place in modern history. A r,an of superior intellect, high social status, possessed of ample means, his wife, to whom lie had been Married eighteen years, and by he had a large family, a lady of exceptional accomplish- ments. be seinned to. have everything within his grasp that would make life plessant. Unhappily, however, the nigbly-intelligent retired army surgeon of 60 in his later years.conceived an aniour for a Miss %inner, who had formerly Served as a governess in the family. There seems to he little doubt that the unfortunate man had been eavrying on a liaion with the lady fbr some time. and lee seems to have finally resolved on the removal of his wife. After a visit to Dublin, Dr. Cross returned to Shandy Hall, his country residence near Dripsey, early in May last. Shortly after his wife, who had.pre- viously enjoyed good health, 'began to sicken, and the evidence for the prosecution suggested that he com- menced from that time to subject her to a'course of slow poisoning. Noother medical practitioner 'Mac called in, Dr. Cross continuing to attend the sufferer himself. The unfortunate lady died on June 2nd. her husband certify- ing the cause of death as typhoid fever. She was in- terred in due course, and then with indecent haste, with Wicked speed, RS Mr. Justice Murphy described it; Dr. Cross married MIFS Skinner and took her to Shandy Hall as its new mistress. • This and other suspicious cir- cumstances led to the institution of inquiries. The body of the first Mrs. Cross was es.'huined, and investigation left little room fordoubt that she had died from arsenical poisoning. It wag proved !conclusively that Dr. Cross ! had purchased a considerable quantity of arsenic, and that he had refused to let anyone but himself see his wife during her illness. After a four days' trial, Dr. Cross was found guilty of the murder at Cork Assizes on lec. 17th, and Mr. justice Murphy sentenced him to lath. . , „.; •

div.head: EXAMINER, SA'rURDAY, JANUARY 14, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA'rURDAY, JANUARY 14, 1888.
GENERAL NEWS.

The Yorkshire coal owners decided on Tuesday not to trlint theitaAdvapce ofi.tkin per cent.chrwages askqd ~ # „ s,ction brought by a blacksmith against the Mae quis of Lansdowne and tlaeHighSheriff of Queen's County for wran?,:fuf eviction has been settled by payment to the plaintiff of £7O and costs. The plaintiff was one of tho Luggacurran tenantry. At the inquest on Wednesday as to the tragic death of the Rev. .1. M. Lowther, rector of Bolton Gate, Cumlier- land, a verdict of temporary insanity was returned. A witness deposed to hearing the deceased, just before he shot himself, invoke a curse on two families ,in the neighbourhood. ; SUICIDE FROM GLASGOW SUSPENSION BRIDGE.—Late an Saturday night an unknown man jumped from Glas- gow Suspension Bridge into the Clyde, and was drowned. Screams of murder bed previously been heard.

The Midland Merchant Traders' Association has de- cided to petition Parliament in favour of the retention of trugtee savings banks under improved regulations; and" in favour of instituting an official inquiry at the public cost into all serious cases of fire. A NEW CONSERVATIVE CUM AT BOLTON.—A Conser- vative club, promoted by influential members of the party in the Bolton distrwt, bas just been opened at Tongs., near Bolton, to meet the wants of Conservatives residing in that populous suburb of the town. The premises ere in every respect well adapted for their purpose, and one of the features of the new establishment will be a rigid adherence to temperance principles. -

To be entombed alive in a safe is a horrible mode of going to the grave. Still more agonising is such a death when the key of the safe is turned by a father on his own son. The incident related from Paris has, we think, no paralleL A boy got into one of the ehatnbers of an office safe in a freakish humour, and kept silent out of mere enjoyment of his "lark." The father came in and locked up the safe, the boy saying nothing. Next morn- ing there was a corpse inside the safe.

TEE Item Ar. IN TROF..—At a meeting of the Glasgow Chamber of Commerce, on Monday, the President (Mr. David Guthrie), in wishing the members the compli- ments of the season, remarked that good vriehes for prosperity were this year more likely to be realised than they were during the preceding two or three years. There was evidence all round that this 7ear would be a year of substantial improvement in business.

THE BADSWORTH MURDER.—The West Riding police appear to attach some importance to the statement made by Pi!more, in custody for murdering a game watcher named Copley, at Badsworth, near Pontefract, to the effect that be murdered and buried his companion. Henry Roberts. The police have just issued a notice stating that "it is strongly -suspected that Roberts has has been murdered and buried in some wood where he and Pilmore hid themselves after the murder of Copley. T ;Amer:can mail received atQueenstown on Tuesday morning brought intelligence of a shocking tragedy which occurred at Macon, Georgia, on,Christmas night. A man named Reid quarrelled with his wife and mur- dered her, afterwards killing his six young children, whose ages ranged from two to 12 years. He then burned the house, the bodies of his victims being almost cremated. After committing thd crime Reid cut his throat with a knife and leaped into a well and was drowned. It is believed that Reid's , mind was temPo- . racily unhinged. THE RECENT BOLTON STRIKE: EXPI7DSION OF LEADERS. The decision of the London Executive of the Amalga- mated Society of Engineers to expel from the society three of the leaders of the men in the recent strike at Bolton, for settling the dispute on their own respon- sibility, is causing much adverse comment in the town, not only amongst the ironworkers themselves but the general public. The three officials concerned, Charles Hough, chairman of the Joint Committee, James Barlow, secretary, and J. Thornton, committeeman, intend to appeal to the annual meeting of the delegates to be held shortly at Cardiff for a reversal of the executive's deci- sion, and in this they are supported by the members of the branch to which they belong, who have met and passed a resolution of confidence in their leaders, and expressing indignation at the action of the members of the executive.

A NOTORIOUS OFFICE BREARER.—At the Liverpool Police-court, on ,Monday, before Mr. Raffles, stipendiary magistrate, William Roberts, described as a clerk, was charged with breaking into a number of offices in the city and stealing a variety of articles. The prisoner has been wanted in the city for some months, and lie is also wanted in Manchester for a good many.siinilar offences. It has been his custom to secrete himself in office buildings where there are no keepers, and when . the street door is locked to set to work to break all the offices open, smashing doors and desks and doing a great deal of injury to property, as well as carrying off any handy thing of value. From the office of Messrs. Lam- pot.* and Holt be stole a blank cheque, filled it up, and obtained money upon it. At the office of Messrs. Adam Douglas and company, 20, Brunswick-street, he stole a signed cheque, but, he never used that, singular to say. It was found at his lodgings, as was a black bag that was missing from the effice of Messrs. Cornish and Osk- shott, solicitors. He tOok a cloak, which was also .10- . duced in court.' Atter evidence was given in three or four cases, the prisoner was committed for trial. He had nothing to say to the charges. A CLERGYMAN' ON FEMALE DRESS.—The Rev. Dr. Gor- don, an Episcopalian, of Glasgow, said in his church on Sunday that the dress of ballet dancers was guitf appro- priate for the stage. He contrasted their attire with the not very modest evening costumes worn by West End ladies. He said that when wealthy Glasgow merchants lived in the Sal tmarket their daughters were not ashamed to tramp blankets in tubs on the public green. These well-shanked, kilted-up damsels thought no more of this thlm of performing other domestic duties. They never 'lost caste or good matches, Mn. GOSCHEN, M.P., ON THE CHIIRCH OF ENGLAND.— Mr. Goschen delivered an address to the Church of Eng- land Working Men's Society, in Pimlico, London, on Monday, but at the right hon. gentleman's request the in ling Was private. Mr. Goschen said it was gratifying 1 o ee the Church being supported by so many gennine W rking men. The Church might congratulate itself on • having awoke to the interests of the people. During the last ten years they had seen a greater mixing of the classes, and many of the more wealthy classes had taken to visiting their poorer brethren, and by the interest • they had shown in their welfare had created a better feeling. SERIOUS DISTURBANCES IN THE HIGHLANDS.—THE RIOT ACT Ilnan.—About 1,000 of the Highland population marched at daybreak on Monday from Portnagumn and other townships to Aiguish Sheep Farm, accompanied by bands of music, arriving at noon at the scene of operations. The military, police, marines, and blue jacket's from the seagull and Jackal left Stornoway at 5 a.m., and for some time bloodshed seemed inevitable. The islanders warned the troops that if a shot was fired they would risk an engagement. So serious was the situation regarded that the Riot Act was read by Sheriff Fraser, who warned the people to disperse. The entire stock was cleared off the farm amid great excitement. Mr. John ,itoss, fiscal, was present, revolver in hind, and was struck with a stick by an old man. Eleven men were arrested, radio are said to have been outside the scene of . the conflicti- and they were marched into the town, by the '•police and militaty. At four o'clock the district around Aiguish- was in a state of siege. Numerous cettars were b.idly wounded in the conflict, and the commander of the Royal Scots and several policemen were also severely wounded. The situation remains extremely grave. THE LITE PROFESSOR BONAMT Pte.—The death is announced of Professor Bonamy Price, the well-known Professor of Political Economy at Oxford. -Pro- fessor Price, who was over 80 years of age, had been for some time in failing health. In February, 1886, he had a serious illness, which caused much anxiety to his friends. But his great vigour of constitution enabled him to rally for a time, though his health gradually de- clined. in November last he became seriously ill, and removed from Oxford to London to seek further medical advice, a deputy being appointed to discharge the duties of' his chair. He died on Sunday afternoon at his residence in London. The deceased gentleman, born in Guernsey, May 22,1807, was educated under private tutors, and at Worcester College, Oxford, where he obtained a double first class in classics and mathematics in December. 1829, and proceeded tb the degree of M.A. He was appointed Assistant Master in Rugby School in February, 1830, and Professor of Political Economy in the University of Ox- ford in February, 1868. Professor Price was the author of " The Anglo-Catholic Theory," reprinted from the , Ediatatrgh Review of October, 1851; "The Principles of Currency, Lectures delivered before the University of Oxford," 1869; "Of Currency and Banking," 18T6; "Practical Political Economy,'" 1878; an Address as President of the Economical Department of the Social , Science Congress at Cheltenham. 1878; and a second at • , Nottingham, 1882; and many articles in reviews and I magazines I

"William Henry Holde,n, residing at 26, Whalley Old Road, Blackburn, has ever since 1872, at frequent inter- vals, been subjected to indescribable suffering, owing to terrible attacks of intense pain and swelling in his eet. CURRENT POLITICS.

The Marquis of Hartingtr, who had been visiting the to qf Wales, ,at Sa.W;mgham, returned to London ‘1 Mr. pradlaugh intelB, n as soon as possible after the session opens. to move a resolution calling upon the Government to give effect to the report of the Select Committee on Perpetual Pensions. Lord Hartington informs a correspondent who ques- tioned him on certain remarks in Mr. Gladstone's Dover speech that he is certainly opposed to Protection and to what he understands to be the policy advocated under the name of Fair Trade.

Mr. John Morley has removed to a villa oq,Walrond- hill, overlooking 'Torbay, where he is the guest of Mr. Stuart Rendel, M.P. The right hon. gentleman has been favoured with very mild weather since his arrival at Torquay, and goes out daily either driving or walking. - -

Mr. Samuel Plimsoll, speaking at Derby on Monday, on Home Rule, said he saw no other way of getting over the Irish difficulties than by trusting to the statesman- ship of Mr. Gladstone and Providence. He had no fear of Ireland forming any hostße alliance against England, and levying protective duties on English manufactures. Mr. Bright's objections to Home Rule did notarise from a lack of love of justice. He was such atower of strength to the Tories that his secession from their ranks would inevitably shatter the present Government He believed Mr. Bright would yet return to Gladstonism, and he op- posed the reversion to Protection.

• The Marquis of Salisbury arrived in London from Hat- field on Saturday afternoon and transacted business at the Foreign Office. Subsequently his lordship left Waterloo Station for Portsmouth, en mule to Osborne to visit the Queen. On arriving at Portsmouth the Pre- mier was met by the Mayor and officials of the port, &e., and was warmly cheered. Several leaders of the local I Conservative party were ,present, and, in reply to con- gratulations, Lord Salisbury said that Winchester was indeed a glorious victory for the Unionist cause. Amid renewed cheering, his 'lordship proceeded to the steam packet Duchess of Connaught, and embarked for Cowes. In response to calls for a speech and cheers for the Win- chester election. Lord Sitlisbury appeared on the saloon deck, and bowed his acknowledgments as the steamer .lepagted. Mr. Charles Bradlaug,h, M.P., writes as follows to the Tinges As Mr. Peters, or some one on' his behalf, has thought fit to forward to you a communication with raerence to his suit against myself, will you permit me to say that it is not true that. lathe declaration or state- ment of claim just delivered,' Mr. Peters avers that Lord Salisbury nas never sent him any cheque in his life and I hat he has never received money in any way directly or indirectly from his lordship? There is nothing to this i-ftect, or in shy way like it, alleged in the statement of claim, which am willing to forward to you, if you wish, though if the matter is to be submitted to a legal tribunal,' fhy own view would be that collateral discussion in the Press is neither respectful to the Courts nor useful to the litigants, and I have purp.sely refrained from any com- ment on the paragraph in your issue of to-daylexcept so far as it relates to this precise allegation of fact." LIBERAL UNIONISTS AT TAUNTON.

_ A large gathering of the Liberal Unionists of West ;Somerset was held at Taunton, on Saturday afternoon, under the presidency of Sir A. Hood.—Lord ONsLow, in the course of a vigorous speech, in which he described the policy of Mr. Gladstone as a policy of plunder, de- clared that at Nottingham the right hon, gentleman held out a distinct bribe to Nonconformists when he said that if they would support him in his Home 'Rule scheme lie would support them in securing disestablishment of the Church. Having eulogised the services of Mr. A. Balfour, his lordship said that they were beginning to see the end of the Irish disturbances. Seditious meetings whiph used to be held openly in Ireland are now held clandestinely. Patriots who were announcing on every platform that they were ready to die and do everything for their beloved -country were crying out that they were being slowly done to death, because, forsooth, they were called upon to change their clothes. What should they say of those who went over from England and made themselves notorious as Mr. Wilfrid Blunt had done? Men who had little chance of becoming otherwise promi- nent were ready to do anything to obtain notoriety; in fact, the patriotism of the Irish party was passing from the sublime to the ridiculous.—Mr. E. R. Wm:mum:me, M.P., moved a resolution declaring the determination of the meeting to uphold the unity of the empire, "and pledg- ing it to support the present Government. The hon. member contended that the present Government was a rational Government, with a Conservative Prime Minister and Chancellor of the Exchequer in whom they ha 4 every confidence.—Mr. Evrox, M.P., seconded the reso- lution, which was carried amid cheers.

div.head: TIIE NOTTS MURDER.-FOUR ARRESTS.
div.p: TIIE NOTTS MURDER.-FOUR ARRESTS.

The greatest excitement prevailed on. Saturday in the little South Notts town of Binghafro, when it became known that four arrests lied been made in connection with a recent case of. child murder, the prisoners being in a good social position, and they are Samuel James Moore, 32. surgeon; Mrs. Jane Rayson, 66: Mary Jane Rayson, 20, all of • Bingham ; and Ada Eliza Sansom, 24, wife of William Wilson Sansom. draper's assistant, 30, Greyfriar-gate, 'Nottingham. The facts of the case were first made public at the inquest, which was held at. Bing- ham on the 27th and 28th ult., when a verdict was re- turned ot wilful murder against some persons unktrm Dr. Moore hakonly resided in the neighbourhood a corn- ' baratively short period, and at one time lodged with the Itaysons. After leaving their roof he continued to act as their mediclal adviser. Miss Rayson, who appears to have been in very delicate health for some time, was found to he ton ill to be removed, and she was therefore left at home in the nominal custody of a police constable. Mrs. Rayson and Dr. Moore, however, were conveyed to the police-station, where they were brought before Mr: Geo. Storer, and fern-tally remanded to Nottingham Prison for a period not exceeding eight days. On.Stiturday morning it came to light that a . fourth arrest had been made—viz., that of Mrs. Sansom, daughter of 'Mrs. Ray.son, who was arrested at Newark op Friday night. taken to Itinghath by the 8 40 express tram, and lodged at Bingham for the night. Her home is in Notting- ham,but on Dec. 3, when her sister was taken ill awl Dr. Moore was sent for, ,Mrs: Sansom was visiting her mother for a few weeks. After jeavingethere she went on a visit to Newark, and VMS at that. borough when the inquest was held. She was called as a 'Witness at .the inquiry, at the conclusion of which she appears to have returned to Newark. She was taken to Notting- ham on Saturday morning, and was brought before Mr. George Storer, at the County Hall, on the charge of murder.

On Thursday, at Bingham, Nottinghamshire, the charge of murdering a newly-born child 'brought against a lady, her two daughters, and a surgeon was gone into before the magistrates. The principal witness in the case was a servant girl, who described what she heard and saw in Mrs. Rayson's house on the supposed day of birth of the child. After a long investigation the magi- strates dismissed the charge against Mrs. lfayson, Mrs. Sansom, and Di% Moore, and committed Miss Rayson for ' trial.

It is reported that an outbreak ,of typhoid fever in a Connemara village has carried off two clergymen and a Scripture reader, that two or three deaths are occuring daily, and that more than forty cases have been sent into hospital. DEATH OF A CENTENAEIAN.—Miss Harriet Williams, an old lady, has just died, aged 104 years. She has resided at Ramsgate about fifty years, and enjoyed good health up to within a few days of her death.. It is only a very short time since she walked to Christ Church, some con- , siderable distance from her residence, to attend Divine service. _ - -

CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WAR- • RINGTON.

The.annual meeting of the ConServatives of the North-west ward waX held in Rolleston-street school- room on Monday evening, when there was a thin attendance. The Chairman of the Ward, Major Litton, presided, and he was supported on the plat- form by Mr. R. Pierpoint, Mr. George Woods, and other Conservative gentlemen. At the commence- ment of the meeting various matters of Ward busi- ness were attended to, and a Ward Committee was appointed on the proposition of Sergeant Bloomfield, seconded by Mr. Thomas Smith.— Mr. John Roberts proposed that Major Litton be i•e-elected chairman for the ensuing twelve months, and referring to political arrangements in regard to municipal elec- tions, said that it had been shewn that they must not put too much confidence in such arrangements, but must carry out their own ideas. Wherever they could do it they had a right to oust a liberal and Put in a Conser- vation in his stead. He did not say that with any feel- ing disrespectful to the Liberal party, but sim- ply because they had a right to do . all that they could to strengthen their numbers. The proposition, having been. seconded by Councillor Heaton, was then unanimously passed.—Speaking after his re-election, the Chairman, who was well received, said that the present Government, with Lord Salisbury, at its head, enjoyed the confidence of the country. The last election proved that the people thought that Ireland should remain united to Great Britain, and Irelandwould remain united. (Cheers.) In consequence of the firmness of the Government there was now a decided jmprove- ment in everything appertaining to Ireland, and there was now a greater feeling of confidence in the financial state of the country, which would tend to the improve- ment of commerce.—Mr. Robert Pierpoint, in a vigorous speech, proposed a resolution to the effect that the thanks of the meeting were due to Her Majesty's Go- vernment for having by a firm and just administration of the law in a great measure released honest Irishmen from the tyranny of foreign-paid traitors to Great Britain.—The resolution was seconded by Mr. George Woods, and carried with applause.—Afterwards Mr. Thomas Fielding, of the National Union, London, gave an address on " Gladstone's Irish Folly." and the usual votes of thanks were passed at the close of the meeting.

LORD SALISBURY'S speech Ist Liverpool, on Wed- nesday, is scarcely up to the high level of his usual platform exhibitions. He seems to have been in anything but an amiable mood. It is stated that he was suffering from a bad cold, and a cold and a fog are quite sufficient to depress either a peasant or a Prime Minister. It was rather hard on the Conservatives of Warrington that they should have gone to the trouble of preparing an ' address, and of inducing our octogenarian member to brave the terrors Of the day in order to be at the railway station to present it, and that, after all, Lord SALISBURY would not so niuch as show his face at the Carriage window. Sir GILBERT GREENALL was determined, however, not to have the address left on his hands; it had doubtless made him sufficiently miserable thus far, so he got rid of it by thrusting it through the window. The bad cold from which the PRIME MINISTER suf- fered runs through his speech. It is an un- happy, querulous, irritable, and irritating speech. Conscious as he is of the bad effect upon the coun- try which has been caused by the Coercion Act creating new crimes in Ireland—by the disgust which all lovers of freedom feel at the malignant way in which editors, printers, and even news vendors havebeen sent to gaol—his Lordship strives to rid himself of the stain which rests upon his name by denying that it is there. But he will learn that the people prefer to trust to their own eyes to looking through his coloured spectacles, and that there will be a heavy reckoning against him at the next general election. With regard to Tory relations to Home Rule, those who are familiar with what has happened during the past three years will say—" Methinks his lordship doth protest too much" when he uses such emphasis in affirming that the Government will never have anything to -do with it. He does, however, make an admission which most people, will think is sig- nificant, and which must be in the nature of a sur- prise to those innocent-minded Tories who have hitherto been unable to believe that any member of a Tory Cabinet hari ever had the slightest hankering for Home Rule. Lord SALISBURY says —"I beg to say that the assertion that there were. other members of the Cabinet of 1865, besides Lord. CABBrAnvoist, who had expressed feelings in favour of Home Rule is an utter, complete, and absolute , falsehood." The cat is at last out of the bag, so far as Lord CARNARVON 18 concerned, and this, too, after strenuous and repeated denials that there
was any cat in the bag. It must be remembered that Lord CARNARVON was Lord Lieutenant of Ireland at this particular period, when, as we know from other sources, he held interviews with Mr.

PARNELL as to the form of Home Rule which would he acceptable to the Nationalists. It is conve- nient, of course, to be able to say that Lord CAB - Naimoli' was alone as a member of the Cabinet in being in favour of Home Rule; but is that nothing? Lord Silmastrair has been asked again and again by Mr. GLADSTONE to state whether he, as Prime Minister, was aware of the negotiations which his Lord Lieutenant was holding with Mr. PARNELL, but he has not yet dared to give an answer. If Lord CARNARVON held these inter- views without the knowledge and sanction of Lord SALISBURY, we do not hesitate to say that it would be treachery to his chief, and that he would be unfit to hold office in the Ministry. Let Lord SALISBURY say, then, if he can, that he knew nothing of what the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland was doing as to this matter in 1885. If he cannot, if we are to infer by his silence that he was privy+ to these negotiations, we may indeed admit that his mind was not made up as to Home Rule, but we should be quite sure that the Nationalists are not far wrong when they affirm that the Tories would have been ready to jump Jim crow if the Parnellite alliance of 1885 had been the means of giving them a working majority. They failed to win with the Nationalists, and so they have since rounded on them. Ha:" toyed once, through their Lord Lieutenant, with the question of Home Rule, we may rest satft that they will be ready to turn to it again soon as they have broken with the Lit Unionists. Mr. GLADSTONE is therefore in the right; if Home Rule be not granted, ere long, bY the Liberals, it will be conceded by the Tories. That is the moral 'of Lord SALISBURY'S speech.

THE Liberal and Radical Year Book for 1888; Published by Messrs. Talbot Brothers, is a volume which should be in the hands of all politicians, and there is no reason why it should not have ex- tensive circulation seeing that—largo as it is—it can be obtained, in paper covers, for as small a sum as sixpence. An interesting feature of this year's issue is a Parliamentary Map of Great Britain and Ireland, showing the representation of parties up to the present time. As different colours are used for different parties, it is easy to pick out the political representation of the various consti- tuencies. The Nationalist colour is green, and when the reader turns to Ireland he cannot fail te be struck with this well-nigh all-prevailing tint. Under the head of "Liberal and Radical Roll Call," details are given of the representation and electorate of ,every constituency in the Kingdom. The results of the poll are furnished for the last three general elections, .so that in case of a bye' election there is a ready means of ascertaining the state of the political tide. There is an alphabetical list of the Horse of Commons, with the age of each member and name of the constituetey represented ; I and with regard to the House of Lords, particulars" are given as to family name, residence, and creation of peerage. Sir WILFRED LAMSON contributes sq.

special paper on "The Popular Veto," which states the case very concisely, and yet very effec- tively. In view of impending legislation on local government, the paper ought to be read by every elector. Miss lIELEN TAYLOR has an article on "The Nationalisation of the Land," which may be regarded as satisfactory in so far as it exposes the evils of the present system, but unsatisfactory in that it fails to show how nationalisation is to be brought about. The idea that the State should hold the land for the benefit of the people as a -whole is attractive; and it is not ‘to be doubted that, if we could begin (7P nqro, tiou would be an excellent thing. But the problem is how to bring about nation- alisation without doing injustice to the present holders of land, or introducing difficulties as great as those which already confront us. The tendency of the times is in the direction of reform .of the land laws by the abolition of primogeniture, entail, and settlements; and by simplifying the registration and transfer of land. It may be that the good which will result from these changes will be less than is anticipated; but the evils of pre- serving remnants of our feudal system are so obvious that we are in duty bound to deal with them, and, if possible, get rid of them. When thia is done, the Legislature may be able to see its • way 'a little clearer in the direction of the national- ' istion of the land. Meantime, the proposal may be discussed as something baying relation to the dun and distant future rather than to the present- day politics. "Readiness for the General Elec- tion" is the title of a valuable article by Mr. W. S. SHIRLEY, M.P. He would have Liberals "educate, agitate, and organise," in view of a con- test which may be Sprung upon the country with little or no warning. The advice is sound; Liberals have everything to gain, and nothing to lose, by educating the masses, and it is work which should be done at once. It sometimes happens that can- didates are hampered with the legal restrictions as to expenditure when in the thick of the fight. They would like to educate the constituency, but it is too late. According to Mr. SHIRLEY'S doctrine, now is the accepted time—now is the day of education, agitation, and organisation. We should add of the Liberal and Radical Year Book, that there is an exhaustive chronology of political events; but we have said sufficient of it, we trust, to induce the wide-awake politician to order apopy at the earliest opportunity.

THE British Prilgrims in Rome were received by the POPE, on Tuesday, amid circumstances of considerable pomp and ceremony. The Duke of NORFOLK presented an address expressive of the devotion of English Catholics; and more substan- tial evidence of their regard was forthcoming in the presentation of the £16,000 which was for- warded by the English Catholic Union. His Roliness appropriately remarked on the manner in Which the QUEEN and the Government of this country have joined in the manifestations of Catholics during the Papal Jubilee. It is indeed a sign of the times—a sign which we cordially acknowledge as indicating legitimate relations between two Great Powers rather than affording evidence of any desire on the part of England to go, as the phrase is, to Canoga. Luo THIS: Tzwrra is at the head of a vast spiritual organisa- tion, having interests that ramify into every civilised State; and, since it is or ought to be the object of Rulers to consider the well-being of their subjects, it is obvious that as regards a section of them• something towards this end may be accom- Plished by being on good terms with the Vatican. This does not mean that the Porn is to be ap- Pealed to to interfere whenever there is a difficulty in secular matters, although we grant that there is always a disposition on. the part of Governments to make use of the reigning Pontiff. Happily, Catholics themselves recognise that, while as to religious matters it is their duty to accept the authority of the POPE, they are• free to take their 4?wrt, course in matters political. Ireland is a case in point, but it is notorious that, while some Catholics are opposed to Home Rule, the majority are enthusiastically in its favour. The leaders of the movement are naturally jealous of anything which looks like an attempt to put pressure on them thrbugh relations with the Vatican; but, thanks to the good sense and diplomatic tact of Leo Thirteenth there has been.no great cause of complaint. In replying to the address, on Tues- day, his HOLINESS is understood to have made a reference to the Irish question. "I pray," he said, "for the restoration of peace between the different parts of the kingdom. I hope that irri- tating questions will be set aside, and that reason and equity will take their place." The opponents Of Home Rule take this as implying that he would be pleased to see the agitation set aside; but in view of the irritation caused by the administration of the Coercion Act of the unreasoning and in- equitable way in which Catholics, and even Catholic priests are sent to gaol—it is certainly not unfair to suggest that the sentence is capable of another interpretation. Taken as it stands, the remark is one which commands the approval of all parties, and as such we trust it will be accepted without searching too curiously for a meaning , Which may not, after all, be there. The POPE is too prudent and too far-seeing to take sides on the Irish questions and especially at the moment when he is receiving congratulations and gifts from all sides upon attaining his sacerdotal • jubilee. i-

I've this day put phwat they call an inshoorance on me loife, an' if I'd fallen down a ladder wid me hod an' break me neck to-morry, begorra an I'd get twenty-five dollars a wake as long as I'm dead. It's a fine country; that's phwat it is!" PENKETH WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT Assocrxrrox.—On Wednesday evening, in the Wes- leyan Day School, a most interesting pape,. was read before the members of the association by Mr. C. B. Parker, "On the moral aspect of the land question." The paper was carefully prepared, and at the close a very animated discussion took place, in which the following members took part : Messrs. R. Garnett, D. Garnett, Dignum, Hobson, Watson, White, and Mesdames Garnett, C. E. Par- ker, etc. Mr. James Fildes, of Bowdon, occupied the chair. Pionurrit PENNY BANK.— This bank was inaugu- rated 33 years ago, being established in 1855 at old . Day Star School, and is therefore one of the oldest penny banks, in Lancashire. From a statement made loy Mr. Garnett, who is one. of the treasurers, at a , meeting recently held in the Wesleyan School, it appears that considerable effort has been made in Penketh to induce habits of thrift and saving, and not without success. At the present time there is in the bank no less than £BO5. During the past -taar there have been 1,119 transactions, 'including both, deposits and withdrawals. Part of the money is in- vested with the Warrington Corporation, and the rest is deposited in the Warrington Savings Bank. The rate of interest on deposits is the same as that allowed by the Warrington Savings Bank. The bank is opened every Monday evening from seven to eight o'clock, when two of the managers (who give their time and labour throughout the year for the benefit of the institution) are present to receive or pay out deposits. Ihr:era's "Roman. floors." acknowledged by all to be the beat, at 42 and 44, Horsemarket-st.reet.—Advt.

"TOUCH AND GO." A dense, damp, dark, and all-pervading fog, That chills one—ay, even to the marrow bones. This, as Ilyron has it, is what some one might, could, would, or should have sung during the past week. ,It has been awful I

The story which is going the round of the papers to the effect that a town in America has been burned down through AI monkey setting itself and then a theatre on fire reads very much like a Yan- kee yarn. If it be true, it must be admitted that Jacko was indeed a mischievous monkey.

There was a thin attendance at a Conservative ward meeting in Warrington, on Tuesday night, and it has been stated that the attendance was .poor because of the dense fog. But this surely is not a good reason; it is a normal condition with the Tories to be in a foe. With a dense fog, there ought to have been a dense attendance.

The "very pretty quarrel" beWeen Councillor Dakin and Councillor John Pierpoint as to the chairmanship of the Markets Committee has beeii an amusement for gods and men. It has been a case of a storm in a teapot—" Much ado about Tithing." It is a pity the members of the War- rington Town Council could not be better em- ployed.than in seeing two of their number make an exhibition of their vanity and littleness.

Lord Bute explains through his lawyer, with reference to the bankrupt savings bank at Cardiff, that, with the exception of once presiding at a general meeting, "he never in any way took any share in the management or the affairs of the bank." More shame for him, seeing that he was President. He ought to be made to pay for his negligence—he can well afford. He should not have allowed himself to be used as a decoy duck.

Mr. R. G. Webster, M.P., has been addressing the members of a London Conservative club on Local Government. He will have something else to think about by-and-by, for is it not written that he was at one time a director of our neutral contemporary? And old-time directors of that journal are being looked up with a view to receiv- ing "invitations to a court" of a kind they little like. But we shall see what we shall see in due time.

Surgeon-Major Cross was hanged at Cork, on Tuesday, for poisoning his wife. He must have had what in vulgar parlance is called a "hard nerve" to see his wife suffer, as she must have suf- fered at his hands, and it is not surprising, there- fore, to learn that he carried his bravado through to the last. If ever capital punishment is justi- fied, it is surely justified in such a case as his. ilt s a relief to know that such a monster is no more.

Thomas Williams and Thomas Williams, father and son, were fined at Runcorn, on Monday, for working a horse whilst in an unfit state. The patient brute was actually hobbling along on three legs when seen by the constable. Heavy fines will be the means of teaching inconsiderate people that it does not pay to abuse dumb animals in their charge. It is the merciful matf who is merciful to his beast; the unmerciful are brought before the magistrates.

Lord rfartington will have a harder fight for his seat at the next election than he had at the last. The Liberals of R,ossendale, on Saturday night, de- cided to invite Mr. Henry Maden, of Bacup, to contest the constituency on their behalf. He is a local gentleman who is highly respected for his earnest and consistent advocacy of Liberal prin- eiPles ; and if he can be induced to accept the in- vitation, it will not be a case, with Lord Harting- ton, of "taking a back seat," but of having no seat at all so far as Rossendale is concerned.

There is a distinct improvement in trade, one evidence of which is found in the fact that there is work to be had. Mr. Win. Rathbone, M.P., stated at the Liverpool Select Vestry, on Tuesday, that there was more demand in Liverpool for rough labour than there was supply at the docks. It will lac well, therefore, if townsmen who are troubled with beggars will head able-bodied tramps off in the direction of Liverpool. Some of them, it is to be feared, are rather disposed to qualify for stand- ing in a police dock than labouring at a shipping dock.

The Widnes Local Board have obtained legal opinion as to the alkali waste heaps, and it is that • they are a nuisance; but when it comes to a ques- tion of taking proceedings they still "Linger shivering on the blink And fear to launch away." Their latest proposal is to invite the nuisance- makers to a conference with the Board; but we do not suppose they will very readily respond to the invitation. Perhaps it is as well to give them another chance, and then, if they do not mend ' their ways, "up guards, and at them."

It is curious to see how dancing comes under the clerical ban. There was an application for a dancing licence at St. Helens the other day in con- nection with a public hail; but it was opposed by the Rev. Canon Eyre, Rev. R. J. Ward, and Father Walmsley. There is nothing wrong' in dancing in itself. Indeed, there is full scriptural warrant for it; for are we not told to praise the Lord in the dance, and that David danced before the Lord ? And as to the place, if a licence can 'be granted for the Victoria Hotel, why should a licence not be granted on behalf of a hall where no intoxicating liquor' is sold?

The Bolton "commercial" who was brought before the Warrington magistrates on Tuesday evidently knew the law. He said :—" I got drunk, I admit, but I think it is not a crime, as I had some one to take care of me. I was within the law in getting drunk. I can do that. I got a man and paid r'him to see me home." His point was that he was not " disorderly " as well as drunk, and so he was not liable to a fine. How- ever, at the suggestion of the Bench, he made peace with the court by giving 10s. to the poor box. The poor will profit, and the "commercial" will be no worse by having 10s. less to drink.

"Yesterday the ,Lord Chief Justice of England was engaged, with Lords Justice Cotton and Bowen, and will probably be engaged all day to- day, in hearing the Chancery appeal upon the question of the validity of the patent for the mak- ing of braided wire •articles that ladies wear for the purpose of protruding their dresses behind." It is not—
0, ye gods and little fishes, What were a man without his breeches? But—

Warrington Workhouse is not, it seems, the only one at which there was too much beer stir- ring at Christmas. "The Liverpool Echo" says: The scenes which take place in many work- houses must confirm the opinion of those who hold that 'festivities' in these institutions should be abolished, or be confined riOdly to the deserving poor. What occurred the other day at Warring- ton WM but a rehearsal of a wider episode in workhouse life at Plymouth. The excitement attendant on a New Year's feast led to the scaling of walls, a breach of all discipline, and an out- rageous mei& resulting in the smashing of scores of panes of dlass." It is to be hoped that, at Plymouth as at Warrington, recent experience will make a certain class wise.

In his speech at the banquet at Liverpool, on Thursday, Lord Salisbury demonstrated very clearly that he has not the courage of his convictions. He said the Land Act of 1881 "was a mistaken course, dangerous to property, and therefore dan- gerous to the best interests of the Empire." But "when a course is begun that course must, be con- tinued." Contrast this with Mr. Gladstone's treat- ment of Ireland; he has come to the conclusion that coercion is dangerous to Ireland and to the best interests of the Empire; but he does not weakly Aespair, and say it must be continued, He says—"We have been in the wrong; we must change our course, and repairtheevil we have done." This marks the difference between the good and strong statesman, and the poor and feeble office- holder. .

He will guarantee that they are not to be equalled in the country for clearness, coolness, and rest they im- part to the eyes: Pamphlet "How to preserve the sight" free on application.—Adet. NEW STORY.—In our next issue we shall commence a new and powerful story with the title of "A GIRL IN A THOUSAND." It is from the gifted pen of Jean Middlemass, author of" Lady Muriel's Secret," "The Spider and the Fly," "Poisoned Arrows," "Wild Georgie," &c., &c.
