- WIDNES SECOND STARR BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY. —ln Connection with this society a meeting was held in Mali's Temperance Hall, on Tuesday evening. Mr. F. H. l'ankhurst presided. After songs and recitations, an appropriation took place, the holder of registered No. 165 being declared entitled to £2OO, free of interest; for 14 years. THB DODS ACT AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Seas- ion. on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynolds and Major Hazleburst the following persons were each fined 2s 8d and costs 8s 6d, for allowing their dogs to be at large ; Charles Lee Evans, agent to Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., Henry Stone, shoemaker, Church-street, John String- fellow, postman, Preston Brook; John Evans, Gilbert- street; Peter Bradley, Bridgewater-St. ; and Benjamin Pickles, gardener to Sir Richard Brooke, Bart. FELONY AT RuNcoux.—Before Messrs. J. Brundrit and G. L. Davies, at Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, Peter Stoho and Joseph Williams were again brought up -on reinand charged with stealing six pairs of trousers, value 15s, the property of Arthur Davies, pawnbroker, Top Locks, on the 28th ult. They were also charged with having.stolen a tin kettle, the property of John Dutton, Devonshire-square, on the same date.—Each prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. WE WILL RETURN the purchase money if one box of Howell's Golden Herb Pills does not cure vou.--:fdet. ROBBERY FROM A WIDNES PAWNBROBER.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Patrick O'Brien, a labourer. was charged with stealing a shirt, value Is 11d, from the shop of C. Ne", pawnbroker, Anne-street West. On Monday afternoon the prisoner went into the shop with the avowed object of 'matching" some ear-rings, and whilst the assistant John Abbott was in an inner room, the prisoner decamped. The shht was afterwards missed.—The prisoner, who pleaded guilty; asked the Bench to deal leniently with him as he had a wife and four Children, and was in employment. It was a drop of drink that caused him to commit the robbery.—As this was the prisoner's first offence, he was only fined 10s, or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment. CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT RIINCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Se:ssions on Monday, Thomas Williams, serm., potatoe dealer was summoned for causing his horse to be worked whilst in an unfit state. His son Thomas Williams was charged with working the animal.—P.C. Thompson stated that about 5 o'clock the lad was in charge of a horse attached to two boats. The horse was only walk- ing on three legs, and the boy. had a bridle over his shoulder and was pulling the amnial along. The elder defendant afterwards told him that the horse had been pricked in shoeing.--Serg,t. Woolley stated that the horse had been blistered and its fetlock joint was swol- len very much. The horse appeared to be suffering great pain. A plsa of guilty having been. entered, the defendants were each fined lOs and costs 9s 6d: total £1 188 Od. THE TALE OFITHE TOVN.—Howells Golden Herb Pills.—

Advt. , SMOTHERED IM SALT AT WESTON.--At Weston 'Point, on Tuesday, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, held an in- quest upon the body of William Other, who was killed on Monday afternoon whilst following his employment at the works of the Mersey Salt and Brine Company. It appeared that the deceased was engaged in loading small carts with salt, which had to be conveyad to and loaded into flats in the dock of tne works. .The salt was deposi- ted at the spot where the deceased was from a higher Level by means of a "shoot," and he getting under- neath was buried beneatn a large quantity. 'He was extricated by some fellow workmen as quickly as possi- ble, but death ensued a few minutes afterwards. A verdict of accidental death was returned. The deceased, who was a native of Moulton, near Northwieh, was 26 years of age, and was married. RAILWAY SERVANTS' DINNER AT Winees.—The annual dinner of the employes of the Coaching Department of the London and North-Western Railway Company took place at Anderson Railway Hotel, on Thursday evening. About 50 persons sat down to the excellent repast pro- vided. Afterwards Mr. McConnell, the station-master, presided, and the vice-chair was taken by Mi. Inspector Career. The toast of the evening "Success to the London and North-Western Railway Company," was proposed by the Vice-Chairman, and responded to by the Chairman. Mr. MeCannell alluded to the new scheme for landing merchandise at Holyhead, which was under considera- tion, and expressed the opinion that the Manchester Ship ' Canal, irateal of injuring the company, wor'd be to its benefit. Other toasts were also proposed andl honoured. PILES are cured by Howell's Golden ,Herb Pills. of all Mel- clue Vendors Vendors.—Advt. WIDNES FREE LIBRARY—The monthly meeting of the committee washeld 'yesterday. Mr. H. W. Deacon pre- sided, and there were present. Messrs. R H Davies, J Mor- rison, S. Robinson, W. Sadler, S. Sadler, F. H. rank- hurst, E. Carey, J. T. Allen (clerk), and Miss Proctor (librarian.)—The Librarian reported that the total daily attendance at the news-room for December was 12,520, being an average of 481 per day. The total issue of books had been 5,528, of which 116 were from the reference department. The average daily issue had been 212. It was decided that the time allowed for reading books— • 7 days--should not be increased. It was resolved that the Librarian sheeld not issue books to people who were known to live where there were cases of scarlet fever, small pox, or any infectious disease.—On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. S. Sadler, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Driffield for his lecture on photography. • APPROPRIATING A BEGGAR'S POSSESSIONS AT RUNCORN:— On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Edward Minton, a middle-aged man, was charged with begging in Regent- street, on Saturday.—P.C. 252 deposed to hearing the prisoner ask for alms at several places. When appre- hended he had 'is Bid in copper and a quantity of bread in his possession.—He was sentenced to seven 'days' hard labour.--Superintendent Hollingworth asked that the money should be appropriated to defray the cost of the prisoner's keep whilst in the police station.—Mr. C. Reynolds asked how the man would get on when he came out of gaol.—The Chief Constable of the county (Colonel' Hamersley), who occupied a seat on the Bench, said such men as the prisoner were a pest to the county and an ex- pense to the ratepayers. If he was worth looking after the Prisoners' Aid Society would do so, but there was no doubt he svorid take to cadging again, as that was his trade.--The Bench thought the application a reasonable one, and impounded the money for the purposes men- tioned. INDIGESTIQN CURED by one ID3x of Howell's Golden Herb Pills.—Advt. THE NEW WIDNE3 TneArrie.—The proprietors and con- tractors of the Alexandra Theatre gave a dinner to the workmen who have been engaged in the construction of that new building on Wednesday evening. Three inenthe have not elapsed since the work was commenced, and Messrs. Sayee and Randle are to be congratulated on the admirable manner in which they have carried out the contract. The structure is now ready for the reception of the interior fittings and the stage appliances, and the proprietors (Messrs. Gerrard, Sutcliffe, and Bray) intend to spare no effort to have the building opened in March by one of the best travelling companies in the provinces.' The repast on Wednesday evening was prepared in the Alexandra Hotel, by Mr. and Mrs. Gerrard, and there were about 70 persons present. Afterwards Mr. R. B. Matthews, CE., was called upon to take the chair, and the usual loyal toasts,were honoured. The Chairman then proposed "The town and trade of Widnes," to which Mr. J. Leatherbarrow and Mr. Lecomber responded, both gentlemen referring in encouragiag terms to the improved trade of the district. The toast of the evening, "Success to the Alexandra new theatre and its proprietors," was then proposed in appropriate terms by the Chairman, and Mr. Bray suitably replied. Mr. J. Rimmer, the architect, also spoke to the toast. The proceedings were enlivened by songs contributed by Messrs. W. Holt, W. Jones, Brouiliton, and G. Sayce. SAD FATALITY AT RIINCORN.—An accident, which had a fatal termination on Monday morning occurred to Mr. William Pownall, of 92, Shaw-street, Runcorn, on Friday night. The facts as brought but at the inquest held on Tuesday, by Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, show that up to a few weeks ago Mr. Pownall was employed as a foreman warehouseman at the docks, and he was out of employment. On Friday afternoon he left home in his usual state of mind with the intention of visiting several of his sons who are married; and he did so. About eight o'clock at night Kossuth Hulme, captain of the flat Rebecca was taking his fiat through No. 4 lock, whea he felt a twitch of the paddle and heard a thud. Several flatmen immediately, got a boathook and brought Mr. Pownall to the surface. He was evidently seriously in- jured, and he was conveyed to his house, where Dr. Mangan attended to his wounds. Besides a fractured skull, he had a broken arm and three broken ribs, and he succumbed to his Wounds early on Monday morning. Mrs Pownall said her husband had crossed the particu- lar lock gate, from which he had fallen, daily for the last 23 years. A juryman said the gate was only 22 inches wide, but there was another gate with a protecting rail a few yards higher up. A verdict of accidental death was returned. Much sympathy is felt for the family of the deceased, who had earned the respect of the townspeople durine a lifelong residence amongst them. He had been connected with Newtown Missions since their forma- tion and had officiated as superintendent of the Sunday school and lay reader.

SMALL Pox AT WIDNES.OR Thursday morning, Mrs. Allen, aged about 35, wife of a labourer named William Allen, of 28, Terrace-road, Widnes, died from small pox, after a few days' illness. This is the second case of small pox within a month. RUNCORN CHURCH INISTITUTE.—In connection with this institute the Rev. W. Paige Cox, M.A., vicar of Rock Ferry; delivered a lecture on "The continuity of the Cke-ch of England, _" in Cie National Schools. The Rev. A. Maitland Wood presided, and there was a fair attend- ance. DISSOLUTION OF PARTNERSHIP AT RUNCORN. The "London Gazette" announced that Mr. C. Wigg has withdrawn from the firm of Wigg Bros. and Steele, chemical manufacturers, and that the business will in future be carried on by Messrs. G. L. Wigg, W. J. Wigg, and Dr. Steele. LIBERALISM AT RUNCORN.—The Annual meeting of the Liberals of the Runcorn District, for the purpose of elec- ting representatives to the Divisional Council, which has control of all party matters in the Northwich constitu- ency, takes place on Thursday evenlng next. As Mr. W. Handley, the energetic secretary, announced a few weeks ago, it is desirable that all true Liberals should attend and take part in the carrying on of what is a most important organisation. ACCIDENTS AT WIDNES.—Thomas LRgAVOrth, aged 27, of 11, Joseph-street, Appleton, hr d his right arm caught between the buffers of two waggons at Messrs. raking- ton's works on Wednesday. The limb was severely lacerated and bruited.—On Tuesday, • Elizabeth Dooley, aged 15, abrva,nt to Mrs. Horan, of Lacey-street, was washing the clothes, when her dress became ignited at the boiler f-e, and she was bay burned. She now lies at the Accident Hospital in a precarious condition. PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.—Mr. F. Beck, of the firm of Messrs. Handley and Beck, having removed to Fred- sham, the scholars of his class at Bethesda Sunday School, with which he has been prominently connected, marked their sense of his services, en Tuesday evening, by presenting him with a handsome parallel Bible, bound in morocco. Mss Edith Riley gracefully performed this ceremony. and Mr. Beck suitably responded. Afterwards Mr, Ake: 'Seed read a paper on "Sincerity" to the assem- bled audience. SMITH'S ILLUSTRATED ALMANAC AND DIRECTORY.—WO have bees favourei with a copy of the tenth edition of the Almanac an I Directory published by Messrs. P. Smith and Co., chemists and druggists, of Runcorn. The book, which contains about 700 pages, is replete with informa- tion of a varied kind, and there is also much literary matter of an enterta'aing and instructive character, the whole being profusely illustrated with views, several of which • ssisess a strong local interest. A most important part of the work is the directory of Widnes, Runcorn, and Frodsham, and the numerous villages around those three towns, this part of the book alone occupying 130 pages. Since the directory was included in their annual, Messrs. Smith have continued to strive to increase the value of the information given by fulness and accuracy, and in the present volume, in adaition to the names and addresses of the inhabitants, there is also given the num- bers of the dwellings, which must be of great advantage to commercial men and tradesmen generally. The fact that the publication has reached a tenth edition is evi- dence that the volume, which year by year becomes more bulky in form, is fulfilting a public requirement in the extensive district in which it circulates. THE WEATHER AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES.—Each day during the past week the district has been enveloped in a fog, more or less dense, and the conduct of traffic on both railway and canal and river has been rendered not only difficult but dangerous. Trains ha^e been' running very far from punctual, and Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, on Tuesday had to engage a special train from Widnes to Runcorn in order to hold an inquest accord- ing to appointment. Trade at the various docks in the I district may be said to have been almost at a standstill. On Thursday night there were about 100 flats waiting at 'Bottom Locks to go to Liverpool, besides about 15 ves- sels. At Weston Point the docks were crowded out with craft, many of which contained cargoes for Lives pool steamships, which in some eases had to proceed to sea without them. The docks at Widnes were equally con- gested, and altogether the trade of the district has been much impeded. Olving to the stoppage of the canal traffic at Runcorn the works 'of Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele were in danger of having to cease operations through a lack of fuel, but so far they have succeeded in overcoming the difficulty. Yesterday, although the fog had cleared somewhat, the sky was altogether obscured, and during the greater part of the day es light had to be used in the places of business.. The river traffic was, however, te some extent resumed. Fortunately no acci- dents have occurred. ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A WIPE AT WIDNES.—James Al- lender, a rough-looking labouring man, was brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Thursday, charged' :th assaulting his wife Jane on the 7th inst. Dr. Hutchinson said he saw the woman on the day named. She was suffering front a contused wound at the back of the head.; the wound was three quarters of an inch long, and penetrated to the bone. The wound could not have been caused by falling, or be self-infficted. It had been caused by a blunt instrument, and not by .a bowl.— , Jrarriett Allender, eight years of age was examined.— , Mrs. Keegan said she heard a disturbance between the prisoner and his wife, and went into the house. Mrs. I Allender was bleeding very much. She told witness to , mind lief own business, and lying on the ground kicked I and shouted.—Cross-examinsa : Witness denied has 'ng: stated, at a former hearing, that Mrs. Allender told her 'her hesba,nd had struck her on the head a ith the tongs, ' and that the prisoner had replied that she struck him on the head ss:th a pan.—lnspector Keighlev, sworn, said he was in the Court on Monday, and heard the witness make that statement.!--Mrs. Allender, called, said she met with an r,ccident through her own fault. She was drunk. At New Year Scotch peonle generally indulged too much in drink, and she had a bit of a squabble with her husband about money. She fell on a basin. and cut her head. It would be a shame to prosecute her husband when he was innocent.—By Superintendent Johnstone : She was drunk, and did not know what she told InSpec- tor Keighley at the time.—The prisoner said he never lie I a finger against his wife.—The Bench said there was a case of very grave and strong suspicion, but the evidence admitted of doubt, and the prisoner would be discharged. RIVAL PILOTS AT WIDN2S.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday. Thomas Hulse and Joseph Ford, both pilots on the Mersey, appeared to answer summonses of assaulting each other. Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared for Hulse.—Ford, who lives in Irwell-street, West Bank, deposed that on Thursday, the sth January, he was act- ing as pilot of the " Coaster " Colonel Gamble. He ran the vessel through Runcorn Bridge, and ordered the anchor to be let go close to the Bridge. Defendant Hulse and a man named Thomas Ashton came alongside the vessel in a boat. Hulse shouted to the captain that "Old Leggy" (meaning Ford).would put the vessel on a bank. Ford replied "You bluff head. I have been up Widnes deep befereever you sawthe place, and it is very strange if I cannot take a vessel up the deep, and been at it all the days of my life." Hulse threatened to run him throegh with an oar, he had raised. Ford remarked that he "could not hurt pussy," whereupon Heise jumped on board, :and dive.sting.himself of part of his clothing and gis:ng his watch to Ashton, knocked Ford to the deck with his fist, and then kicked him.—By Mr. Knowles: He had served six months for attempting to drown a pilot, and had been fined for assaulting Harry Peacock, of the "Edward Whitley."—The case for Hulse was that he had been engaged to pilot the vessel into Widnes Dock, and when he went alongside the vessel. Ford attempted to prevent, him getting aboard. He used threats of a most colent kind, and pushed and hustled Hulse to such an extent that in 'self defence Hulse strulck him a 'blow that knocked him to the ground. Ford afterwards attempted to strike Hulse with a bucket and a pump handle. Hulse informed the Bench that Ford was like a lion after its prev.—The Bench considered cash defendant had committed an offence. Hulse was fined 10s. and costs Bs. 6d., and Ford was bound over to keen the peace for three months, himself in £lO and two sureties of £5 each. DATIESBURV HIGHWAY BOA:RD.—A meeting of this Board was held at Daresbury Court House on Thursday afternoon. Mr. Mclntyre presided, and there was a large attendance of members.—A Dan- gerous Ditch: A letter was read from Mr. Wools, of Hatton, calling the attention of the Board to ditch on the side of the road from Acton Grange to Moore, which made the road extremely dangerous: —Mr. Parr said the road as at present was very dan- gerous, and be proposed that a small committee be appointed to visit the spot, and see what should be done. He thought Mr. Walker, the Ship Canal con- tractor, would he willing to supply plenty of mate- rial to fill the ditch up with. (Laughter.)—lt was agr6d to appoint a small committee for the pnr- pose named.—Old Books, : Mr. Burgess reported that the sub-committee appointed at a previous meeting to look over the books and papers handed over by the late surveyor had done its work arid destroyed all those books and papers which they thought of no use to the Board.—Roarl Scrapers: 'lt was decided that a number of hand road- scrapers should he obtained at a cost of 50s each.— The Ship Canal Works: The Surveyor (Mr. Peerman) said that one of the engineers of the Ship Canal mentioned to him the other day that it was their intention to bridge over the road in Moss-lane, so that they might excavate and run their wagons UTI- - and also to make a drain to drain the water.—The Clerk (Mr. H. Linaker) said he had supplied the surveyorwith all the acts and bye-laws bearing on this subject. The road could not be touched unless a sufficient way was provided for the public.—The Surveyor said he told the engineer that if he wanted to make any application he could make it to the Board that day, but no application had been recess-ed.—The Clerk said he had told the surveyor not to allow the road to be touched until a bridge sufficient for public traffic was provided. —Mr. Knowles suggested that a small committee should be appointed, with which the surveyor could take advice in this matter, and this was agreed to. —The surveyor having been instructed to make in- quiries as to the cost, Sm., of a steam roller, the meeting terminated.

DRIVEN FROM HOME AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sesaions on Thursday, before. Mr ,T. Brock and Mr H. Wade Deacon, Joseph Keating, 14 years of age, was charged with sleeping upon the works of Messrs Gasket!, Deacon, and Co. P.C. Holbrook, who found the prisoner, stated the boy said his mother had turned him out.— The boy's stepmother said he was well treated at home. —Mr Brock said this Was disgraceful. There were many cases where children were brought up, and the parents owTht to be.—Mr Deacon said he had known the woman for years at the School Board, and it was not the boy's fault.—ln answer to the Bench, the boy said he would like to go to an industrial school.—The boy was there- upon set at liberty until Thu-sday next., MISSION SERVICES AT WIDNES.—Each evening during the past week mission services have been conducted in Milton Congregational Chu •ch, Widnes, by Mr. George Green, the Warwickshire Evangelist. The congregations, if not quite up to the expectations of the promoters, have been of fairly large proportions, and much good, it is hoped, has been done. Mr. Green, wl-o is a powerful' and convincing speaker, has delivered lecture's on the. fo"owing subjects :—Monday, " The most wonderf al thing ever written ;" Tuesday, "The three musts ;" Wed- nesday, "Born in a Tent ;" Thursday, "The wanderer brought home ;" Friday, "A woman did it." The musical portions of the services were rendered by the choir, assis- ted by friends from other churches, the hymns used being from Sankey's collection.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meetilig was held on Tuesday at the Town Hall. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Carey, Gas- kell, Taylor, Heves, Wright, Brown, W. W. Gos- sage, Houghton, Handley, Sadler, J. T. Allen (clerk); T, lligginson (surveyor), Care (engineer). NEW YEAR'S GREETING. The Chairman said this was the first meeting of the Board this year, and he was glad to meet the members once more, and to thank them for their services during the past year, and to wish each and everyone of them, a happy and prosperous New Year. That the business of the Board would be conducted as amicably and as successfully as before, was his fervent hope. (Hear, hear).

THE WASTg HEAP NUISANCE. The Clerk read the following letter from Messrs. Oppenheim and Malkin, solicitors, St. Helens, with re- ference to the "waste heaps" in the township :—" Such deposits as these are, in our opinion, clearly nuisances within the meaning of section 91 of the Public Health Act, 1875. They need not be "injurious to health" to enable the magistrates to convict (Bishop Auck- land Sanitary Authority, and Bishop Auckland Iron and Steel Company, Authority, 138). In our opinion, however, in consequence of, among other things, the saving words in sub-section 1 of the proviso attached to section 91, summary proceedings would not afford an adequate remedy, and we advise that proceed- ings should be taken under section 107 in the High Court of Justice to enforce the abatement or prohibition of the nuisance. The Attorney-General would be a necessary party to these proceedings. See Wallasey Local Board v. Goacey L.J.R. 56, Ch. D., p. 739." In reply to Mr. Heves the Clerk said that since the last meeting there hadbeen no official inspection of the waste heaps by the committee, or by any officials alithorised by the committee. He had visited the place of deposit in the neilhbourhood of the Central Station, and found considerable nuisance.—The Chairman sug- gested that a committee should be appointed to confer with the depositors of waste, and endeav- our to come to some arrangement by which, the nuisance can be stopped by the discontinuance lof the eposition of waste in objectionable places. He thought that to take extreme legal steps upon the Board's presumed right of law would be extremely objectionable. They had got to live together, waste or no waste.—Mr. Wright proposed the appointment of a committee con- sisting of the Chairman, Dr. O'Keeffe, Mr. Gaskell. and Mr. Heves to deal with the matter.—Mr. Gaskell said he should not like to serve upon any committee unless they had clear and full instructions what they were to ask for. He moved a resolution that the depositors should confer' with the whole Board.—Mr. Carey seconded the motion, which was carried. Mr. 'Kright's proposition, having no secondn, fell to the groand.—lt was decided to invite the depositors of waste to a special meeting of the Board at two o'clock on the afternoon of the 24th inst.

_ 'FOOTPATH AssoctizioN. The Clerk said he had received a circular letter from the above association asking the Board to become mem- bers. For a subscription of O. per annum the Board would be entitled to the best legal advice gratis on the question respecting public footpaths or encroachments made on the road side land.—Mr. Carey said this was a useful society, and was doing a good work in many places.—The letter was referred to the Highway Com- mittee on the motion of Mr. Heyes, seconded by Mr. Wright.

GAS AND WATER COMMITTER. The Engineer directed the attention of the committee to the dangerous state of the old chimney at the works of the Widris Alkali Company in Earle-street. In the event of a collapse the gas works would sustain great damage.—The CrAnx was instructed to give notice to the Alkali. Company that they would be held liable for any loss or damage sustained. The mean rainfall for the month had been 2.605 inches, and the water in stock on December 28 liwas 8,388,297 gallons. The illumina- ting Dower of the gas during the month had averaged 17-63 candles. It was recommended that the following charges be made for the use of the hose reel in addition to the warns of the Fire Brigade. Within the district let hour, 7s 64; each succeeding hour when w.u-king. 55; each hour when waiting orders, 2s 64. Outside the dis- trict Ist hour. 12s 64; each succeeding hour when working, lOs ; each hour when waiting orders. ss.—Mr. Gaskell moved, and Mr. Taylor seconded the adoption of the minutes.

TIT?. NETFIRTIVEY BROOK. The Chairman asked if the committee were satisfied with the way in which the affluent water from the Huy- ton-with-Roby Sewage Farm was now being conveyed away by a line of pipes.—Mr. Gaskell said the pipes had been taken a greater distance than was at first intended. but what the result would he the committee could not Possibly tell. Sewage water still flowed from the farm into the brook in abundance. The committee could not say whether it would be satisfactory until the arrange- ments had been thoroughly carried out.—The minutes were adopted. -- •

HIGHWAY MATI'EDS. The minutes of this committee included the following: —Moss Bank Sewer Outlet: Letter, 31st December, from Mr. Bibby, respecting easement and about a sewer in Proposed newstreet between Alexandra-street and Moor- lane. Mr. Bibby Attended the meeting by request. Re- commended that an offer of 5s per lineal yard be made to Mr. Bibby for easement through the Marsh, provided he gives the two sites for ventilating shafts. This offer to be without prejudice.—Mr. Bibby to submit plans, of new street and sewer.—Public Roans : Tenders as follows for fencing approach road to I. D. Hospital—R. Balshaw £l9s 6s 6d, C. Hemingway £l9 10s, and T. Sadler £22 103. Recommended that the tender of R. Balshaw be accepted. Plan of proposed alteration to footwalk from the Police Station to the Alexandra Hotel submitted and approved. Letter, 2nd January, from Mr. Super- intendent Johnston, stating that the justices agree to pay the cost of flags (£34 10s) opposite their property. Re- commended that tenders be obtained for the carrying out the proposed alterations. The Dian for theatre in Alex- andra-street, for T. Ge-rard and others, be approved.— Mr. Carey moved, and Mr. Hought-in seconded, the con- firmation of the minutes.—Mr. Wright said he had heard some disparaging remarks as to the manner in which the committee had given the contract for the fencing.—Mr. Carey said both Mr. Allen and himself, after an inspec- tion of Mr. Heminzwav's tender. came to the conclusio that the amount was £l9 10s.. It now SACITA that Mr. Hemingway intended the figures for £l9, and it was un- fortunate they had made a mistake. The other pOrsons had written the amount of their tender tw;ce, once in figures and once in words, and it would have been better if Mr. Hemingway had done the same.—Mr. Allen said the matter could not have been cooked, because there was another tender that had not been examined at the time.—Mr. Wright: I am perfectly satisfied.—The mi- nutes were passed. THE INVECTIGIN DISEASES HOSPITAL.—A COMPLAINT. The Medical Officer of Health reported to the Health Committee that during December there were 75 births and 65 deaths, being at the rate respectively of 30 and 26 per 1,000; 32 deaths occurred amongst children under five years. Zymotic diseases caused six deaths. The Nuisance Inspector reported that there had been four cases (woman and four children) of typhus fever at No. 52, Major Cross-street, and one case at No. 7, Charlotte, street. There had been one case of smallpox at No. 30, Terrace-road. The woman and children had been re- moved to the new hospital: the other patients were now convaleseent.—lnfectious Diseases Hospital: Tenders for forming roadway, kc. as follows examined, Sayce and Co. £93 12s. S. CovvbZirn £lO6, W. Smith £76. and H. Edgerlev £ll5 Is. Recommended, that the tender of W. Smith. £76, be iccepted. Tenders for cupboard, table, Sze., T. Sadler £l2, R. Balshaw £ll 7s ed. Recom- mended, that the tender of H. Balshaw be accepted. The Clerk reported that it had been necessary to engage an assistant nurse and a servant, and that the matron stated a second servant is required. Recommended, that the assistant nurse (Miss Winter), at a salary of £2O per annum, and the servant, £l2 per annum, be appointed, salaries to commence from the dates on which they com- menced duties. 28th and 15th December reSpectively ; and that another servant be engaged—all to have uni- forms and to be subject to a month's notice. Miss Downie, matron at the Accident Hospital, applied for an increase of salary, and the committee recommended an advance of £7 per annum (making £52 per annum).— Dr. O'Keeffe moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Wright said if, as some people thought, the Infectious Diseases Hospital was going to be a white elephant, it was not the •fault of the Board. They had it pushed upon them, and they must make the best of it. He should like to call the attention of the Board to the fact that a family was removed into the hospital before it was fairly fit to receive anyone, and from the Wednesday, when theyemtered. until the following Tuesday, there were no disinfectants of any description about the whole building. The rate- payers in the locality of the hospital thought everything

would be thoroughly disinfected, so asto prevent disease spreading, and yet a whole week was, allowed to pass without any attempt at disinfection. The danger of spreading the disease was increased by the fact that workmen were still on the job, and were going in and out of the place where the dirty clothes were. As they had got the hospital let them look after it thoroughly.— Dr. O'Keeffe said the hospital was scaicely fit for the re- ception of patients when these cases,arose, but th •atigh the strong representations of the medical officer the com- mittee were compelted to send the patient, to the hos- pital. There was a mother and three childr-• • living in one miserable room, the capacity of which wa... not suf- ficient for the mother alone, and they would have been a danger to public health. With regard to the rooms not being disinfected, he knew nothing at all about it. That was a matter for the doctor attending the patients, for the inspector of nuisances, and the matron and nurse. Disinfectants could have been had or the ask- ing. If he had known about *'-ie matter he muld have taken good care *hat disinfectants a., well as every other necessity had been sent to the hospital. If the matron allowed the workmen to come in cont.zt with the per- hons suffering from infectious disea.se, o • with their clothinov, the sooner she received instructions that this should not recur and the better. The Nuisance Inspector explained +-hat the disinfectants ' were not sent to the hospital earlier because the cart was engaged in other business. The matron could have had what she wished by asking for Wright said he simply raised the question so .that such a stat af things might not occur again.—The Chairman said. was glad to see that the committee recommended an increase of salary for Miss Downie. She had been with the Board many years, and had been a most efficient servant.— Tenders for the erection of a mortuary and amhulance shed were opened, and that of Mr. 11.13alshaw, being the lowest (£B9 14s) was accepted.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee reported that the Local Government Bpard had sanctioned the borrowing of £2,120 for 30 years for Moss Bank sewer, and it was recommended to borrow that amount from the Public Works Loans Commissioners. Accounts amounting to £5,940 12s 5d were passed for payment. The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. T. Handley.

AMATEUR DRAMATIC PERFORMANCES AT WARRINGTON. On Wednesday, Thursday; and Friday evenings of this week amateur dramatic performances have been given, to large and appreciative audiences, in the Public Hall, by the members of the Warrington Amateur Dramatic Society, the object of the per- formances being to aid the funds of the Warrington School of Art. The stage was tastefully adorned with plants, and several of the scenes, which were very effective, had been prepared aad painted at the School of Art. The music was furnished by Mr. T. J. Down's orchestral band, and it is due to them to say that the selections were admirably played. Mr. Downs is to be congratulated on the success which has attended his untiring efforts, and it is to be hoped that the public of Warrington will have many further opportunities of listening to so excellent a band. On Wednesday evening the entertainment opened with the following prologue, written by Mr. W. C. Copeland, and admirably spoken by that gen- tleman :

One word of welcome Friends assembled here, We wish you all a very bright New Year. You've entered now on eighteen eighty-eight. ' Without attempting to vaticinate, We'll hope the future may eclipse the past— Yet, shade of Robertson, this is forecast ; So, why not prophesy good times in store, Not" good old times," but brighter than before, When, notwithstanding veto, clique, cabal, Our ship wales in along the Ship Canal? • 'Twixt Mersey's port and Camp our fortune's made,— A halfway house must drive a roaring trade; Or, say, while others tug at horns and tail, Like flogar..'s lawyer, we can Jill the pail; Won't one look blue, the other town grow green, To see midway shine forth—the golden mean. Good reaton have we also as a nation To bless this year. The story of invasion— What armaments sailed forth, then how they fled, And England was delivered from great dread— No need to tell aguin ; all schoolboys know What happened just three hundred years ago. Another hundred, sixteen eighty-eight— Invasion then salvation to the State! When next those eights come round, behold a wonder! The printing press begins like Jove to thunder; Comes forth the "Times," admonisher of nations,— It costs you threepence at the railway stations. Each to his taste; endeared to us those days, When dram L flourished, and produced the plays Which focussed all the fervour of the are, And shed a glory round our English stage, But to descend from this highilown excursion, Our true intent, not Meg's, but your diversion. For your amusement, too, the "Ticklish Times," Let merry laughter ring like Christmas chines; We ask no thunders for our lightsome play, As greei.s the melodrama of the day; • Yet, gods behind, of plaudits don't be chary! Ye goddesses, Asonanum eat errare. You know the casz, now though they're not "perfection," By former feats they've won your predilection. Great credit this. •Me motive and occasion Most even win our critic's approbation; " Observe" us well, not harshly, and "Examine," Our "Guardian" angel back us, don't backgammon; Supporting us, you benefit a cause Which asks 'or somethir g more than mere applause, The muse of art. Since on the roll of fame This town is wedded to an artist's name, 'Ti, meet each townsman play, or pay his part, To propagate the principles of art. This school of hers (you lately passed its portal) May well, who knows, train up some new immortal. While yet the marble is beneath the tool, Adore the goddess, says the golden rule. (Applause.) Mr. H. T. Craven's much-admired two-act drama, entitled " Mer°'s Diversion," was next pre- sented. Mr. Alfred Woods, as Jeremy Crow, a , Devonshire farmer, was very successful. He might, perhaps, have made up so as to look a little more like the father of two grown-up daughters. Mr. Arthur Browne was not less effec- tive as Ashley Merton, Esq. The part suited him to a nicety, and he made good use of his oppdrtu- nity. The Jasper Pidgeon of Mr. Percy Davies was, however, the hit of the evening. He looked and played the part, admirably, and in the pathetic parts he managed to put the tears in his voice" in a really clever manner. Roland Pidgeon, who is in I truth a foil to his brother, was sustained by Mr. W. E. Atkin with 'distinctive freedom and grace. Mr. W. H. Cookson made the most of Eytem, an Exeter lawyer, for he succeeded in making it quite a char- acter. The actresses, it should be stated, were pro- fessionals, and it is, _perhaps, the highest compli- ment that we can pay the amateurs to say that there was not that marked difference in style be- tween the ladies and the gentlemen Which might have been expected. Miss Annie Darncombe repre- sented Cornelia with great care, and with ,fine dramatic feeling. Miss Clara Lemore was also very effective as Margaret, while the Airs. Netwell of Miss C. Elton left nothing to be desired. The farce "Ticklish Times" followed, and was well received, though it was obvious that it would have been all the better for a little more rehearsal. Mr. J. E. Davies kept the house in aroar as Launcelot Griggs. He has genuine talent for parts of this class, and was seen to great advantage. Mr. J. T. Picton was pirhaps a little too demonstrative as Bodkins, but he was certainly suc- cessful in helping to keep the fun going. Mr. Percy Davies had little to do as Jansen, a Dutch smuggler, but he did that little well. Mr. H. D. Barkas, as Sir William Ramsay, a Jacobite leader, was too con- scious of playing a part, and was consequently somewhat stiff and awkward. Miss Clara Lemore, as Mrs. Gigs, Miss A. Darncombe, as Winifred, end Miss Caroline Elton. as Dot; acquitted them- selves admirably throughout the farce. It may be remarked that, on the first evening, both pieceswent too slowly, and, with the extra music of the band, it' was late—considerably after eleven o'clock-.-when ht to a close. On Thurs- daythe performance was brought night the same programme was presented. It is almost needless to say that the various performers had profited by their experience of the previous evening, and the result was that there waa alto- gether much more "go." and the entertainment was broueht to a close at a reasonable hour. Mr. Jos. Davies, who is an old hand at stage work, lent valu- able assistance, as stage manager, in keeping every- body up to the mark. The series of performances was last evening brought to a close by the representation of Mr. T. W. Robertson's comedy "Caste." There was a crowded audience, and in all other ketycets the performance was a decided suc- cess. In this. play perhaps the most distinctive part is that of Eccles, the tippling parent of the two heroines of the piece, and it is certainly a part which affords endlms amusement to the audience when well sustained. In this respect the Warrington Society is particularly fortunate in having in its ranks a comedian like Mr. J. E. Davies. It would be difficult to find a more capable exponent of the ways and weakne.sses of the bibulous Eccles, and as a result the house was kept in a continual roar during Mr. Davies' appearances on the stage, and his exit was always markod by hearty applause. The important character of the Hon. George D'Alroy found a competent representative in Mr. W. E. Atkin, whose playing VMS distinguished by a naturalness and ease particularly commendable in an amateur. Mr. W. Cookson as Captain Hawtree was also a success, though it might perhaps be suggested that he empha- sised the sang froid, which is the great characteristic of the Captain, to such an extent as to militate against the subdued humour of the character. Sam Gerridge, the very practical plumber, found a capital exponent in Mr. Alfred Woods, whose performances were a source of much amusement, and contributed largely to the success of the evening. The three professional ladies, Miss

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: Caroline Elton as the Marquise de St. Maur, Miss Annie Darncombe as Esther, and Miss tiara Lemore as Polly, were, it is scarcely necessary to say-, an invaluable aid to the amateurs. Each actress was admirably fitted for her part, and it would be difficult to say whether Miss Lemore as the vivacious and irrepressible Polly, Miss Darncombe in the love-making and pathetic parts which fell to her lot, or Miss Elton as the haughty and blue- blooded Marquise, displayed the most effective acting i . The on'y other character n the piece, apart from the inevitable baby, was that of Dixon, a servant, who only once appeared, and that for a brief period. Mr. H. A. Barka.s played the role of Dixon admirably. It shorld be said that his "get up," like that of the other performers, was very appropriate. At the conclusion of each of the three acts the applause betokened in an un- mistakeable manner the appreciation of the audience, and at the close of the second the players were twice called before the curtain. The music was again sup- plied by Mr. Downs' band, whose selections were de- m redly admired. It should be mentioned that the furniture and ap- pointments had been lent by Messrs. R. Garnett and Son, Sankey-street; and dresses weresupplied by Messrs. Holmes and Powell, of Bridge-street, and others. The hon. trease-er for the undertaking was Mr. H. Fair- dough, and the hon. secretary, Mr. W. Milner. There is reason to believe that the committee will have a respect- able balance in aid of the School of Art.

div.head: " COMMERCIAL " ON THE SPREE.
div.p: A " COMMERCIAL " ON THE SPREE.

A commercial traveller named Frederick Gore, who gives an address at a Bolton hotel, has been hav- ing a spree in Warrington. He was seen in a:state of intoxication in the Market-place, and, as he was also in questionable company, the police, with a view to his safety, conducted him to the bridewell. When interrogated he made it known that he was under the impression that he was in Bolton, but when asked if he knew anyone in Warrington he gave the names of several very respectable people. Subsequently two of them attended at the police station and bailed the man out, each making him- self responsible in the sum of £5 for the appearance before the magistrates next morning of Gore, who was himself bound over in the sum of .£lO to ap- pear. When taken charge of by the police. Gore had upon him a sum of .£ll and othey valuables. On Tuesday morning the sureties put in an ap- pearance at the police court at the usual hour—ten o'clock—but the defendant himself was not forth- coming. Consequently the case was adjourned, and, there being no other business, the magistrates left the court. Soon afterwards, however, defen- dant arrived at the court-room in company with one of his sureties, and it was explained that he had been taken to the County Court by mistake, under the impression that it was the Police Court. The attendance of Mr. Francomb having been secured, the case was proceeded with, defendant being charged with having been drunk in Bridge-street on the previous evening.—ln reply to the charge, defendant said he would plead guilty to being drunk, but at the same time he had to inform the magistrate that he hada man in charge of him whom he had paid to look after 'him. He knew that he was drunk, but he thought he was within the law by having a man to look after him.—Mr. Fran- comb: You plead guilty, I suppose, to this offence. I think it is -better that you should do so under the circumstances.—Defendant: If you will allow me to explain, I will tell you why I do not plead guilty. I did get drunk, but still that was allowable, I understand. When I get a man to look after me, I believe I am safe from the interference of the police. —Mr. Francomb; But you see the police authori— ties thought it was best that they should look after you _Defendant: From what I know of law—of course, I don't want to dictate to you, sir—l know that I was within the law in getting drunk. I can do that. 1 got a man and paid him to see me borne. —Chief Constable Hunt; We don't want men to come here and get drunk, and render themselves liable to be robbed, thus adding to the crime of the town.—Defendant: I would not have said a word if I had been robbed. It was my own fault.—Mr. Francomb: If you will pay 10s. to the poor box, that will end it. Will that suit you ?—Defendant: Well. sir, I shall pay it,‘but I should like you to give yourjudgment upon the question whether the police were within their right in arresting me when I had paid a man to look after me.—Mr. Francomb: You see you were in the hands of a." corner " man, a man who gives the police authorities a great amount of trouble, and I think you ought to be very thankful to them for the action they have taken in the matter.—Defendant; I will pay it like a shot, sir: at the same time I hope you will say that they have no authority over me.—Defendant then handed over the 10s., thanked the magistrate for his kind- ness, and left the court with his filends.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

in the Irlam and Cadishead district the bulk ef the Ship Canal works now in operation are situated in the meadows at Hollins Green, North of Warbur- ton Bridge, where there is a vast tract of fiat coun- try lying between the river Irwell and the highway leading from Manchester to Warrington. This bridge connects Lancashire with Ch9shire. and is the only public thoroughfare over the Irwell between that district and Barton, a distance of over seven miles. Amongst the officials on the ground are Mr. Strover, engineer to the contractor, and Mr. lien- way, agent. In the meadows named about half a mile of a ballast line has been laid in the direction of Irlam, which is to meet another section of the line now being constructed on the east side of Irlam railway station, by which the contractor and sub-contractors will be enabled to get their plant and material along the banks of the river. A large quantity of timber has already been laid, which is being cut into lengths at a sawing mill by a power- ful stationary engine for the contractors' offices, store rooms, and huts for the navvies. A start was made with these on Monday, and in the huts provi- sion is being made for at least 1.500 men. For sani- tary reasons the huts will probably be erected in blocks of six each. The contractor has already on the grounds four six-wheeled and two four-wheeled coupled locomotive ballast engines, 'and several steam cranes and other machinery. The sub-con- tract for the Irlam and Cadishead length of the canal, it is stated, was let on Monday to a gentle- man who has just completed the bridge at Rhyl for the London and NorthlWestern Railway Company. On Friday last week a steam navvy arrived at Irlam station, ant: has been conveyed to the scene of opera- tions at Rixton. During the week operations have been carried on as vigorously as ever in connection with the con- struction of the canal in the neighbourhood of Acton Grange and Moore, anti material is constantly arriving by way of Latchford station. Negotiations are being carried on with the object of acquiring land at Lvrom, and it is probable that within a few days work will be commenced in that district. From a report in another column of the Lynam Local Board, it will be seen that arrangements are in progress for the gale of the sewage farm belonging to the Board to the Ship Canal Company. Mr. Walker, the contractor of the canal, has, it is stated, applied to the Rey. Chas. Garrett to select five evangelists to work among the navvies during the construction of the canal. The directprs of the Ship Canal Company have recently been in communication with the Corpora- tions of Manchester ind Salford with regard to the pollution of the rivers Irwell and Mersey and their tributaries, with a result that a conference will be held on the 24th inst. at the Town Hall of Manches- ter, to consider what means can be taken to prevent the pollution of those rivers. A circular has been issued to town councils, local boards, and other bodies interested, asking them to send representa- tives to the meeting.

SUDDEN DEATE.—Joseph Unsworth, an old resident of Earlstewn, died somewhat suddenly on Tuesday morn- ing. The deceased, who Nim.s 70 years of age, and re- sided at 51, Sankey-street, rose about seth o'clock on the morning of the day named for the purpose of light- ing the fire and preparing breakfast. He left his wife and grand daughter in bed, and after lighting the fire he went into the back yard. As he seemed absent for an unusual length of time Mrs. Unsworth,went in search, and found him lying on the floor of the closet with his bead against the wall. He was quite dead, and when Dr. Mounsey was called some time afterwapas he found that the immediate cause of death was spasm of the heart. Dr. Mounsey had attended the deceased for about three years past. NEWTON FOOTBALL7LIIII BALL.—The annual ball under the auspices of the Newton Football Club was held in the Town Hall, Ne,a, on, on Friday evening, and wai a most suceessful gathering. The halt had undergone an attractive decoration by Mr. E. T. Evans, of Market. street, Earlestown. The windows were draped with curtains, red cloth lined the seats along the sides of the room, and the orchestra was resplendent in red and black stripes, the colours of the club. The arrangements were carried out by Messrs T. Appleton, W. Parks, Geo. McCormick. George Lane, T. Egan, and A. Lane, with Mr George Thompson (hon. secretary). Mr W. Pear- son's string band from Wigan. rendered an excellent selection of music, and dancing was kept up with much spirit from nine o'clock until about half-past five the following morning. Mr F. Appleton and Mr George Thompson ably officiated as masters of ceremonies. and excellent refreshments were provided for the company by Mr. R. Walmsley, of the Legh Arms Hotel.

Til'E SANITARY COMMITTER.-TRE LONGFORD MANURE CON- TRACT. - TICE COUNCIL AND THE RURAL SANITARY
AIITHOItITY.

The minutes of the Sanitary Committee contained the following items :—Resolution, that the tender of Mrs. Charlotte Lunt to supply horses and men during the next twelve months be accepted.—Re ' solution that the tender of Mr. John Bonnell to supply an iron tank delivered at, Longford depot be accepted.—Minute, that a letter was I read from the elerktothe Newton-in-Makerfield Improve-. ment Commissioners, giving notice, to terminate the agreement between the Commissioners and the Corpora- tion respecting the Hospital for Infectious Diseases, and suggesting fresh terms .—Resorution, that this committee believing that the terms of the existing agreement are fair and equitable cannot see their way to alter them, but are quite willing to continue the present agreement. —Resolution, that a contract be entered into with the Warrington Slate Company, Limited, for the sale to them of the whole of the manuie manufactured at Longford from this date up to the end of April, and that the Town Clerk be instructed to prepare the contract.—Resolution, that this committee contribute the sum of £3O per an- num towards the cost of working the boilers and com- pressors at the gasworks, required for the ejectors at the intercepting depots.—The minutes also contained copy. of some correspondence which had taken place with the Local Government Board relative to the outbreak of small-pox at Sankey Bridges, in the district of the Rural Sanitary Authority. alderman BURGESS, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said they would observe that the tender of Mrs. Charlotte Lunt to supply horses and men at es 10d per day during the next 12 months had been accepted. This, bethought, was so reasonable a thing that it was hardly necessary to take up their time with it. He thought they would all agree it was a very reasonable price, and that the committee had done the Council good service by getting it at that price. (Hear, hear.) The next minute he would call attention to was with refer- ence to the letter from the Newton-in-Makerfield Com- missioners giving notice to terminate the agreement be- tween the Commissioners and the Corporatism respect- ing the Hospital for Infectious Diseases, and to

which the committee replied that they believed the terms of the existing agreement were fair and equitable, and that they could not see their way to alter them, but that they were willinp to continue the present agreement. He might remind the Council of what many of them knew, that a few years ago an arrangement was entered into with the Commissioners by which the latter were authorised to send patients into the Warrington infectious diseases hospital on certain terms. The terms were the payment of something like £lO4 a year for the right, and 16s per patient per week during the time he was under treat- ment in the hospital. What the Commissioners wished now was that the £lO4 should be reduced to say £5O a year, and that the amount chargeable per patient should be raised to say 20s instead of 16s. The Sanitary Com- mittee however, thought that the arrangement they had had with the Commissioners was of so fair and equitable a character that they would not be doing the Corporation justice in acceding to the proposition of the Commissioners. They were quite willing to renew the arrangement on the pld terms. (Hoar, hear.) Alder- man Bure-ass, no:zt referre4 to the contract proposed to be entered into with the Warrington Slate Company for the sale of the manure manufactured at Longford. He thought they would see that that was a resolution which required that whatever _was said about it in that room should be carefully said, and he did believe that the less said upon the subject the better. They had nothing they wanted to keep back. The members of the com- mittee knew, or were satisfied in their minds that they 1 had made a very good arrangement for the Corporation.' They did not want it to be considered that they wero the custodians of a great secrete and that that Council was to be kept in ignorance on any subject whatever. This they did contend, that as they were selling to people who would have to resell, they should not put the buyers from the slate company in possession of the terms upon which the slate company haa that material placed in their hands, for in that rase their ; customers would have an advantage they were not en- titled to. If that Council had had confidence enough in' the committee to believe that they 'had made a proper, satisfactory and equitable arrangement with the slate company, they would confirm that resolution; if they did not think so, he hoped they would express their opinion in such a way that the committee should under- stand that it had not the confidence of the Council to the extent it ought to have if it was to carry on the de- partment with usefulness to the borough. With refer- ence to the correspondence that followed relative to the outbreak of smallpox in the district of the Rural Sani- tary Authority it was not for him to do more than call the attention of the Council to the fact that that out- break was close to the borough—betwixt there and San- key Bridges. It was very much too near to be satisfac- tory, and it was a menace to the borough. They had thought it to be such a grave matter that through thel town clerk they had put themselves in' communication , with the Local Government Board,calling their attention to the condition of things. The Board of Guardians not having any hospital of their own to which they could take a patient suffering from infectious disease, they thought that the safety of the borough required that they should urge upon the Local Government Board to require the Guardians—and he was sure the Guardians would not find fault with them for doing so—through some instrumentality or another, to have some place where people suffering from infectious disease could be taken. He would just, in passing, correct a mis-state- ment that appeared to have been made, that that Cor- poration declined to accept patients of the' Poor-law Guardians in their hospital. Now, that was not accurate, for as the correspondence itself showed that the Rural Sanitary Authority had at one time an arrangement with them that their patients might go into the Corporation hospital. That engagement was terminated by the Rural Sanitary Autho:ity, but a few months ago they made an ap- plication to the Corporation with a view of again hav- ing the right to use the hospital, arid the Mayor and himself were deputed to meet the representatives of the Sanitary Authority to discuss the terms. They sub- mitted the previous terms with this addition, that they said that as far as they were concerned the question Of whether a patient was a pauper or not, should not be allowed to interfere. The MAYOR: That was so.

Alderman BunoEss said that merely to clear away any misapprehension that might exist, for it did appear that there was an erroneous impression in the boardroom. Whatever was done would be satisfactory to him and the Sanitary Committee if the Board of Guardians would take care to do what it was their bounden duty to do, through one instrumentality or anothtr—that was to say, to make provision for cases of such extreme danger as had lately occurred, and so place the borough in a posi- tion of greiter safety. (Hear. hear). Councillor DARIN seconded the proposal to adopt the minutes. Councillor JOLLEY said he did not think Alderman Burgess had given a very clear definition of the position of the Rural Sanitary Authortty. To the best of his re- collection the terms of the agreement with the Corpora- tion were these : That the Sanitary. Authority pay the Corporation £l3O a year, and 16s. per week for every patient; and what the :Sanitary Authority objected to was that there was a proviso in the agreement that the Corporation would only receive patients from the Sani- tary Authority when there was room in the hospital. If the hospital were • full the Sanitary Authority paid the £l3O and got nothing in return. ' Alderman BURGESS aid it was only within the last fertr,;itt er time wceks that he learned that the proviso was in the agreement; , Councillor JOLLEY said that, speaking al a member of the Sanitary Authority, he thought it a very one-sided bargain. The MAYOR: How were we to provide accommodation if we were already full up? CouncillorJoway There comes irl the inconsistency, and I think the Rural Sanitary Authority acted wisely in breaking through that bargain. ' '" . . .

COUOAIIOr BARKER, refercring to the resolution relating to a contract with the Warrington Slate Company, said that as the terms Were not made public he expected that every member of the Council would be able to get at the prices. He wished to know whether advertisements for the contract had been issued, or it had been entered into with that one firm only irrespective of any others being asked for tenders; and also whether the Slate Company would only take the manure manufactured be- tween then and the end of April, or take it all the year round at the same price. They knew that at the end of April the demand was less, and it was difficult to get farmers to take it away. Councillor DIXON moved, as an amendment, that the minute referring to the contract with the Slate Com- pany should be referred back to the committee. This amendment, however, was not seconded,. _ _

Councillor HurcniNsoN thought it would have been better to have invited tenders for the manure on the same conditions as the Slate Company had undertaken to buy it. He thought that in that *ay they might make a little more money by it. Councillor BURGESS, in replying, said with regard to the hospital question, it would probably neVer have oc- curred that any patients a( the Sanitary Authority would have been refused admission owing to their being no accommodation. The Corporation would not stand by and see an infection spread, but would without hesita- tion adopt extraordinary means to provide accommoda- tion, as they did on a former occasion, by erecting tents. (Hear, hear.) With regard te Councillor Barker's que,;- tion, they had found by experience that after the end of April the demand for manure ceased for that year—the quantity required after that time was infinitesimal. The suggestion that had been thrown out as to advertising would not be lost sight of. The Maven said with regard to the hospital it Might satisfy the Rural Sanitary Authority with a clause that if at any time the hospital was so full that none of their. patients could be admitted, the part of the £l3O for the privilege of the use of the hospital should be deducted for the time the patients were not admitted.
Alderman BuitoEss remarked that they should in honour be bound to provide for the patients, and in the interests of the public. The minutes of the Sanitary Committee were then passed.
