div.head: MARKETS COMMITTEE.-ANIMATED DISCIISSION.
div.p: MARKETS COMMITTEE.-ANIMATED DISCIISSION.

At a meeting of this committee it was resolved, "That the resolution of this committee of the 14th November, appointing the chairman and deputy-chairman, be rescinded ; " "That Mr. Councilor Da.kin be appointed chairman, and Mr. Councillor Graenall the deputy-chair- man, of this committee for the ensuing year ; " and "That Mr, Councillor 131ackhurst be elected a member of the sub-committee, in the place .of Mr. Councillor John Pierpoint."
The confirmation of the minutN wai proposed by Councillor DIN, seconded by Councillor J. SHAW GREEN.

Councillor JOIN PIERPOINT, who addressed the Coun- cil at some length, referred to a letter sent by Councillor Dakin, which was read to the committee on the 28th of November last, and was read before the Council on the 6th of December. Mr. Dakin prefaced that letter by saying "I beg to enclose copy of a letter I have for- warded to the ,Chairman of the Markets Committee re- signing my seat on the committee, but, as I understand it will not appear on the minutes, I desire that you and the Council should be in possession of the facts which compelled me to take that step." It would be his (Mr. Pierpoint's) duty to show them that the preface was alto- gether illusory. He (Councillor Pierpoint) did not attend the meeting of the committee on the 12th December on account of the way he had been used at the Council on the 6th December. At that meeting the resolution ap- pointing the chairman and deputy-chairman was rescinded, and he was given to understand on very good authority Mr. Dakin was invited to take the chairman- ship. of the Markets Committee, when he positively re- fused. He (Mr. Pierpoint) was accused of making a mis- statement in Mr. Dakin's letter. He was accused be- cause, unfortunately,through alittle omission of memory,

div.head: TILE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 14, 1888.
div.p: TILE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 14, 1888.

he did not exactly remember how many years he had been a member of the Markets Committee—Mr. Dakin accused him of misrepresentation, and hinted that he had falsely jumped into the position Of the Chairman of the Committee. On the 13th December, the day after the meeting, the Deputy Town Clerk called upon him at his office, no doubt under the *authority of the commit- tee, and he asked him this question, which he took down in writing :--" Is it your intention to remain as a mem- ber of the Markets Committee ? " He discussed the -matter,with him for a considerable time, and did not give him a definite answer. But he thought it better to consider the matter over, and afterwards wrote to this effect :—"4, Bold-street Chambers, Warrington, 14th December, 1887. Dear Sir,—Markets Committee.—ln reply to your enquiry yesterday as to my continuing to remain a member •of the above committee, I can only say, after due and deliberate consideration, that under no circumstances can I consent to act on the committee, except Mr. Councillor Dakin is pre- pared to make an apology at the next monthly meeting of the Council, withdrawing his unwarrantable and un- gentlemanly letter relative to my_ appointment to the chairmanship of the Markets Committee. I may here express my extreme sorrow that Mr. Dakin. whom I have at all times regarded in the highest degree as a per- fect gentleman, should so far have forgotten himself (no doubt under pressure of a little temper) as to have writ- ten the abusive letter referred to. As there is at present neither chairman nor deputy chairman I send this letter through you to be submitted to the Markets Committee at their next meeting.—Yours faithfully, Jrro. Punt- POINT. J. L. Whittle, Esq., deputy town clerk." Under the circumstances he thought it was his duty to remain on the committee, and he was not going to retire. A little bird came to him one day, arid told him a story. Between the 12th and 19th, the 12th being the day that Councillor Dakin refused to accept the chairmanship, that gentleman, whether bethought himself incompetent or,timid—looked out for some worthy alderman to take the position as chairman. He looked out for an alder- manic fish. (Laughter.) He did not state this as a fact, but he had heard it. If there was anything in it those to whom it applied would feel it. (Hear, bear). Alderman Bottoms: Did he take the fish with him? Councillor PIHRPOINT : I am going to tell you that he did not get the fish. Alderman Hammon ; What kind of a fish as it? . w_

Councillor PIBRPOINT Aldermanic. If Councillor Dakin had succeeded in catching this particular worthy alderman, and had induced him to join the committee, there is no doubt he would have been a great acquisi- tion, but I was at a loss, and I said "Who is the mm- bar of the Markets Committee who is going to re- tire in favour of the alderman coming .in P " I did not know. Perhaps Councillor Dakin will tell us in his reply. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS: You said at the last Coun- cil meeting that you would never serve on the committee again. Councillor FLBACI/id: You would not sit for a thousand a year. (Laughter). ' COURCHIOE PIERPOINT (continuing) said that after Councillor Dakin returned from his journey to the alder- man some of the members suggested that one or two members of the Council, who were resident in the North- west Ward, should take the chairmanship, and he (Councillor Pierpoint) was still at a loss to know who would retire from the committee. He said most posi- tively that he should not do so. Fie should leave him- self in the hands of the Council, and they should deter- mine whether he had been treated fairly or not. He entertained not the slightest animosity to any mem- ber of the committee—neither to Mr. Dakin nor anyone else.

During a short discussion that followed Councillor PIWRPOINT said that he had met Councillor Dakin in the Market-place as he was on, his way to Mr. Dakin's shop to buy some cheese, and when he said "Good morning Councillor Dakinturned his head another way and would not look at him. Continuing, Cceincillor Pierpoint said he was determined to remain a member of the commit- tee, and he felt insulted because Mr. Blackhurst had been allowed to take his plane on the sub-com- mittee. _ _
Councillor BOLTON then proposed and Councillor Boum seconded, that the minute referred to be sent back to the committee.

Councillor SH&W GREEN said that Mr. Pierpoint's letter did not state whether he retired as a lumber of the committee, but it said that he would not continue to act on the committee. He took it that it was his determina- tion to remain a passive member. They must have an active member of the sub-committee, as it would never do to elect one who had determined to do nothing at all; and, therefore, they thought it right to elect a member who would do the work required. . _ .

Councillor BLACILEURST said that if it was he wish of the Council that Mr. Pierpoint should bs elected he ha,d not the slightest objection to give way to him, as he had never sought the position himself. He was asked to serve, and he did so in the belief that, as Mr. Piefpoint told them, he would not serve himself. -

Alderman BURGESS said it appeared to him that the 1 matter required a little consideration at home; and if 1 Mr. Pierpoint would allow him to make a suggestion,. and he did so in all fairness, and with a desire to promote, harmony, it was that he would go home and take his wife into counsel, and they would arrive at a successful conclusion. (Laughter.) Councillor H. ROBERTS : The Markets Committee made a serious mistake when they were in the dilemma to which reference has been made with regard to the ap- pointment of a chairman. There was a member of the Committee of wide experience and in- telligence, and also a member of the Council, who would have been willing to have occupied the post. The committee made a very great blunder in not appointing Councillor Dixon. (Loud laughter.) The amendment was then put to the meeting, when five voted for it and 15 against. The minutes were, therefore, confirmed. Subsequently Councillor PIERPOINT informed the Council that it was his intention, had matters gone on in the ordinary way, to have publicly, through the Mayor, retired from the committee; but he had been so trifled with he would not make way for anyone else. Councillor DAMN said that when he was asked to be- come chairman he refused. He had no wish at all to be chairman, and it was only when he had been urged on both sides to take the chair, and that ' he learned it was the Council's wish he should do so that he consented. They did not know whether Mr. Pierpoint Was a member of the committee or not; He had neveractually resigned, but it was generally held that he had done so. ' The reason why Mr. Bla.ckhdrst was appointed a. metnbcr of the sub-committee in the place of Councillor Pierpoint . _ .

was simply because the latrter was an ex-ofrio member of the committee, he having been chairman, and as they wanted an active member, and as Mr. Pieipuint said he would not come to the meeting, they appointed a suitable person in his place. The subject then dropped. GAS COMMITTRE.-A COMPLAINT. _ _ _
Alderman HOLMES proposed, and Councillor WRI6HT seconded, the adoption of the minutes or this dom-. mittee.

..... Councillor FLEMING remarked that the complaints out- side the Council Chamber with reference to impure gas were both loud and deep, and they came " from all quar- ters of the town; not within the last few days, but dur- ing the Christmas holidays. Perhaps the chairman of the committee could explain the matter. His impression was that the committee were using inferior Coal, and he believed that if they paid more for it they would be a great deal better off than they were at the present time.

Alderman HOLMES in reply, said that no complaints had been made with reference to the quality of the gas.. They had received complaints about the deficient supply, but he wished to explain that • there was a stoppage m the gas pipes in the Bank Quay district which tireven- ted a continual volume of gas passing along' and in that part of the town great complaints were made, but the stoppage had now been remedied. During the Christmas week there was a tremendous demand for gas, and the gas went away from the works as fast as it could be made; therefore, there was not a full supply in the town. They had never made so much vas at any :,par- ticular time as during two or three days in the Christmas week.
The minutes were confirmed. THE LONGFORD DEPOT AND THE PUBLIC.

In accordance with notice, Councillor DIXON proposed —"That the resolution of this Council of the 3rd of Juno, 1884, which was as follows. :---‘ That no person other than a member of the Town Council be allowed to visit the depot at Longford, without the permission of the chairman of the committee '—be rescinded, and to substitute the following :—‘ That any member of this Council may take a friend at any reasonable time to visit either the Longford or Intercepting Depots., and may give an order for the admission of any ratepayer to visit the same during working ,hours." During the past rear, he said, many complaints had ;leen made regard- ing the depot. A great number of people wished to see tho depot, and that was the reason he proposed his reso- lution.

Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT seconded the motion. He thought any member of the Council should be at liberty to take a friend whenever he thought fit. There was nothing very secret about the place, and nothing that they might be afraid would be run away with. Why object to a member taking a friend? Councillor PERCIVAL supported the resolution. He thought that ratepayers should have as much right to visit the place as members of the Council had. Councillor JOLLEY thought that the proposition went too far. There was nothing improper in a Councillor being able to take a friend during the day time, but he thought it would be unueccessary for anyone to go at night. It would interfere with the work, and do no good to the ratepayers. Alderman PICIMERE agreed with Mr. Jolley, but he did not see how any member of the Council could induce a friend to visit the works; he thought people 'would rather remain away. He couldtagree with the first part of the motion, but should object to a Councillor giving an order to any number of ratepayers to interfere with the working of the place.. _

Councillor BOLTON said he should like to know why the ratepayers should be debarred from ' seeing what they could so frequently smell? (Laughter.) Councillor BARKER intimated that he was prepared to support the first part; but not the latter, of the resolu- tion. .„. ,

Alderman Buttaass asked the Council to refuse to pass the motion. As far as the intercepting depots were con- periled, the public had never been preventedzoing there, and if more of tha public wctuld go there _would be, less said that did not contain the whole truth and suggested a good deal that was not true. Every member of the Council could go to the Longford deppt when he liked, but he intended to resist, on behalf of the Committee, the addition that a Councillor should take a friend. They believed it wa.4 not possible to induce a friend to go, and the person who would go would be an enemy. The people that Mr. Paoli would take would be the people who would be prepared to make the public be- lieve that the machinery was gool for nothing. They would go there for nothing in the world else.
• Coun'cillor Winsurr said that he should be loyal to the committee. They woresati-saed that the best interests of The Council would not b.: served by adopting the mo- tion. •

Councillor GRESNING said he should vote aguinst the resolution, because he believed that the proper course was now being adopted. If the public could go to the depot at any time, it would interfere with the proper carrying on of the work. Councillor BARSIIR : How is it I received a letter from the Town Clerk forbidding me to take a friend through the intercepting depots? Alderman &mows, : I did not know you had had such a letter.

Councillor H. Roberts said that they need only try to realise how the resolution would apply to the gas works to see the difficulty which would arise in this case. Any member of the Council could go to Longford whenever ke thought fit, and up to the present no member who had asked for an order for a friend had been refused. Practically, if a member wished to take a friend with a right and proper motive there was no difficulty. He thought that if the names and objects of persons could not be disclosed, such persons should be kept out of the depot. . .
after a little further discussion, the motion was put to the meeting and negatived, only three members Councillors J. Pierpoint, Dixon, and Percival—voting for it. This was all the business.

cock, W. Stubbs, J. Gayter, E. Andrews' W. Hughes, W. H. Broady, G. Wainwright, J. Clarke, andW. Faulk- ner,Jorwards. Oldham: 4. Fullalove, back; A. Greaves, Eteourt, and W. Johnson, threequarter backs; J. R. Mills, and G. F. Iforden, half backs; J. Armstron,g (captain), J. It. Ripley, E. Wood, P. Ingham, W. Leos, J. H. Mallalieu, F." Mayer, E. Blornley, and Acton (sub.) forwards.

WARRINGTON (" A " Team) v. LITILERLAND This fixture was brought off on Saturday on the ground of the Litherland Club, Seaforth, near Liverpool, in fine weather, and before a goqd number of spectators. The " A " team • were not very strongly represented, being without the services of such players as Appleton, Cra- ghan, Molyneux. and Adamson, although able substi- tutes were found in Lloyd, Bate, 'Holland, and Nield, J. Warburton taking the vacant position at three-quarter. Having in view, the reputation of the visitors, the home club had got together 'their strongest team. The home captain kicked off at 3-30 p.m, against the wind, Antro- bu.s making a good return, and Donoghue following up prevented a return being made. T. Larkia got nicely away, and passed to Whalon, this player making a good run, being brougkt down by Samson. The home forwards, who were a heavy lot, went away with great dash, tak- ing play to the Warrington 25. Warburton relieved with a kick, and Bate sent the ball into touch. M. Larkin next passed to Quigg, who kicked to Bate, this player, making his mark, and Holland, following up, collared Ives before he Could part with the ball. Play raged in the home quarters, when T. Larkin , passed to Quigg, who put in a good kick, Warburton returning well, the , ball going dead. Holmee dropped out, Antrobus carry- ing the ball into touch. The home forward's, headed by Murphy, Singleton, and Roberts, dribbled to the War- rington quarter-flag, J. Warburton saving well. Sanson got the ball away by a splendid kick to the home full beck, who returned, Antrobile being pushed into touch by Ives. The home forwards next broke .away and dribbled over the line, Jolley touching down. Jolley ' dropped out, and Jonas and Eyes dribbled well into the I helm half. Isherwood,- took play' to the line, where Whittle got possession and passed to Evans, this plaler making a splendid bid for goal, the ball going just under the cros-bar. Warburton retuthed the drop-out to centre. Neat passing between Larkin, Qtfigg, and Whalon took operations to the' Warrington 25, but Sanson responded by a beautiful kick, Jore returning into touch in midfield. Good passing between the home backs was witnessed, 'but Warburton neutralised their efforts by charging down Ives' kick. The Warringtonians now pulled themselves together, and rushed the ball over the line, Whittle gain- ing a meritorious try. Jolley took the place kick, but failed to notch the premier poiht: Holmes re-started, the ball going in touch. Quigg next tried to get away, but he was stopped by Whittle, and Sanson put in a long , kick, the ball going dead. Quigg dropped out, Antrobus I returnine• well, Jore 'saving by touching down. Splen- did passing between Whittle, Evans, and Sensor', re- sulted in another minor for the visitors. From the drop- out kicks were exchanged between Evans, Ives, and , Warburton, play settling dowa in the home territory. ' Whittle next passed across the scrimmage to Antrobus, who almost got over, being brought down by Ives. The home team were again forced to touch down, and on call of half-time the score stood—Warrington 1 try and 5 minor points, to Litherland 1 minor point. The second half developed into a rather rough game, and was not, therefore, near so interesting as the first half. Whittle restarted for Warrington, Jones kicking to Woods, ,this player being held by Lloyd. From a liee-out, Quigg kicked to the visitors full back, who failed to return, and play rested near the line, Jolley saving by touching down. Jolley dropped out, the ball going into touch'. Thornley, Lloyd, and Donohue next showed up with a dribble, but T. Larkin, by a nice kiek, transferred play to the Warrington line, another minor 'accruing to the home team. Soon after the drop-out, Whalon got nicely away and passed to Holmes, who grounded the ball oYer the line. This point was disputed, owing to the ball having apparently been passed forward, but the referee (Mr. Wilcocks) allowed the point—no goal resulting from tho place kick. The visiting forwards now broke away with a dribble, Ives returning into touch. Whalon next got possession and put in a fine run, being brought down near the line. The Warrington forwards worked the ball to centre, where Whittle got hold and put in a short run and kick, Jore returning into touch. Time was now called the score standing—Warrington I try and 5 minors; Litherland I try and 4 minors. 'Teams; —Warlington Full back, Jolley three-quarter backs, Samson, Evans, and J. Warburton; half backs, Whittle (captain) and Antrobus ; forwards, Eyes, Jones, Thorn- ley. Donohue. Bate Lloyd, Holland, Isherwood, and Neildt,

STOCKTON HEATH V. SUNLIGHT RANGRRS.—This match was played on the grotind elf the former before a goodly number of spectators, and after a fast; *'mine resulted in a win for the heme team by 1 try and 3 minors to nil. For the home team Hughes, Daly, Quinn, Riley, and C. Hughes in the forwards played a good game, whilst Sam- mon and Baldwin were the pick of the backs. WYCLIFFE V. PENKETH (IST TRAMS).—Theretlllllmatch between these teams took place at Penketh on Saturday, the game resulting in a win for Wycliffe by one try and 2 minors to nil. Arthur Jones scored the try. The score does not fairly indicate the state of the play, as the home team had to act on the defensive the greater part of the time. Several of the Wycliffe players, too, notably J.. Knowles and H. Hayes had hard lines in not scoring. Arthur Jones played a good back, and J. Knowles a good forward game. Ruecoaat FREE WANDERERS (IST TEAM) V. RUNCORN RANGERS ("A" TEAM.)—This match was played at Run- corn on Saturday, when Nevitt, the home captain, kicked off for the home team. The ball was well re- turned to the home quarters, when A. Horton gained a splendid try. Hough took the place kick, but no goal resulted. On resuming play, Horton made a splendid run down the field, and gained another try, but no goal resulted. On restarting, the ball was played out until John Molyneux gained another try, which brought time, with the score—Wanderers, .3 tries 5 minors to nil. ST. JOHN'S, RAVENHEAD (2ND) V. SUNLIGHT ROVERS, WARRINGTON.—This match was played 9/1 the St. John's ground, at Grange Park, St. Helens, and resulted in a draw in favour of the home team by three minors to one. Winstanley, the home team skipper, kicked off, and a feeble return being made, theftrst pack was formed n the visitors' half. Foulkes showed up with a short run, and passed to "Nipper," who made a little further ; headway, and then kicked: Massey replied with a run, ' and kicked to half-way, and smartly following up pre- vented a return. Several scrimmages ensued, the visi- tors gaining ground. Foulkes passed to "Nipper," who handed over to Critchley, that player making the best run of the game, starting from near his own goal, and handing off half-a-dozen of his opponents in grand style,. and only being brought down when within a few yards of the visitors' line. From the ensuing pack the visitors were forced to save. Facing about, both teams strove hard te score, especially the forwards. Kilroy, Garrity, and blassey made several nice runs for the visitors, which were respectively neutralised by Critchley, " Nip- per," Foulkes,' and "Sparrow." The Rovers scored a minor and the home team two minors in this half, and 'when the whistle blew, a pleasant and evenly oonteeted game ended as stated. SUTTON RECREATION V. WARRINGTON ROVERS (Ist Teams).—This match was played at Sutton on Saturday, but owing to the late arrival of 'the visitors, who had 14 men, a short game of fifteen minutes each way was played. The Recs, were without the services of Bicker- staffe, Birchall, McKennon, Rigby, Owen, Ralphson, and Wilde, and klayed a man short, but they managed to beat the " wirepullers " by one goal, one try, and three minors to one minor. Immediately, after the kick-off Murphy got possession, and nimbly eluding his oppo- nents, grounded the ball between the uprights. Fowles landing an easy oal. On turning round J. Johnson dribbled the ball over the line and scored the second try for theßecs. Fowles again took the place kick, and made a splendid attempt at goal, the hall striking the posts. Nothing further but minors were scored, and at the call of time the Recs. were declared the winners. D. Johnson, J. Atkinson, and T. Evans were in grand form. Teams :—Sutton Recreation: Quillin, back; Watkin- son, A. Johnson, T. Fowles, three-quarter backs; E. Murphy, T. Barton, half backs; D. Johnson, J. Atkinson, T. Evans, John Johnson, W. Lathom, S. Saxon, and P.) Dale, forwards. Warrington 'Rovers Welsby, back; Glover, Nome, Dixon, three-quarter backs; Sutcliffe, Ansell; half back Lee, Stacey, W. Evans, Green, Owen, Bate, Hardy, Milner, forwards: Referee, Mr. J. Itythian, Sutton Fdotball Club. _

Wimies V. EncLEs.— layed at Widnes on Saturday. A g,aMe of two 35's was decided on, and Worthington kicked off at ten minutes past three. Widnes returned the ball, and dashing runs by Plumpton and Farrel com- pelled the visitors to save. Widnes still continued to have the upper hand, and having added- another minor the ball was scrimmaged near the visitors' lines, kicked over, and Parkinson rushed in and obtained a try be- neath the pots. Farrell took the place, and the ball, hit .the bar. Subsequently Widnes had repeated hard lines, and at half-time the score was Widnes 1 try and 6 minors to nil. Smith re-Started, and again the home team showed their superiority. ' After fine play in the Eccles territory, Woods, Penning'-von; and Hughes carried the ball over the line, and Eccles were forced to save. Sub. sequently the visitors played with more dash, and at last succeeded in scoring a dead ball. This advantage, however, was only for a moment. Tough play S followed in the Eccles' quarters, Widnes adding two more minors in fine style; and at the close the home team wore vic- torious by a try and nine minors to one minor point. Plumoton, Parkieson, Farrell, 'liughes, Kiddie, Smith and Bingham played well for Widnes. Teams :—Widnes S. Bingham, back; Plumpton, Parkinson, and Barker, three-quarter backs; Farrell and Wilkinson, half-backs; Smith (captain), Hughe.s, Kiddie, J. Bingham, Gandy, Woods, Pennington, Bather, and Sampson, forwards. .Eccles.: Foote, back: Daley, Chambers, and H. Wood- -head, three-quarter backs ' • Halsall and Drury, half- backs ; Worthington (captain), Edwards, Lithgoe, Tay- lor, Woodhead, Blackley, Shaw, Nunn, and Pickup, forwards.

Rusreolis v. OLDHAM.—The first meeting of the above clubs was brought off at Rsincorn on Saturday, the Cheshire men winning by one. goal, one try, and five minors, tp one minor. Both teams were weak. Oldham lion the spin, W. Hughes giving the initial motion to the ball, and at the outset it was patent that the visiting forwards were overmatched, a dead ball being noted after some scrimmaging within the Oldham 25. After the drop out, Armstrong led his forwards in a grind rush, which was only stayed when the leather had reached the home lines. Stubbs relieved, matters being further improved by Cawley with a short run, but Arm- strong, Lees, and Wood regained some of thp lost ground. Further improvement in the visitors', position was occasioned by a Auncorn forward kicking the ball into the hands of Escourt, who, after a short run, passed to Greaves, H. Hughes bringing the latter down at the home 25. Stubbs and W. Hughes, however, came through the scrimmage and dribbled well up die field. From the Oldham 25 Speakman was nearly bringing off a drep, Fullalove running the ball out grandly. Runcorn still had the advantage, and after some fast play the ball went into touch near the Oldham 25 fla„a. Before the visitors could get up, Speakman bounded the ball into play and ran over and grounded, this manceuvre taking the Oldhamites by surprise. W. Hughes failed at the diffi- cultplace. There was nothing iurther of a substantial na- ture noted up to half-time, Runcorn crossing over with a try and three minors to their credit. Won after resum- ing, T. Davies was Conspicuous with a good dribble, and from the Oldham 25 the home forwards rushed the ball liver the line, but only a touchdown wed the result. Nice passing by the Runcorn backs was replied to by Holden and °reeves with good runs, the former being well tacked by Woods. The Runcorn captain relieved his lines by a fine dribble, and after a short period of even play -Armstrono• came through a scrimmage and dribbled up the fieldf and, aided by his fellow forwards, reached the Runcorn 25 mark. Woods mulled, and, Greaves rushing up, dribbled oVer the line, the home full back bringing him down when it try seemed certain, Wainwright kicking the ball dead. The drop-out trans- ferred play to the Oldham 25, whence Speakman effected a clever run and planted the leather behind the posts, Woods kicking a goal from an easy place. Another dead ball to Runcorn was all that was scored up to timelbeing called. Teams: Runcorn: T. Woods, back; H. Cawley, Speakman, and T. Davies, threequarter backs • 11. Hughes (captain), and W. Riley, half backs; F Han.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. RUGBY.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. RUGBY.

The famous Midland organisation visited Warrington for the first time on Saturday. The visitor's came with a strong team and a good repntation,-and quite 4,000 speetators assembled on the Wilderspool enclosure to witness the encounter. -The home team mustered its full strength, Massey making his reapre-3aranee• in-the team after an absence of ten weeks. A hearty reception was accorded each team, and the cheers were renewed again and again when Massey entered the arena. Splendid weather prevailed, and two thirty-fives hav- ing been agreed on, Frank Turner started- the game, Swire returningto Jolley' who as promptly replied to the Rugby quarter flag. F. Stannard held Barnes, after the Warrington skipper had put in some tricky evork, and a run by Edmonds found the game in neutral territory. Nevins, by a huge .kick, was the cause of the Midland men beating a retreat, and Jolley threatened dartg,ee by a strong run to the Rugby lines, The Warrington Men lacked combination during, the first few Minutes of the game, and failed to take opportunities that preeented • themselves, but when the play had settled, the game as chiefly confined to the Ruby quarter, the Warringto- nians , working in machine-like fashion. From • a pack close to the Rugby line,Warren passed smartly to Barnes, who put in a useful run and transferred to Massey, the latter being pushed into touch close tieehe line. Loose play followed, and Rugby were forced to save, but from the drop out the Rugby goal was in, jeopardy. Jolley put in a useful kick to the Rugby quarter flag, and after some give-and-take play, the wirepullere " dribbled over the line, Povey grounding. Barnes took the place, but failed after a good attempt. Mason re-started, play resting at neutral ground. From a pack at mid-field, the', home forwards dribbled with smartness, and forced the game on the Rugby line. Warren ran round the scrim- mage, but Richardson was on the alert. Mason relieved the pressure to half way, but a rush, headed by Dillon, Ashton, and .Littlewood, ended in the latter scoring. Speakman essayed the kick at goal, but 'failed- to noteli the premier point. Exchange kicking soon after the re- commencement was 'witnessed, Nevins, Barnes, and Swim being repeatedly applauded. Hopewell put in a huge kick from a' return by- 13arnes' and a kick by Ed, monds over the line scored the first minor for Ibigby. Franle Turner dropped out, and again some tall kicking, by the opposing backs, Nevins and Hopewell, called forth cheers. This pretty play was supplemented ,by, a grand dribble, in which the brothers Turner were prominent. From a pack formed on the line, passing by Speak- man, Warren, Barnes, and Massey ended •in the latter dropping at goal, the half only missing its des- tination by a few inches. Jolley replied to the drop out; and was the means of carrying the pine to the Ruelty 25. Barnes effected-one of his tricky runs, and almost got in. Individual efforts were made by Massey, Jolley, and Davies to add to the score, and the much-coveted goal was nearly scored from a free kick awarded Barnes, the Place being taken 'bv Fair. Turner. Massey Was to the fore by a, smart run to the Rugby fines, but from a dribble headed by . Ashton and Frank Turner Randlei got over, the kick at goal again failing. F.Stannard re-commenced, and Massey again forced the visitors back on their lines, but no addition was made to the score from new to the call of half time, when War- rington were in the majority by three tries and three minors to one minor. Rugby re-started, Barnes return- ing in fine style. Littlewood, by a smart kick, invaded ' the Rugby quarters, and. Fair. Turner made a grand effort to score. Loose play relieved the pressure,, but the superior combination of the Warringtouians again forced the Rugby men to act on the defensive. Jolleyput 1 in some grand work, and forced Hopewell to save on , several occasions. The drop out gave a little relief tol the visitors, but what chance they had of scoring was mulled, and the advantage gained was neutralised by Jolley running the leather back to the visitors' lines. Hopewell replied to a kick by Barnes, but: Jolley again got in a grand kick to Hopewell, and from the succeed- ing pack Fair. Turner scored- the fourth try close to touch in goal. The place was taken by the same player, and he landed a goal amidst ringing cheers. The game was re-started from centre, and Edmonds was awarded a free kick for off-side play, but it availed his side little, Ashton, charging it-down, Jolley now made off, and forced another minor. The visitors were forced to adopt' these tactics several tithes in quick succession, and, after some give-and-take play, Speakman almost got in after a good run. Warren looked like scoring after a fine run; but the defence of the visitors was too good to allow of any more liberties to be taken, and only minors ,were scored. In the end Warring retired victors of a pleasant genie by one goal, three tries, nine minors, to Rugby two minors. . •

The Warrington team were certainly not seen at their beat during the first few minutes of the game, and missed several chances. However, as the game pro- ceeded, they showed grand combination, the dribbling of the forwards Using perfection. If ,special praise must be awarded, W. Dillon, Povey, Littlewood, Ashton, and Fair. Turner deserve it. In theback- division Speakman and Warren never tired, and showed all their old fire and dash. The play of the trio of three-quarters is too well known to call for comment, and to single but any one of them would be an injustice. Nevins was particularly safe at full back, and it may, be safely, said that he is the right man in the right place. Of. tha Rugby team, Hopewell, Swire, Mason, Moulds, and Hillier were the pick.

The following were the teams :—Watrington : Full back, W. Nevins ; three-quarter baeks, J. Jolley, T. Barnes (captain), and J. T. Massey; half backs, J. E. Warren and W. Speakman ; forwards, 11. Ashton, Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, T. Davies, W. Hayes' W. Dillon, W. Povey, R. Littlewood, ,and W. Ra.ndles. Rugby: Full back, Hcipewell ; three-quarter backs, Edmonds, F. Stan- nard, and Swire ; half backs, Mason (captain) aLd Richardson; forwards, Moulds,'Cowley, Flllller,Clements, Phillips, Ivan, Lee, H. Stannard, and Coekerill. Re,ee, Mr. Vickers, Salford F.C. •

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The first visit of the Rugby team to IVarrington7drew a large crowd of spectators to the Wilderspool ground, on Saturday. A good game was expected and in this the specta tors were not disappointed, though the home team showed a superiority throughout the game that had been scarcely anticipated. This was certainly altogether due to better play and not to any physical advantages for the visitors were very aptly described as a " lot •of giants." The two centre three-quarters, in particular, were a, masked contrast in point of size. but " Tommy " very dex- trously managed to keep out of reach of the long arms of his antagonist', and in fact by his quickness and -Unsel- fish passing put in some of his very finest play. . Another advantage for Warrington, which they have been without for some time, was the presence of Massey, who met with a very cordial welcome from the 'lookers- Although some of the effects of his recent injury were still to be detected in the style of his running, Massey displayed all his old pluck aud coolness and very nearly all his old quickness of movement. Speaking of the play generally it w.ould be very diffi- cult to call to call to mind a time when the Warring- tonians exhibited better all-round form than they did against Rugby. Their play was remarkably well com- bined, and each played to the others in a very fine, fash- ion. Their superiority over the Midland men was chief- ly seen in the back department, where each player showed up at his very best, but the forwards, also, more than once did some capital dribbling and passing with the feet. Dillon, Hayes, Davies and Povey -were prom- inent in this respect, betas a matter of fact all the forwards were seen at their best. The best we can wish for War- rington when they meet Wakefield Trinity to-clay is that the' may be in Rugby forrn and have Rugby weather. The meeting of the famous Preston North End club and Aston Villa in the fifth round of the English (Associa- tion) cup contest seems to have excited more interest than any football contest before it. The meeting took place on the ground of the Aston Villa club, aud it is said that the attendance of spectatoss reached the enor- mous figure of 27,000. The total receipts were £l,lOO the largest sum ever taken at a football match. In the end the game resulted in a victory for the North Enders by three goals to one, but as the spectators on more than one occasion broke into the ground it seems to be still an undecided point whether the tie will not have to be replayed. Since the above was put in type it has been stated that a telegram has been published from • the referee denying the report that he ordered the cup tie to be abandoned. ha reply to this a Birmingham paper publishes a telegram from each of the umpires stating most empha- tically that the cup tie was abandoned by the referee after a consultation with the 'umpires and the captains of both teams, who consented to a re-arrangement. Mr. M. P. Bette, one of the umpires, states that the referee stopped the cup tie under rule 21 of the Association, which required a fair field to play. Under these circum- stances the match will have to be replayed. After three succeasive defeats Ruhcorn broke through the spell of their ill-luck on Saturday, when they succeeded in vanquishing that strong Lancashire combination, Old- ham. This victory is all the more creditable, as the win- ners were trying the important experiment of substitut- ing five of the usual players-by second team men. The new men amongst the forwards played with a dash, a vigour, and a judgment that did much towards the pleasing result of the game, and if they display the same form against Salford to-day, their permanent inclusion in the first fifteen may be regarded as certain. Riley, at half back, worked hard, but his energy will have to be better directed before he is fit for the responsible posi- tion he occupied on Saturday. Doubtless a few lessons from the captain, who played a magnificent game, would make him into a valuable colleague. The shining light of the match was Speak-man, whose running, dodging, and tackling were a treat to witness, and the two tries he scored were obtained after very meritorious pla3. • i Although only half the season s aver the victorious career of Widnes has already borne fruit. On Tuesday night the first and second teams-and a number of friends were feasted at the Central Hotel, the cost being borne conjointly by the committee of the club and Mr. A. Parkes, the landlord. Full justice was done to the sumptous repast provided, and after the clearing of the cloth Dr. Richards, an enthusiastic admirer of the club, took the chair, and Mr. .1. H. Smith, the captain, the vice-chair. The customary toasts were proposed and honoured, and with the aid of music a 'pleasant evening was spent. That the exertions of the club deserved recognition, may be gathered from the following rzeord. Since the season opened the first team have played 20 matches, of which 16 have been won, 3 lost, and 1 drawn. The total score is 18 goals, 24 tries, and 120 minors, against 7 goal, 8 tries, and 31 minors.' With Saturday's victory over Eccles, no less than 13 matches have been won in suc- cession. The second team have shown themselves equally able to uphold the honour of the town, only two games having been lost. It is to be hoped the recOrd wilDnot deteriorate before April arrives.

Two boys, aged 10 and seven years, sons of a far- - mer residing at Malkin's Bank. Cheshire, were sent to town, a mile distant, about five on Wed day afternoon, and on returning w..-re lost in t! e fog. Search was made, but the boys were not discovered until late this morning, when they were almost starved to death. The eldest lad pulled his jacket off and put it on his brother. Toth boys are in a critical condition, the eldest boy being the worst. Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at Ince on Thursday on the body of a collier named John'Johnsen,' 17. Deceased on Monday night went-. an errand for the canal lockkeeeper, but not return- ing, and _no information being fortheoTing. the canal was dragged, and the body found next morn- ing. The night was very foggy, aud apparently de-, ceased fell into the water when walking along the canal bank. Verdict accordingly. , On Thursday evening an express train from Ac- crington to Todmorden ran into a goods train which. was standing on the line near Hapton station—the - fog being very thick at the ,time—and smashed , the guard's van to fragments. The guard of the goods train, Thomas Hill, of Miles Platting, was killed, and several persons who were in the passen- ger train were injured; none of them, however. very . seriously.

div.head: DENSE FOG,--SERIOUS ACCIDENTS AND
div.p: DENSE FOG,--SERIOUS ACCIDENTS AND
LOSS OF LIFE.

The fog which has prevailed &tiring the week seems to have been general, and the result is a large number of railway and other accidents. During a dense fog, a trap belonging to Mr. Wil- liam Fisher, wholesale butcher, Drake-street, Roch- dale, collided with a , steam tram, near Rycroft Farm, Heywood, about nine a.m.,-on Tuesday. The horte was knocked down, and dragged about 20. yards. In South Wales the railway traffic was much de- layed. An accident which occurred owing to --tile fog at Aberdylais on Monday, by the colliding of gds and passenger trains, resulted in somewhat serious injnry to thebrakesinan of the goods train, and considerable damage to the rolling stock. There was a dense fog on the Mersey, on Tues- day.and a large number of ve.Seels. including six American liners, were detained off the bar. No casualties are reported. • Guernsey has been enveloped in a dense fog since Saturday evening, with a dead calm. - ‘7:. Daring the fog on Tuesday is goods train ran into and demolished a temporary bridge placed over the rail Way at Chatham Station for the accommo- tion of passengers. Another train shortly after- wards destroyed a second bridge. No person was injured. • At Birmingham two goods trains, ranning through a suburban station. came into collision, the engine: of one running into.the other as it was going over a crossing: A- large number a trucks were upset, and the contents thrown. down an embankment, and rolling stock and the ' permanent way were so seriously damaged that traffic as entirely blocked for eight hours. Th 4 guard .of the train run into. was somewhat severely injured, but the other guard and drivers and firemen escaped with- out injury. A fog, the duration of which has not been equalled there for several years, prevailed ,over Bolton on Tuesday. At Trinity-street Station of the Lanca- shire and Yorkshire Railway, about 7 pan, on -Monday, a man named Jamea 'Greenwood, a marble sculptor, Who was on his way te his home at Man- chester, was endeavouring to reach the train, when he missed his footing, through tha fog, and fell upon the metals. He was immediately caught by an in-Coming train, and run over, receiving terrible injuries, his right arm being literally torn from his shoulder. The poor fellow was conveyed to the Bolton Infirmary. There was no improvement in the condition of the atmosphere on Thursday morning. A dense canopy of fog Overhung the district, and traffic of all descriptions was carried on With considerable danger. Quite a cannunade of fog signals was kept up in the vicinity of the railway stations. On Wednesday evening, in coming across Swin- ton Park, near Manchester, a woman walked into a pit, and a man, in attempting to rescue her, was also drawn- into the water. Fortunately both escaped. During.the dense fog, on Wednesday evening, in Accrington, a steam tramcar Iran into a shilibier near Haslingden: One horse was injured, and the shilibier was badly broken; fortunately, the vehicle was empty. The fog still thickly envelopes Northampton, and there is great interruptiOn to afl kinds of traffic. Trains are greatly delayed.. In South Yorkshire, on Thursday morning, large numbers of colliers, who have to walk considerable distances, could not get to work owing to the fog, consequently many pits are working with consider- ably less hands. A similar state of things has pre-7 veiled for three mornings past, causing colliery owners to suffer great losses. The navigation ot the English Channel is seriously impeded. The South-Eastern Company's cargo boat. which left Folkestone on Wednesday morning in the fog, had not reached Boulogne on Thursday morning. A chief boatman of the coastguard, named.. Dare, on Wednesday fell over thq cliff at Babbicombe in the fog, and was killed. Abraham Collier, seaman, of the Whitstable vessel Onyx, walked into the water during the fog while returning to his ship at Rochester, on Wednesday night. He was drowned.' The steamship Birnado and the barque America wew in collision off Sandgate during the fog On Thatsday morning. The America was badly in- jured. , The Liverpool police have received an intimation that during the.fog on Wednesday afternoon ,E 1 of the lads of the.,reformatoty ship Akbar seized a boat and escaped. Two of them were concerned iii previous events. _ .
- During a dense fog in the Bristol Channel, on Wednesday night, the Cardiff pilot boat Lyn was run down by a steamer. The crew werp saved.

div.p: :NEW BOOKS, &c.

What is .popularly known as "Young's Practical ' Arithmetle,' prepared by Mr: Samuel Young, and . published by Mr. John Heywood, of Manchester, has deservedly reached a second edition. It is deacribed as "a system of practical arithmetic adapted to the . use of schools, containing the fundamental rules,' and their application to mercantile, cotton-spin- ning, manufacturing, and mechanical calculations." It comprises "numerous rules and ex Amples in the various departments of cotton-spinning, mechanics, &c., useful to cotton-spinners, Wheelwrights, en-- gineers, and artizans in general." It is a matter - of course to say that the new edition is an im- - provement on the original issue. The boy, or marl,. who masters it may be said to be a practical' arithemetician, for nothing in the way of calcula- tion will come wrong to him. We strongly recom- mend the work for general use, and as a text book for schools. . Mr. James Croston, F.S.A., is to be complimented on the completion of the first volume of the new issue of Baines's History of Lancaster, which he is editing, and which is being published in monthly shilling parts by- Mr. John Heywood. Title and index with part fourteen: complete the first volume. The greatest care seems to have been taken to rectify errors and to bring the record down to date. It will be seen how much' is due to Mr. Croston when it is stated that more than one-third is really new matter. A beautiful engraved portrait of Mr. E. Baines accompanies the firstvolume. Perhaps Mr. Cros- ton will favour his ' admiring readers by letting them have his own portrait in the next volume. The publisher supplies- a handsome cover for binding, price 2s. 6d. Part one of the second volume deals with 11Ianchester Parish as part of the Hundred, of Salford. Plans are given of Manchester as known to the Romans; and there is quite . a wealth of illustrations of the 'numerous finds, not omitting the Roman coins found in Manchester. A view is given of " Woden's Cave of Orsdall as it existed in the last century ; " and the, part alio furnishes the des- cent of the Barons'of Manchester!

"The Westminster Review" for January, holds its place as the leader of advan'ced. thought in politics. The paper entitled "Dr: 'Johnson on li•eland " is all too brief —it is so re,adable.- Johnson,--though an old-fashioned 'gory, was a hater of oppression., How characteristic of lum to say--L" Let the authority 'of the English Govern- ment perish rather than be maintained by iniquity. Bet- ter to hang or drown people at once than by unrelenting persecution to beggar and starve then!' The writer of the article on "Count Cavour " does full justice to that eminent Italian statesman without taking sides : he carries the reader with him—picturing Cavour, diplo- matist though he was, as fired with a holy zeal for the freedom of Italy. Other papers are on "Free Trade in Banking," "Adulteration of Food and the Remedy," " Manxland." "Seven Weeks in Anstra-: ha,""A reply to Dr. Ingham by the Right Hon. W. E. -Gladstone,- M.P." ; while in the Independent Section we have "The Pisheries Question; •an American View of it." There is, beside; the usual 'review of Contemporary Literature and of Home Affairs, ," Scribner's Magazine "leads off with an exhaustive and profusely illustrated article on "The Man at Arms." It is a- historyin brief of the mail-clad warrior. "The Great Pyramid," -by Mr. E. L. Wilson, contains a large amount of information presented in an attractive form, and there is a series of • pictures and photographs of a striking and realistic kind. The reader who studies this article will, feel that he has "done the Pyiamids." Mr. H. C.' Runner contributes the first part of the story of "Natural Selection—a Romance. of: Chelsea Village and East Hampton Town "-; and there is an article on "Japanese Art, Artists, and 'Artisan:" with illustrations from drawings by a Japanese artist. Mr. B. L. Steven- son-furnishes "A Chapter on Dreams," wiitten in his usual vivid style; and there is excellent verse by Mr. T. B. Aldrick, Andrew Lang, and 'other well-known 'Writers.

" Whittaker's Almanac" is to hand, and it is larger and better than ever. The earlier portions, which form the popular (shilling) edition, live been somewhat ex- tended', and..everything has, of course . been re-rimed-and brought, down to date. The inforniAlon is fuller than hitherto, arid the lists of official's connected with :different branches of the public service . have been con- siderably extended. . In the .supplementary portion of the bound Almanack, the Colonial and Foreign section has been enlarged, and a variety of useful o additions the ns havels Iden introduced, including a corriPh Consu- lar Service. Papers on the Military and Naval "Medals, Ger/inn Trade and German Competition, Mag,aneßifies and British Small Aims, Shipbuilding, FA.lucational Pio- gr,lss, Chronological History of Astronomy, and many shorter articles, including a. sketch of the Fcrth Bridge, are amongst those given for the first time. The County and Municipal Directory, Citizen's Diary and other well- known features, are continued as hitherto, making the .AlManac the most complete Of its kind. • .Cassell's Magazine of Art for January, is a particularly strong number. ,• An article of -especial interest to.War- rington readers (since the author is &Warrington Man) is Mr. E. F Brewtnall's paper witlrtho title of !`,.lslotes by an. artist 'living in The country.'" It is illustrated-from Mr. Brewtnall's Own drawings, and is charming alike as to text andillustration. He has a:genuine love of nature, and, a genius for expression which is made Manifest .1.-)y pen as well as pencil. The frontispiece for this num- ber is a powerful etching of Mr. J. W. Waterhouse's fine painting of " Mariamne." Amongst the illustrated articles we have "The Black Arts—a Reverie in the Strand," "The 'Portraits of 'Napoleon the First," "Louis gas- tour," "Gerard Terberg, ' and "Art in Christmas Decora- tion."

"The Woman's • edited by Mr. Oscar Wilde, keeps its promise of good things. This month the frontis- piece is a full page illu,stration of the Princess Of Wales in her academic robes 'as a doctor of music. Hers is a face which is always pleasing, despite its lack of expres- sion., "Historic Women" is the title of a blank.verse poem of some length and no small merit:by- Lady Wilde. Lady Constance Howard contributes a _paper on Kirby Hall, he home of Sir Christopher Hatton. It is illus- trated by Mr. Herbert Milton, who is unrivalled in work of this class ; he.catches the spirit as well as the form of ancient mansions, Stc. Amongst other articles we may name " Medicine as a Profession for Women," "-The Truth about Clement Ker," "Greek Plays at the Univer- sities." and one on "The Author of John Halifax, Gentle- man," which is illustrated, and graced by a beautiful portrait,.

Cassell's Magazine :for January is in no Wise lacking. The frontispiece, " Anembne, illustrates a graceful triolet ' Mr: G. Weatherby; the' 'Family Doctor has something of Moment to say to those Who are getting bald.; . and there is an interesting illustrated paper on "The Capital of Oyster Land." Then we'haye "The Garden in January," "What to Wear," "The Gatherer," with a full supply of finished and unfinished stories. "The Quiver" is also strong. in tales which are admira- bly illustrated. The Rev. Dr. Hitchens writes on ‘.` Bible TM.des," the Bishop of Gibraltar on "The Presence of God in Holy Places," and the Dean, of. Canterbury con-, tributes his third paper on "How God Preserved the New Testament." "Christmas Eve in Montreal" (illus- trated), is excellent in its way; and there are the cus- tomary scripturo lessons, short arrows, Sze. "Little Folks "for. the new year is'the first part of a new and en- larged series. There is no sign with the increase in quan- tity a any falling off in quality, so the juvenile readers will be delighted.. The coloured' frontispiece; with . the title of "Gee-up," is as pretty as it is homely. ' We have also to hand from Messrs. Cassell the,current issuos, of the Encyclopaedic , -Dictionary, Illustrated Shakespeare, Dictionary of ' English History, Life and Times of Queen- Victoria,- the Sea, and Familiar Wild Flowers.

Dressmakers. can buy no better sowing cotton than Bagley and Wright's. which for strength is unequalled.—Ackt. . Two. brothers married sisters, and lived in the same house, and in course of time a girl was born to each of.' them, making six in the family. But some wag declared there were sixteen of them, and being asked-to name them, he wrote them down thus :—"Two fathers, two mothers, two brothers, two sisters, two uncles, two aunts, two nieces, and two cousins—making sixteen in all." TifE WELSH TITJIES AGITATION.--On Tuesday, Messrs. Peterson and Todd, solicitors to the Clergy Defence Asso- ciation, accompanied by, two appraisers, visited a number of farmers under distraint for tithe, for the purposes of selling the hay seized. They were escorted by a strong body of the I.th Hussars, and also by 60 policemen and a number of special cOnstables, with semi-military uni- form. The appearance of the military caus,d the great- est excitement. we farms were visited, and in each case the hay was purchased either ,by the tenant or his friends. There was no disturbance. .

' THE LATE CAPTAIN REYNOLDS, J.P. . • PRESENTATION TO MRS. REYNOLDS. . Mrs: Reynolds, widow of the .late Captain •Syle vanes Reynolds. JP., of 'Redden Court, Latchford, . Was on Monday afternoon presented with a hand- some marble bust of her late husband, by a depute,- tien whci undertook that duty on behalf of the 2.500 persons who had given subscriptions, in order _ to evince their regard for the deceased gentleman. The project for providing the blast was set on foot some time before the -lamentable accident Occurred that terminated in the loss of the captain's life, and, It was intended, a course, that it should be pre-' aented to him. A commission was given to the late Mr. Warrington Wood, the eminent sailptor,' who' himself died unexpectedly before' the but was 1_ quite completed, and this sad event preeente(l its 'being ready for' presentaticin as soon as was ex- pected.. After the death Of 'Captain Reynolds, it was decided that the beet should 'be presented to MM., Reynolds, and the ceremony took place quietly on Monday afternoon, in the drawing-room at Raddon Court. The- late Captain Reynolds, who was' chair- man of the Conservative Association, was held in the greatest esteem, not only by the Conservatives • of the borough, but by all classes, and his honest ; • and straightforwarctdealings'gained him the appre- ciation of the working-men -in particular. The Bust Presentation Fund was started by his Conser- vative working-men friends, by whom most Of the - subscriptions were given, but it should be mentioned that many persons subscribed te it who hold poli- tical opinions different to those held bV,the gentle- man for whom the testimonial was intended. The -coat of the bust was 150 guineas, and with the illu- minated address and the pedestal on which the but was placed, the total cost was increased to abode, 170 guineas. The deputation which consisted of Mr. John Roberts (chairman, of the Bust Presentation Committee), Mr. Thomas Mason (hon. sec.); Mr. Alfred 'Jolley (hon. treasurer), and Mr. George Woods. met at the Conserva- tive Club, in Sankev-street, shortly before five o'clock in The afternoon, and drove thence to Ra,ddon Court. Here 'they were' received by 'Mr. W. H. Brook, a friend of the late Captain Reynoldseand conducted to the drawing- room, where • ehe marble :bust had already been con- veyed, the plaster pest, the last completed work of the late Mr. Warringtot Wood, having been placed in the morning.:room. • Mrs. Reynolds having been introduced ‘, to the deputation,. .Mr. Jonx Rowans proceeded to make the presenta- tion. He had, he said, on behalf of the- subscribers, most a whom were working men, to --present to Mrs. Reynolds abust of her late esteemed husband. The task was a pleasant one; inasmuch as the proceedings testified that the late Captain 'Reynolds was highly respected and beloved by his fellow-townsmen generaLly,no less than by his purely political friends; and it was also a sad one be- cause he foe wheel-it was'intended eves no longer with ' • them to receive it. They pow begged her to accept the bust, one of the best specimens of the sculptor's art, in his stead, trusting that whenever she looked upon' it it would serve to retnind her, were it neeessary,-of one who had earned not only the love and-respect of his wife and family, but of all with wheal during a very,active life ; he had come into contact.. The subscribers deeply sym- pathieed with Mrs. Reynolds in the great lose she- had sustained, a loss felt by the inhabitants of the town' and district generally. :He then presented the bust, and the address, which reads as follows :—" Presented to Cap- tain Reynolds, chairman of the Warrington Conservative Association, and the first chairman of the new Conserva- tive Chin. We, the Conservative workingenen of War- rington, have long desired to give 'Yee some' Substantial -- recognition of our high appreciation of your great ser- vices tel the Coneervative petty of Warrington. In 1880, , the first year of your office as Chairman of the Conser- vative Association, you 'found Lis disunited and disor- , relied, but by your intelligence, patience, tact . and indomitable courage, you rallied our party and letl us on to the mat victonesof 1885 and 1886. We mainly owe to you the erection of our splendid new Conservative Club, and, under your able and daily guidance, Censer- , Yatives of all classes find a home there for recreation and Political instruction.. To every, . loyal , Conservative in Warrington your name is a household word that Will not be forgotten. Accept then, this proof of our high esteem and regard for you and your family. Our testimonial to you is a bust of yourself in marble, the last completed work of our much esteemed and highly-talented fellow- townsman, John Warrington Weed. May this recogni- tion of your worth stimulate those who follow you' to, work as you ungrudgingly have done for the Coaserva- tive estuse in Warrington. JOHN Reimers. chairman ; THOKAS MASON, secretary; ALFRED JOLLEY, treasurer." This address, it was explained, was prepared before the death of Captain Reynolds. In concluding, Mr. Roberts asked Mrs. Reynolds to be kind enough to allow the Marble bust to be placed in Mr. Boothroyd's shop window at the Conservative CAuleto allowthopublic to inspect it, and Mrs. Reynolds consented to do so., Mr. Kum, the hon. sec. then read a letter apologising for the absence of Mr. William Atherton, and proceeded ' to explain that it Was just a year and nine months since \ the commiSsien was given to 'Mr. J. Warrington Wood, to execute the bust of Captain Reynolds in ins rble. About four weeks, afterwards Mr. Wood was stricken - down with a serious illness, and was advised by his medi- cal attendants to go to Switzerland. He did so, and hy- ing remained there a few months the doctors advised him to go to Baden-Baden to take the waters, and -when his health was restored he returned to Rome, and in the month of August he wrote saying that he was as well as could be expected,' and that in September he would come to Warrington and carry out ale work which had been given to him. In September he came to Warrington, did he told him (Mr. Mason) that the bust would be the greatest work of hie life. He said it would be a perfect work, and that it would give satisfaction, to the commit- tee ae well as to his fellow townsmen. The captain gave Mr. wood no fewer than 24 sittines • and soon after the work was sent away to be finished in marble in Rome, Mr. Wood died. After the east had gone to Rome Mr. Wood's affairs were uneettled,and the committee thought the work would never be finished, though Mr. Roberts did all in his power to hasten it on. They wrote to Mrs Wood and had the satisfaction to learn from her that the ,work which had been entrusted to her late husband was in progress, and that in a short time' it would be ready for presentation. On the Sunday morning when Captain Reynolds died, Mr. Roberts received a letter from London to say that the bust had arrived in that , city. It was a most curious fact that it arrived at the . very same hour that the late captain received the fatal gunshot wouncl. He 'deeply sympathised with Mrs Rey- nolds in the great affliction which had befallen her. Her late husband was a thorough-going gentleman, a; man of upright character, one who led a blameless life, and one who was gifted with the great attributes of a business life, endowed with great perceptivenees .of character and an earntnes9 of purpose which made him beloved and respected by all who came into contact with him. He was a man, take him for all in all, . , We shall not look, upon his like again. Mrs. REYNOLDS, who was deeply affected, briefily thanked the deputation, and on her behalf. Mr. linoox said that Mrs Reynolds desired him to say that it was . her wish, if the workingmen would accept it, to present to them a similareiust to the one they had jest presen- ted to her.—Befere the deputation withdrew, Mr. JOL- LEY said that on looking over the ,subseiiption books, he found there were about 250 subscribers at 2d; 310 at 3d; 493 at 81; and about 1,030_ at a shilling each. That Showed the good feeling and respect entertained for the late captain Reynolds.

An English tourist sought refuge in an Irish cabin in a heavy shower, and finding it about as wet inside as out, said to the owner, "Yon have quite a pond on the floor:" " Yis; shure we have a great lake in the roof," was the owner's reply. MR. J. My wife always says she knows they saved her life, and I quite think they did. She was ill for years and although we had the best of Doctors, no one seemed able to do her any real good. PROMOTION.—"MaITiage is promotion," says George Elliot. In the eyes of such a reasoner a man with his third wife would doubtless pass for a brigadier-general. A. WINTER'S TALE.—A massive intellect in Islington did not have to clean the snow from before his house last winter. He pinched his wife till she screamed, and the neighbours trod down the snow. A BREEZE.—We are willing to take a certain amount of stock in newspaper accounts of western cyclones, but when an American paper tells us about a zephyr carrying a bed-quilt sixty-one miles and then going back for the sheet, we aren't there. ' A SONATA.—Host (something of a. musician, who is entertaining a country friend at dinner); "Would you like to hear a sonata before dinner, Squire ?" The squire: "Weil, I don't mind. I had two on my way here, but I guess! can stand another.' AT tsz Cosyreriosaa's.—He (afraid she will 'order the second plate) : "Did you know they make ice-cream, of glucose, oleomargarine, cayenne pepper, and strych- nine!' She (finishing the plateful) : "No, I didn't know that, but I've noticed they are so stingy in filling their dishes that one has to eat two plates in order to get enough." POOR TERRA COTTA.—Among the visitors to a fine art exhibition were two old ladies fresh front the country, engaged in examining with great interest a statue re- presenting a young Greek, underneath which were in- scribed the words, Executed in terra-cotta." "Where is Terra Cotta?" asked the elder of the two, turning to her companion. "I haven't the least idea," replied the other; "I never heard of the place before." " Ah, well," observed the first speaker, "it doesn't much signify The poor man who was executed there is not the less to be pitied, wherever it may be." LOVE AND Harz.—" Yes," he said to his confidential friend, "I am engaged to her, and I suppose I ought to be very happy; but somehow I am worried about a former attachment of hers. There's that Jones. Who—" "Why, bless rae, you stupid fellow," exclaimed the Ifriend, "she hates him like poison !" "Yes, yes, I know," he said, "that's what troubles me. She hates him too bitterly not to have loved him once." • THE SErrrso SUN.—The intensely poetical editor of a Texas paper describes a recent gorgeous sunset in that vicinity as resembling a ripe pumpkin wrapped in the American flag." Brier SHOPICEEPERS.—An Englishman went to New York, and put up a sign "Established 1804," and rather prided himself upon the antiquity of his establishment.' The next day. his Yankee rival across the way bur- letqued his sign in this way—" Established yesterday. No old goods on hand." CRUEL DECEIVER.—" You must kiss me twice in Us; very same place, George, or I can never be your bride." "Are you certain of this, Myrtle? • Is there no appeal from this decision?" • "None whatever," answeted the girl, giving her improver a hitch to the left: Looking lovingly into Myrtle's deep blue eyes, George bent over and kissed the sunny-haired beauty on her right cheek, just aft of where a beauty-spot was crushed silently alongside her jaw. "And if! do not kiss you again we mist part for ever ?" he asked.. "Yes," replied Myrtle. "Then good evening," he said, in cold, cruet tones. "And shall I see you to-morrow evening as usual?" said she. "No," he replied, "you have unwittingly released me from my vows," and, with a hoarse, piratical laugh, he jumped over the mat and was gone. MORE HOSE.—Aunt Jane came down to visit Leicester for the first time. During a fire in her vicinity on the third night after her arrival the cry of the firemen for "More hose" aroused her from peaceful slumber, and like a philanthropist who had no waste timber in her heart, she threw out of the window all but three pairs of her best woollen stockings. As yet they have not been returned to her. Flys Sall:uses IN THE POUND.—On one occasion Lord Alvanley had promised a person £lOO as a bribe to conceal something which would have involved the repu- tatibn of a lady. On that person pplying for the money, his lordship wrote a cheque for £25, and presented it to him. " But, my lord, you promised me a hundred , pounds." "True," said his laydship. "I did so; but you know, Mr. --, that I am now making arrangements with all my creditors at ss. in the pound. Now, you must see that if I were to pay you at a higher rate than I rimy them, I should be doing try creditors an injustice ." Is HASTE.—A man was hurrying along a street the other night, when another man, also in violent haste, rushed out of an alley way, and the two collided with great force. The second man looked mad, while the polite man, taking off his hat, said, "My dear sir, I don't know which of us is to blame for this violent encounter, but I am in too great a hurry to investigate. If I ran into you, I beg your pardon; it you ran into me, don't mention it." And he tore away at redoubled speed. HITHBLE Pig.—" We are goin' to have pie for dinner," said Bobby to the schoolmaster. " Indeed!" laughed the dominie, amused at the little boy's artlessness; "and what kind of pie, Bobby ?" "It's a new kind. Ma was talking this morning about jia bringin' you to dinner so often, and pa said he didn't care what she thought, and ma said she'd make him eat humble pie before the day Was over; and I s'pose we're goin' to have it for dinner." A DOT'S WAYS —Calling a boy up in the morning can hardly be classed under the head of pastimes, especially if the boy is fond of exercise the day before ; and it is a little singular that the next hardest thing to getting a boy out of bed is getting him into it. There is rarely a mother who is a success at rousing a boy. All mothers know this, and so do their boys. And yet the mother' seems to go at it in the right way. She opens the stair- door, and insinuatingly observes, "Johnny." There is no response. " John-ny." Still no response. Then there is a short, sharp "John," followed a moment later by a prolonged and emphatic "John Henry." A grunt from the upper region signifies that an impression has been made, and the mother is encouraged to add, "You'd better be coming down here to your breakfast, young man, before I come up there and give you some- thing you'll feel." This so startles the young man, that he immediately goes to sleep again. And the operation has to be repeated several times. A father knows nothing about this trouble. He merely opens his mouth as a soda-water bottle ejects its cork, and the "John Henry" that cleaves the air of that staircase goes into that boy like electricity, and pierces the deepest recesses' of his nature. And he pops out of that bed and into his • clothes and down the stairs with a promptness that is commendable. It is rarely that a boy 'allows himself to disregard the paternal summons. About once a year is believed to be as often as is consistent with the rules of health. He saves his father a great many steps by his thoughtfulness. I

• NIAREET-GATE POST OFFICE. Sir,—Now that letters are again collected from the out- side Of the above office, I would suggest that the postal authorities should extend the hours of collection. Eight o'clock is a very early hour in the evening for the last collection, and it would be an undoubted boon to the tradespeople and public generally if the letters could be collected at the game hour as at the pillar box in Sankey- street, viz., 9-30 p.m. The time of opening this office also calls for remark. The notice in the window states that the office is opened at 8 a.m., but I should like to ask when was the last time it was so opened. I think a little investigation would be useful as a matter of HISTORY. January 10th, 1888.

div.head: TITHE _ QUESTION:
div.p: THE TITHE _ QUESTION:

Sir,—l would very much like to know if the foil -wing is true, which I copy from a contemporary of last week: —" But they must also remember .(Mr. Raikes said) that the Government brought in a bill to relieve tenants from paying tithe by placing the charge upon the landlords, but they were prevented from carrying that measure in consequence of the obstruction of the Radicals. They therefore knew whom to thank for what was taking place around them." Well, sir, if it should be as Mr. Raikes says, all I can say is, it is very damaging to Liberalism, and the reverse to Toryism. I need not tell you, sir, that with very few exceptions tithe is paid the most reluctantly of any money the farmer is compelled to pay. He would rejoice if the burden was re- moved, whether by a Liberal of a Tory Government.— Yours, &c.

EX-FARMER. [Mr. Raikes know perfectly well that the fanner world not be " relieved" by the passing of Lord Salisbury's Tithes Bill. The only difference would be that, in- stead of paying the parson, he would have to pay the money to his landlord.—En. Er.]
