Sir,—Your mud-larking correspondent, John Peers, evidently gets on the wrong "tack " whenthe abandons the geographical descriptions of his explorations of mud- banks, gutters, and guts, and takes to moralising on sub- jects he knows nothing about. Like a local Wesleyan minister, he seems to have seized the first opportunity of having a tilt at faith-healing, and then giving the medi- cine man a gratuitous advertisement. Your nautical narrator speaks in high terms of the " skill, experience. and medicines of a physician," but for my'part I fail to see where these qualities come in. Anyone who has read anything at all about the practice of modern medicine must know that it is nothing more or less than a huge humbug, and that our drug distributors have no more control over disease than the medicine men of the fast disappearing Indian tribes. It would be a waste of time for me to assure Mr. Peers that there is such a thing as faith-healing, and that I know of such cases. Suffice it to say that I have not such faith in the healing properties of physic as he seems to possess. My experience of the use of drugs is that they are useless and injurious, and the so3ner the public begins to realise this fact the better. But so long as people continue in disease-produciag habits of living, so long will they find constant employ- ment for the ever-increa-dng number of " doctors "in this town. The British people, it is said, will swallow anything, and certainly, if it be in the drug line, they wir swallow it with avidity. But with increasing educational facilities, Englishmen will learn to kcep their mouths closed to many things that now find a ready entrance; and when they begin to give a literal interpretation to -the scriptural injunction, " Cease to do evil ; learn to do well," there will be less room for drumming up the doctors by such physician-loving pilots as Mr. Peers. At all events, it 'mill save them from practical acquaintance with a less picturesque "poverty nook," and from fall- ing into "further straits" in that direction.— Yours Szc
CALIFORNIA AND BRITISH MEN.

div.head: ANTI-QUACK.
div.p: ANTI-QUACK.

Sir,—l saw in your issue of January 7th a statement which, I think, must have been written in a trades' union spirit, and calling my statements in question re- garding the wages of joiners and builders in particular. I can verify-every statement I have made by actual ex- perience, andl havesent yourcorrespondent'sletter toLos Angeles. It will no dcubt be contradicted by those on ' the spot. Last winter, when I was in Los Angeles and Pasadena, I conversed with men who, as joiners and builders of wooden houses, were earning Zl. and Ll 4s. a day, and many more could have found work at the same price. Now trade is even brisker and men cannot be got. I copy the following from the Los Angeles " Times" of November 4th:—" There is a great scarcity of labourers. I have to refuse contracts continually be- cause I cannot find men to do the work." A leading builder said the other day "I refused a 5,000 dollar order for the simple reason that I could not get men to do it." There is a great demand fcr skilled mechanics in all building trades. Another employer of 75 men said: —" There has been for months a scarcity of mechanics. and the wages of bricklayers at 245. a day. The prices of labour range from Bs. to 24s a day for common labourers, bricklayers and carpenters. Plasterers for eight to nine hours work earn from Ll to El 4s. a day." This is a cutting from the leading paper in the very town where men are warned by your correspondent to keep away from. Could a respectable Warrington paper hold its own if it made statements that men earned Ll and more a day, and the truth being that not half that could be earned ? I have no motive to mislead anyone, but I do sympa- thise with the toilworn men and women of Britain who so heroically fight the battle of life with such fearful odds against them. My experience of California has given me actual demonstration of the greater possibili- ties of that sunny land for all who believe in the dignity of labour, where A man is a man if he's willing to toil, And the humblest may gather the fruits of the soil. • I gladly point to that golden gate to happy independence. —Yours, &c., MARGARET E. PARSER.

div.head: IRISH QUESTION:T.-BY A 'PROTESTiLNT HOME
div.p: THE IRISH QUESTION:T.-BY A 'PROTESTiLNT HOME

RULER.—No. 3. would be glad if some of your Conservative readers would visit Ireland and see for themselves the condition of this country, which is a blot on the fair fame of England. Our population is yearly decreasing. During the past 46 years we have lost over three millions of our people, while the population of England and Wales has increased by 12 millions. Our towns decaying, our lands going out of cultivation, misery and starvation constantly with us, and the workhouse the only refuge of large numbers of the people. The number of inhabi- ted houses has enormously decreased. No less than 270,000 have been levelled to the ground. Who that has a heart can read these details without emotion? Two hundred and seventy thousand houses swept away! And in these the pulse of affection once beat warmly, for nature has endowed the peasant with feelings as well as the prince. To these the poor man proudly brought his bride. In these they no doubt spent years of humble contentment, cheered amidst their sorrow by each ether's love. And there too, have they -knelt around dy- ing embers, and in their own humble way and simple strains, presented their evening prayers to heaven. Emi- gration still continues, and I cannot too often refer to the anguish endured by my warm-hearted countrymen, when thus turn, from their humble, yet well beloved home; what this must be, the heartrending cries of emi- grants who throng the quays of this city, but too pain- fully show. Who could witness such scenes without feeling all that one of our poets has so touchingly ex-

pressed : " Good Heavens! what sorrows gloomed that parting day 'That called them from their native walks away; When the poor exiles, every pleasure past. Hung round the bowers, and fondly looked their last— And shuddering still to face the distant deep, Returned and wept. and still returned to weep." I am quite satisfied, after a visit to our shores, your Conservative readers would admit the justice of our claim to self-government, and would freely give us, what they themselves enjoy: "the right to make our own laws in our own land." In common with the majority of my fellow countrymen, I rely on the justice of the English people, and I am quite satisfied we shall not ap- peal to their sense of justice in vain; and at the next general election they will reverse their decision, which their more perfect knowledge of the situation will fully justify them in doing. Before concluding, I wish to say a few words on the subject of RELIGIOUS INTOLERANCE, which has been made so much of at your side, and can say as an Irish Protest- ant, that such does not exist in the South of Ireland. I have a very extensive knowledge of the country, and can vouch for the fact that Protestants and Catholics work together in the greatest harmony and good will. In the Corporation of this city (which is the most Catholic city in Ireland), 11 members out of &total of 50 are Protes- tants. The Corporation selected a Protestant High Sher- iff this year, and have sent up Protestant gentlemen as first and second on the list for next year. The Harbour Commissioners of Cork, on which Board the Catholics have a large majority, have now for the past three years elected a Protestant chairman. I have been elected to the Corporation by the Catholics of the ward which I have the honour to represent, and as a Protestant have not the least fear to trust my civil and religious liberty in the hands of my Catholic fellow countrymen. Eng- lishmen should not be led away by the cry of SEPARATION. No sane man in Ireland wants it. All men of position laugh at the idea; with your population, your wealth, with your navy and army, and every offensive appli- ance on your side, I cannot understand how Englishmen could for one moment entertain the idea. No, sir, Irish- men do not want separation. but look forward to the true union when Ireland will enjoy self-government, and when the Rose, the Shamrock and the Thistle shall be united in a firm bond of amity and peace. With many thanks for inserting these letters.—l remain yours faith- fully Cork, Jan. 10, 1888.
RICHARD A. ATKINS, T.C.
TFfE IRISFI LAND QUESTION. Sir,—lt appears according to your last week's issue that there is such a parson here and there in Ireland as- suming the term Protestant Home Ruler, and, as he

gives us his name, I presume it is true; otherwise I should have had some doubt. Mr. Atkins draws out a list of tenants, who have obtained great reductions in their rents, and gives this as a reason for the justice of the Plan of Campaign. What does he mean? Are we to understand that justice is unobtainable from the Land Court, unless it is preceded by a Plan of Campaign 'amongst the tenants? If such be the ease, Mr. Wad- stone in his Land Act should have granted full license, to the National League to fix the annual rental of the land in Ireland. In that case' what is now done under the name of the unwritten law, would have been' done in accordance with the law of the land. But sup- Pose we take another view of the case, and say that be- cause the Plan of Campaign had been inaugurated, the Sub-commissioners had yielded to the terror of the Na- tional League, at the expense of the landlords, by unjus- tifiably reducing the rents. How are we to decide in that ease, whether the cases he has alluded to, have been rail-rented to the extent he assumes? We must not forget that the sub-commissioners were, to a great ex- tent, nominated lw Mr. Gladstone's Government, and we are not in a position to know whether the same effect, that has affected such men as Lord Spencer and Sir W. Harcourt, has reached the sub-commissioners. Mr. At- li-ins must not come to the conclusion, because I have been trying to reason in this way, that I believe that rack-renting has never been resorted to by a great many of the landlords in Ireland. I have believed that ever since I knew what politics were; I know that there are bad landlords in Ireland, and always have been; more than that, 'believe they exist in England as well. But are we to assume ix .:ause there are bad landlords, that there are no good landlords? Does Mr. Atkins give us these cases that have been rack-rented as a reason why we should accept Mr. Glad- stone's ill-considered plan of giving Ireland a separate statutory Parliament, with executive powers? If so, how would he deal with the numerous cases of rack- rented farmers in England and Scotland? Nay, he may carry the system into the large towns, and he Si ill find that the artisan classes have to suffer very largely from this system of rack-renting. If this system, which un- fortunately has been carried on in Ireland, is because of English rule, and, as the Parnellites say has a foreign garb, what is the course we should adopt? We cannot rsv that we are under a foreign garb. To lay all blame of mis-government on England is a myth. To say that no mis-government would take place again, if Mr. Gladstone's'Bill had become law, and that Ireland had her own Executive Government, is absurd and foolish. If injustice exists in Ireland, it can be re- medied in Westminster, in my opinion, far better than on College Green. If the !British Government has not shown a desire to conciliate Ireland, by giving her good laws during the last twenty years, I really don't know what will convince them. the land in Ireland has been unremunerative of late years, but has it always been so? If so, how is a that the sub-conimissioners did not fix the rents, which they have just re luced, at the first whan they had the power granted them? Simply because the rents they have now fixed did not apply to that period. I have said thatland in Ireland for some years has been unremunerative don't mean all the land. But I would ask Mr. Atkins how it could be otherwise consider- ing the methods that have been adopted by the Land League after 1880 in letting the land go to ruin ? Even when the food was ready for the bar zest, farmers were forbidden to gather it in for fear of their lives. The order went forth that it. had to lie and rot, and yet now people wonder because the land has become unremunerativel Having reduced it to ruin, coupled with reduced prices, rents have of course to come down, although it is a strange fact that the increase in the sale of whisky in Ireland amounts to about the same sum as the reduced rents come to. We are told times with- out number, that Ireland cannot obtain justice and re- dress from British Ru'e and yet, strange to say, Home Rulers are dangling before our eyes the great reductions, that are taking place in the Land Courts. Is this not a proof that her greivances are listened to, and remedied? I have before me a list of rack-renting that is taking place in Ireland. by tenant-farmers who sub-let part of their tenancies for a sum considerably larger than they themselves have to pay to the landlord. Why does not Mr. Atkins and his associates agitate against this? Who is to bame for this? Will this rack-renting on the part of the tenant-°armers be laid at the door of British Rule? Let me give you a case that has been brought before our notice by Mr. 'Maude in the columns of last week's "Union." Mr. Maude asks, can it be possible that a landlord is rbliged to allow a reduction under the Land Act of 1887 to a tenant who purchased within the last three months uncle:- the following circumstances :—Old rent of holefing, £l4 2s 9d, which was reduced by the , Sub-Commissioners to £l2 10s in the year 1883, and has now changed hands by public auction at £445 exclusive of auctioneer's fees. Let Mr. Atkins reckon this up, and he aal find that this is only £5 short of 36 years' pur- chase. Had this farmer obtained the land direct from the landlord, he would have had it for less than one-half he has now undertaken ta pay. A remarkable ease was heard before Mr. Justice Monroe during the month, where a tenant in County Limerick held a large farm from the Earl of Devon at £BO a year. This was sub- let to a relative at over £2OO a year, notwithstaading which fact, he demanded and received a large abate- ment on his original rent. During the sitting of the Sub- Commissioners at Armagh a case was heard on the estate of Lieutenant Colonel Richardson. "The name of the tenant was William Irwin; area: sa. 2r. 25p.; rent £5; and valuation £6 ss. The tenant swore that a fair rent would be lOs per acre. He had paid £lOO for his hold- ing, and he could easier have paid the old rent seven years ago than half of it now.. On cross examination by Mr. Gallagher, solicitor, who appeared for the land- lord, he admitted that he had half an acre of the hold- ing sub-let to a tenant named Allen, at £3 per year, al- thouoia he was himself paying only £5 for the entire holding. Mr. Brush, the agent, had offered him a re- duction of 4s. in the pound, but he would not take it.— "Irish Times." November 17th, 1887." This is a typical

_ case of an Irish tenant, and similar examples are com- mon in the South and West of Ireland. The methods adopted by Gladstonians and Parnellites in order to get their plan of a separate Parliament for Irelard are any- thing but straightforward.—Yours Respectfully RADICAL UNIONIST.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

CONCERT AT HEISBY.—A very successful concert was held. on Monday evening, at the Church Schoolroom, Helsby. The place was crowded long ,before the time an- nounced for the commencement. The chair was taken by Mr. James Reynolds, of Fox Hill. The members of the Helsby Brass Band, who have been under the tuition of Mr. James Woods, of Runcorn. rendered very credita- bly a piece called "The Village Festival." Mr. Morris's quartette party, from Runcorn (the Misses Jones and Birkett, and Messrs. Morris and Birkett), sang three glees with their usual taste and ability, and were loudly applauded, being once recalled. A duet on cor- nets, played by Mr. J. Woods and Mr. Knight, was ren- dered in splendid style. Mr. R. T. Bibby sang ""le anchor's weighed" and " Rodked in the cradle of the deep "in an effective manner. One of the features of the evening was the playing by the Brothers Guest. AsSisted by Mr. James Wool (cornet) they gave quite a treat to the audience by the manner in which they rendered the two pieces set down to their names, and on each occa- sion they were deservedly encored. A cornet solo. "My pretty Jane," was beautifully played by Mr. J. Woods; then Mr. Morris, to fill up a breach (caused by the ab- sence of two gentlemen from Frodsham), sang in his usual happy style "The tar's farewell,' which was much enjoyed by the audience. The proceedings con- cluded by the singing of the National Anthem. Mr. J. Ravenscmft very ably presided at the piano.

. - PAROCHIAL TEA AND CONCHRT.—The annual tea meet- ing in connection with the parishioners of Frodsham was held in the National Girls' Schoolroom, Frodsham, yester- day afternoon week. The following ladies presided at the tea tables:—Mesdames C. Reynolds, C. E. Linaker, J. C. Sutton, J. Ashton, C. Hutchings, R. Bate, Duns- ford, Hurst, and Murray Misses Crosfield, Ashley, Simpson, Linaker, Weaver. Davies, and Malleson. Sub- sequently a concert was held in the Town Hall and the room was well filled. Mr. Ellison's String Rand opened the proceedings by Frost's "Evening Thoughts," which was well performed. A quartette, "Foresters sound the Cheerful Horn;" by Miss E. E. Riley, Me.-isrs. R. Holland, R. Jones. and W. M. Turn- bull followed. An encore was awarded to the song', "Fid- dle and I," by Mrs. J. Wilkinson, of Chester, with violin obligato by Mr. Holland. Mrs. Wilkinson also gained an ncore for her rendering of the song, "I'm going a milking!' Mr. A. W. Dolby caused much amusement by his contributions, • The Lads in Red," and "Old Pilot Jim," each of which re- ceived an encore. "Yes! let me like a soldier fall" and "There is a Flower that bloometh," by Mr. F. Spencer, were creditably rendered, and the latter was encored. Miss K. S. Rigby gave "In the Chimney Corner" in her usual excellent manner Mr. G. Maddock contributed much to the enloyinent of the evening by his comic songs," John the Masher "and "Nobody knows what trouble was there," and ho was twice recalled. Mr. John Holland's songs, "The Boat swain's Story" and "The Little Hero," were well received. "Kathleen Mavourneen was delightfully sung by Miss E. E. Riley. and was subsequently encored, as was also a duet entitled "The Spirits of the Wood," by Miss K. L. Rigby and Mr. B. A. Rigby. The Vicar. Rev. H. B. 810g,,g, M.A., caused much mirth by a reading which he gave, called "Mr. Butterwick's Horse," an American story. • The Band brought the proceedings to a close by a selection from the " Bohemian Girl," and the National Anthem.

Never trouble another for what you can do for your- self. "I have never given you credit for knowing vtry much, madam," said a blunt old bachelor; " but—:" "Sir," she interrupted. "do you wish to insult—" " But," he continued, "I have :ilways admired your grace and beauty." "I accept your apology," iaid the lady.

Three college boys were having a spread and a sor;e in their rooms, when there came a thundering knock at the door, and they asked who was there. "Me," said the angry voice a the college president. "Oh, no," said the boys, "you can't give us that. If it were President he would have said 'lt is I.' Go away." And the baffled dignitary went. .

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 14, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 14, 1888.
ST. MARY'S ROMAN CATHOLIO CHURCH.
THE NEW ORGAN.

A new organ, which is being erected in St. Mary's (RAI) Church in Butterrnarket-street, Warrington, , at a cost of about £l,OOO, will Ahortly be completed, and it is expected that it will be formally opened before the end of the present month. The instru- ment, which is practically already built, is under- going a few "finishing touches" at the hands of the builder, Mr. E. Franklin Lloyd, of Chester-street, Liverpool, who takes a great interest in his work. The building of the organ was commenced in April last, and everything has been done under the per- sonal supervision of Mr. Lloyd, who is now engaged in voicing, regulating, and tuning it. The pedal organ has the tubular action, the great organ the pneumatic action, and the reed work, of 'which Mr. Lloyd has made a speciaßty, is very line. The fol- lowing is a description of the instrument —Swell organ: double diapason, 16ft.; open diapason, Bft.; Liilich gedacht, Bft.; iuticional, Bft.; vox angelica, 81t4 principal, 4ft.; fifteenth. 2ft.; mixture, 3 ranks; , hautboy, 81t.; cornepean, Bft.; clarion, 41t. Great • Organ :—Contra gamba. 16ft.•, open diapason, Bft.; gamba, 81t.; stop diapason, Bft.; flute 4ft.; princi- pal, 4ft.; twelfth, 21ft.; fifteenth, 21t.•, mixture, three ranks; trumpet, Bft.; clarion, 4ft. Choir Organ :—Open diapason, 81t.; clarabella, Bft.; dal- mans, Bft.; suabe flute, 4ft.; gemshorn, 41t.; corm di bassetto Bft. Pedal Organ :—Open diapason, 16ft. ; bourcion. 16ft.; violone, 16ft.; violincello, 81t. Couplers :—Swell to great, choir to swell, great to , pedal; swell to pedal, choir to pedal, tremulant. There are three composition pedals to the swell, organ, three to the great organ, and a horse-shoe pedal to the great-to-pedal coupler. The full , width of the organ shows 28 feet of metal frontage. The gallery on which it stands has been lengthened several feet, and ample accommodation is thus provided for the choir. Mr. Joseph Dolan, joiner and builder, has had charge of this portion of the work, and has, also supplied the wood work for the organ. In s little room at one side of the organ gallery an Otto gas engine has been erected, and motive power is thus supplied without the aid of "organ-blowers." • The new instrument will be an ornament to the church, and there is no doubt that at the hands of the organist, Mr. T. Mather, it will receive full justice. ' LORD SALISBURY AT LIVERPOOL.

The Marquis of Salisbury addressed a large gathering of Conservatives in Hengier's Circus, Liverpool, on Wednesday evening. Replying to an address of welcome presented by Mr. A. B. Forwood, M.P., on behalf of the South-west Lancashire and Wirral Conservative Associations, Lord Salisbury urged that the prospects of the Conservative and Liberal Unionist. forces for the future were of a very promising character. They had had a difficult battle to fight. Their political opponents had relied upon the conviction that Ireland could not be governed unless the Executive conceded all that the Irish agitators demanded; on that imagina- tion all the hopes of the Opposition had been based, and they had directed all their policy to secnre that that imagination should be fulfilled. He did not, he remarked, like to attach too much inportance to the results of by-elections, but it seemed to him that the difference between those in the summer and those jn the autumn was due to this, that in the former case the judgment of the elec- tors was warped by the strange and monstrous descriptions of the Crimes Act in which Parliamen- tary orators indulged, and that in the autumn the people saw that the Crimes Act was" doing no harm but only good." He stigmatised as a" monstrous charge " the assertion that the Conservative party were insincere in their opposition to Home Rule, and said the statement that in 1885 there were eminent members of the Conservative Cabinet, be- sides Lord Carnarvon,who favoured Home Rule was an "utter, complete, and absolute falsehood." After ridiculing Mr. Gladstone's suggestion that the Con- servative and Liberal Unionist leaders were not to be trusted on the subject of Free Trade, the noble Marquis maintained the truth of the historical ex- amples about the consolidation of related nationali- ties which he set forth at Derby on a recent occa- sion. While admitting that England had been guilty of many crimes against Ireland, he asserted that England's greatest crime had been her vacillation 'in the government of Ireland. He entreated the English democracy to justfy its existence as a sys- tem of government by resolution anti tenacity. Having suppressed conspiracies to murder or to steal, let it firmly • and consistently rule for the welfam of Ireland and the preservation of the Empire. On Thursday Lord Salisbury attended a private luncheon given by Mr. A. B. Forwood, at his resi- dence. the Priory, Gateacre. Afterwards he visited in succession the Conservative Clubs at Wavertree, Edge-hill, and in Abercromby Division. and at the first made a speech commending such institutions as aids to temperance. In the evening he attended a grand banquet in the Philharmonic Hall, presided over by Lord Lathom. Responding to the toast of his health, he expressed the deternlination of the Government to carry out the law in spite of all abuse and resistaFe. He stated his conviction that the country was in process of extrication from the calamitous depression of trade, and that the touch of the magic wand Of prosperity would untie the knot of many of our political troubles. The Government were entering upon a hazardous session, and he hoped Conservatives .would remem- ber their difficulties. To maintain the Union, they depended upon the sepport of the Unionist party, consequently their measures must bear, to a certain extent, the colour which the Unionist party gave to them. In the event of any adverse vote, they must - be guided in deciding whether to appeal to the country by their sense of the overwhelming respon- sibility of submitting the constitution to the elec- tors at a time not suited to obtain their real and deliberate decision. He thought that appeal should be deferred, if possible, until the result of the recent measures in Ireland was displayed to the minds of the people. Dealing with the rumours of war in Europe, his lordship said he should be sorry to induce anybody to carry his conviction to• the certainty of it permanent peace. PRESENTATION OF AN ADDRESS AT WARRINGTON.

The train in which the Marquis of Salisbury journeyed from Hatfield to Liverpool en Wednesday, was due to arrive at the Central Station, Warrington. at 3.27 in the afternoon, but a considerable time before this the approaches to the station were closed, and many persons were refused an entrance. Notwithstanding, however, a number of persons, mostly members of the Warrington Conservative Association, got on the platform, and waited patiently the arrival of the train, which was a quarter of an hour behind time. Among those who assembled to greet the Premiet? were Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P. for the borough, Mr. W. C. Jones (Conservative candidate for the Leigh Division), Mr. John White, Mr. H. Greenall, the Rev. W. H. Price, Mr. Wynne Jones, Mr. .T. Fairclough, Messrs. Speakman, Eddowes, Bloomfield. Fligeinbotham, H. Collins, R. Isher- wood, and others. Chief Constable Hunt and a staff of police were also present on the platform. When the train entered the station a rush was made for the car- riage containing his lordship, who, however, did not seem anxious to present himself to his admirers. Several minutes were thuS wasted in finding the Premier, who was seated in a first-class compartment. The crowd then gathered round the carriage, and the Marquis was presented with the following address by Sir Gilbert Greenall
TO THE RTOT TWN. THE MARQUTI SALTSBDT4Y, R.C3. - - - . _ .

, 11Iy Lord.—The Conservatives of Warrington cannot permit , your lordship to pass through their town without taking the opportunity of congratulating you on the success which has so far attended the efforts of the Government to restore tran- quility to Ireland, and they beg to assure you of their sym- pathy in the arduous struggle for law and order in which you are engaged, and of their continued and unrelaxing efforts to support von and the Government in the object you have in view.—Signed, on behalf of the Warrington Conservative Association, by the President. . 11th January. 1888. There was no time to read the address, but in handing it through the window to the noble lord, Sir Gilbert As- sured him that the Conservatives of Warrington held him in the highest regard, and they had every confidence in him and the Government of which he was the head. They hoped further that the efforts of the Government to maintain peace and order in Ireland would be crowned with success. The noble marquis thanked Sir Gilbert for the address, and said he was pleased to hoar of the loyalty of Warrington Conservatives, at the same time reciprocating a hope that success would attend the Government legislation in Ireland. Very few of those who had assembled to greet the Premier were able to catch as much as a passing glimpse of him, and consider- able disappointment was expressed.

The Prime Minister passed through Warrington at 11-45 yesterday mornin,". on his return journey to Hat- field. There were very few people on the platform at the time, and only the railway officials seemed to be aware that his lordship was in the train. Mr. Chalton; assistant district manager of the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee, and Mr. Winders, of the detective department, travelled in the train.

div.head: BOLD-STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL.
div.p: BOLD-STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL.

' The innual tea meeting was held in,.ld-street , Wesleyan School-room, Warrington, on Thmisday evening, when the proceedings were of a very suc- cessful nature. A large number of friends sat down to an enjoyable ten, and at the sabsequent meeting there was a ;zoool attendance.—the chair was oc- cupied by the Rev. G. E. Toe, superintendent of the Warrington circuit, who, after the meeting had been opened with singing andprayer, said that he remem- bered a similar occasion twelve months ago, when they had a good meeting; but he thought that the attendance that night was more numerous than on the former occasion They were glad to see an increased interest in Sunday school work. So far as he had been able to judge, he thought thateverything had been goiag on fairly well during the past twelve utenths. There had of necessity been some changes dulltg the year and one of the earliest Sunday school superintendents, Mr. Silcodes colleague, had removed to Manchester, to their deep re- gret. Mr. Sikock ocenpied one of the highest positions that the circuit could confer, upon one of the members, and was one of the circuit stewards. He was also a local iireacher, and A very good one too. By the unanimous approval of the teachers of the Sun- day school, Mr. Evans had been appointed to be Mr. Silcoc'k's colleague as superintendent. They had also a large number of teachers, whose duties involved a great deal ,of self-denial•aud hard work. He thought that they were very fortunate in having such a set of teachers and officers in connection with the school. They had also an important young men's class. If they, could only get hold of the young men and women, they had a good chance of keeping them. Although they had a . large school in Bold-street that was only a poition of the work. They had another large school in connection with Bewsey-road, at Silver-street, and he was glad to see that several of the friends from that school were pre- sent that evening. They had also all the machinery at • work in connection with the Methodist system, both in town and,country. On'the whole they were doing fairly , well, and they thanked God and took cour- age. He hoped that the present would be a happy year in connection with their Sunday school work.—Miss S. Pigot and Miss A. Gill ' having played a duet on the piano, Mr. Henshall, the secretary, read a statement of the progress of the school during the last twelve months. Ordinary routine work had been energetically carried on. and they were glad to ' report that the school had had a very peaceful and pros- perous year, and that its efficiency and discipline had been fully maintained. There was no very material al- teration in the statistics. The number of teachers was 55, as compared with 47 last year, and 48 out of the 55 were members of the society. The scholars numbered 491, there being 249 males and 242 females. In the pre vious year there were ca scholars-255 males and 223 females. The average attendance of teachers was— morning 21, compared withl9 ; afternoon 32, being one more than the preceding year. The morning average attendance of scholars was 151, and the afternoon average attendance 338. The school library had been actively used throughout the year, and the librarian re- ported-that the demand for books was more than equal to the supply. There were 405 volumes in the library. , The Band of Hope was doing good work, having 1101 members, that being an advance of 18 on the previous year.—Subsequently addresses -were given by the Rev. W. Brookes, the Rev. E. J. Jackson, Mr. Silcock, Mr. S. . B. Stringer, and Evans. Anthems were given by the choir, Mr. R. E. Garnett gave recitations, Mrs. C. Parker and Miss F. Garnett contributed a .pianoforte duet, and the Misses Toft gave selections on the violin. and piano. During an interval, Mrs. Young distributed certificates of merit to the scholars.

div.head: LYIIII.
div.p: LYIIII.

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.-012 Monday Mr. James Dodds read a paper to the members of this asso- ciatiOn on the" National balance sheet." Mr. Welford presided. The FoG.—Along with other places, Lymm has dim- ing the present week been enveloped in a dense fog, and considerable inconvenience has been thereby caused to the inhabitani,s. The railway traffic having been im- peded by the fog, many of the trains were late in their arrival at the station, and borne of them were more than half an hour behind time.

BAPTIST MUTUAL IMPROV2MENT SOCIETY.—The weekly meeting was held on "Wednesday evening. Readings were given by Messrs. Hollingsworth, Perkin, Eaton and Bragg, and an impromptu speech on " Pride " was given by Mr. Eaton, Messrs. Knowles, Clarke, Diamond, Grif- fiths, and G. Clarke taking part in a discussion that fol- lowed. Mr. Perkins gave a recitation. A paper on " Disestablishment," was read by Mr. E. Clarke. DEATH OF MR. THOMAS MOSTON.—Mr. Thomas Mos- ton, Winer and carrier, who for a long time has journeyed between Lymm and Warrington, died on Tuesday in his 06th year. The deceased, who had been a cari:er for more than thirty, years, was highly respec- ted. He was an ardent Liberal in politics, and, mdee 1, was so when it was almost an unpardonable offence in Lymm to be a Liberal. The funeral of the deceased took place in the churchyard yesterday afternoon, a con- siderable number of relatives, and several inhabitants of the village attending. Shutters were up at many 'shops, and blinds were drawn, as a mark of the respect in which the deceased was held. TEA MEETING AT OnoirratywroN.—The annual tea meeting in connection with the Parish Church, was held on Monday evening. The tables were presided over by Mesdames G. B. Dewhurst, Everton, Knocker, 0. G. I Smith, Howard, and Whitelegg, and Misses Brereton, King (2), Ethel Wright, Thornley, and Everton. After tea a public meeting and entertainment was held under 'the presidency of theßev. W. O. Knocker, rector, who, in a speech of considerable length, touched upon all the subjects of interest in the parish which had taken place during the year. Addresses were also delivered by Mr. G. B. Dewhurst, Mr. Parr, and Mr. Everton, and a mis- cellaneous programme was afterwards carried Out. CHURCH OF ENGLAND TRMPERAMCR SOCIRTY.—About fifty members of the Juvenile Branch of the above so- ciety were entertained to tea in the Parochial Schools on Tuesday e••ening. Mesdames Guest and Ardern, and the Misses Dearden, Ardwick, Bayley, and Cookson pre- sided at the tables. After tea an entertainment was given, to which the friends of the members were invited. The Rev G. W. Guest occupied the chair, and delivered an interesting address on temperance. A 'pianoforte duet was given by Misses Grundy4ind Bird, a violin solo by Miss Mildred Thew, and a song by Mr. Blakemore. The chief feature of the programme was the performance of the school cantata of "Red Riding Hood," the chief characters being sustained by the Misses Grundy, Swan- wick, and Dutton. WARM:ft/TON CONGREGATIONAL TEA PARTY AND CHOIR CONCERT.—This annual social gathering was held in the schoolroom, Warburton. The tables were presided over by Mesdames Egerton-Warburton, Newton, Moore,West, Beckett, and others. After tea a concert was given by members of the choir of St. Werburgh's. The chair was taken by the Rector (Rev. G. Egerton-Warburton). The programme included songs, &c., by Mr John 13olton' Mr A. Walton, Misses West, Holt, Collins, Green, and Bol- ton and Master Scattergood. Mr R. Newton proposed a vote of thanks to the Rector for presiding, to the ladies for presiding at tea, and to the choir far the good enter- tainment they had provided, which was responded to by hearty applause. Mr Oliver West, son of the choir- master, presided at the piano. WESLEYAN ANNUAL TEA MEETING.—OR TURSdareVSTl- ing the annual tea party in connection with the Lymm Wesleyan Sunday School was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. A very substantial tea was provided, and the tables were presided over by Mrs. Dodds, Mr. and Mrs. Brown, Miss Ashton, Miss Halford, Miss M. A. Jones, Miss Moston, Miss Bate, and Miss Rowlinson. After the tables were cleared a meeting was held, the Rev. G. E. Young presiding. After an address by the Chairman, Mr. Brown read a statement as to the Sunday School, which was as follows :—Number of scholars on the books, 146; the largest attendance on one day dur- ing the past year was on Sunday, November 13th, when 111.11 scholars were present. This was the best, in the history of the school, so far as they had been able to trace back. The average attendance in the morning was 52; in the afternoon 97. They seemed to have kept very I close to (he year before, for last year it was 52 and 94. Ten years ago, in 1877, the average attendance in the morning was 48; in the afternoon, 81. He was glad, he added, to see that their school was in a very healthy and flourishing condition. (Applause.)—AddreesPs were also given by the Rev. W. Evans, Mr. Ward, and Mr. Ford. The meeting was brought to a close in the usual way.. .

SPECIAL REETING OF THE LOCAL BOARD.—A special meeting of the Lymrn Local Board was held on Thurs- day evening, the members present being Messrs. Came- ron (in the chair), Thomason, Gibbons, Harrison, For- ster, Dutton, Rogers, Bra zendale, and Appleton, with the clerk, Mr. T. J. Ridgway.—The Clerk reported that he ha 4 received the sum of £lO from Mr. Stubs, and he had Nen promised a further sum of £lO from Mr. Mc- Iver, towards providing work for the local unemployed. At the last meeting of the Board, he added, he offered to be at the cost of making a road through his ground, if the Board would permit their surveyor to take charge of the work. Since that time the Board's surveyor had es- timated that the cost would amount .to £45 .13s 4d, and he (the clerk) had paid to the Board's account a sum of £5O for the purpose in question.—On the motion of Mr. Rogers, seconded by Mr. Harrison, it was resolved to pass a cheque for £25 to enablethe surveyor to proceed with the work.—A circular, signed by Lord Egerton of Tattun, was read. In it the Board was asked to send a representative to a conference that is to be held this month at Manchester for the purpose.of considering the pollution of the rivers Mersey and Dwell. It was re- solved, on the motion of Mr. Thomason, seconded by Mr. Rogers, that the chairman and the law clerk be ap- pointed a deputation to attend the conference.—Mcssrs. Thomason and Harrison lodged protests against the Board taking legal proceedings against Mr. Brazeridale in reference to the falling of a wall on Mr. Henshall's premises .—The Clerk mentioned the subject of the dis- posal of the Board's sewage farm to the Ship Canal Co., and the chairman said that as the final arrangements could not be Come to that evening, it would perhaps be advisable that the reporters should not be present.—The rest of the meeting was held in private.

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
[FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.]
23, Old Broad-street, E.C.

There have been few features of interest on the Stock Exchange during the past week. The fortnightly settle- ment which commenced on Tuesday and terminated on Thursday has absorbed nearly the whole attention of brokers, and what business has been done in other mat- ters.was of a characterless description. . _

With the close of the settlement, there is a very general belief that an all round rise in prices will take place mote especially in mining speculation. The activity in this market during the past two months has been almost without precedent for several years, and it is considered by those who are sup- posed to be authorities on the subject that the activity, as far as the general public is concerned, is really only conimencing. Whether this be so or not, there can be no question that the value of the Transvaal gold fields of South Africa is acknowledged to be without rival, and the profits to be divided are undoubtedly Feat. This statement presupposes that existing cornpatues, and the new enterprises which are shortly to be launched, are , worked honestly and in the interests of the share- holders.

There is room for the absprption 4 a large amount of capital in working the sound mining schemes, but, as it has been repeatedly pointed out, intending investors should take the ordinary precautions which apply to all new undertakings before embarking their capital in schemes which may look very tempting, but which, on closer perusal, would not fail to reveal the greed of. pro- moters, and not the bona-fide wish to start a genuine enterprise. There are in existence at present several companies whose • shares are consider- ably below par which are far better. deserv- ing of attention 'than any new ones, as it is not too much to say that every mining company through various phases, the chief of which is a rlaerS 7 decline after a time on the par value of its shares until its actual working has been started. finally on the value of things mining enterprises are purely specula- tive, and those who cannot afford to lose should never , touch them.

Home rails have commanded attention during the past week, and are considerably higher than at the close of the year. On Wednesday the dividends of the London, Brighton, and South Coast Railway were declared. On the dividend ordinary stock of 4 per cent. fon the half year, making 5 per cent, for the year and 3 per cent, for the half year on the, preference stock, . This gives 5 per cent, for the whole year on the defferred stock, leaving £6f300 to be carried forward. For 1886 the dividend on the deferred stock was 41 per cent. The directors of the Metropolitan Railway Co, subject to final audit, will recommend a dividend on the ordinary stock at the rate of 2/ per cent, per annum, carrying for- ward £20,000. The dividend on the surplus land stock will be at the rate of 2/1 per cent. For the second half of 1886, the dividend on the undivided was at the rate of 4f per cent.

Tag roue)] Altana-axon Ctiss.—The members of the constabulary in the Newton Division who formed the recent class of the St. John Ambulance Association, and underwent a creditable successful examination by Dr. Garton, of St. Helens, received their newly-designed badge on Sgturday afternoon. The whole of the mem- bus of the class were successful, and they have each been presented with the token of their success and of their ability to render first aid to the injured. The badges, which are to be worn on the left arms, are silver plated, and round the circ eof the badge are the words "Lancashire Constabulary." In the centre is a space showing the Cross of St. John, or, as it is better under- stood, a Maltese Cross. This cross is in red, and gives the badge a pleasing appearance.

Tim FOG: Accinatir AT Nowrox.---The heavy fog which has enveloped the Earlestown and Newton district each day during the present week has caused consider- able inconvenience to vehicular traffic, especially in the outlying country roads. On Tuesday morning the at- mosphere was clearer, but in the afternoon a thick fog again enshrouded everything in darkness. Many of the trains were late, especially the 8-0 p.m. from Earlestown to Liverpool, which did not leave until .9 o'clock. The discharge of fog signals on the line has been con- tinuous, resembling the firing of cannons, at intervals of a few minutes throughout the day. On Wednesday night, an elderly man named Struthers -was returning to his home at Golborne from Messrs McCorquodale's print- ing works, l'srewton, when he made a false turn, got in some fields, and subsequently stumbled into an old pit. When discovered next morning he was ma deplorable condition, and nearly starved to death, having been lying out for fifteen hours within a few minutes' walk from home.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The miners of Fife and Clackmannan were on Friday warned of a reduction of 10 per cent. Mt. Barnum has made an offer to buy the Great East- ern steamship, for the purposes of a travelling show. Dr: Thomas Wheeler, a well-known Belfast physician, drank on Friday some prussic acid, and died two hours afterwards.
The trial of Henry Bowles for the Camberley murder was resumed at the Old Bailey on Friday. Medical evi- dence was given. _

Mr. J. G. Gibson, M.P on Friday formally intimated to his committee in the Walton division of Liverpool, his acceptance of an Irish judgeship. The island of Lewes is still in a very disturbed state. In the districts of Carloway, Shabost, and Ness, the cotters have invaded the sheep runs, and demolished the fences and dykes.

• SERIOUS CAITBREME OF TYPHOID FEVER IN IRELAND.— Typhoid fever has broken out at the village of Inver, in Connemara, two or three deaths occurring on the average day. The Protestant rector, his curate, and a Scripture reader have died of the malady. More than 50 patients have been sent to hospital. ALLEGED MURDER BY A WlFE.—Mary Ann Phillips, an old woman, was committed for trial at Cardiff, on Friday, on the charge of murdering her husband, aged 79. The old man was found lying in the back kitchen covered with wounds and bruises alleged to have been inflicted by the prisoner with a.broom and coal pick. DEPARTURE OF LORD SALISBURY FROM LIVETtPOOL.— Lord Salisbury left Gateacre Priory on Friday morning, and visited the Liverpool Conservative Club, where he was shown over the building: He then drove to the Central Station, where he was joined by the Marchion- ess and Lady Gwendolyn Cecil, and proceeded to Hat- field.

SUICIDE OF A CONVICT.—An Indian convict, named Munshee Shiek Gheesa, aged thirty-five, has committed suicide in Chatham Prison, by hanging himself to the bars of the closet window by his braces. He was a native conjuror, and was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude at Manchester Assizes in 1884, for unlawfully wounding. He was under the delusion that hewas going to befogged and thrown into the river. PROPOSED LINE OF AMERICAN STEAMERS TO WALES.— The Welsh newspapers of Friday announce on authority that negotiations have been opened between the Milford Haven 'Estat,e Company and an influential syndicate of &pitalists for the purpose of constructing spacious docks at Milford for the use of a special line of express passen- ger and mail steamers between NeW York and the Principality, to vie with the Liverpool steamers. The expenditure on the new docks will, it is stated, exceed £300,000, _ _

MORE CoEucum—Mr. Roche, poor law guardian, Mr. P. Boland, and tone other Nationalists were arrested in Woodford and its neighbourhood, late on Thursday night, and lodged in the adjacent police barracks, on warrants charging them with having been present at an illegal assembly on the night of the 21st December, on the occasion of the release of Mr. Martin Egan from im- prisonment in Galway Gaol. The prisoners were all admitted to bail to appear at a special petty sessions, convened under the Crimes Act, and to be held at Wood- ford, on Monday next. This is the third time Mr. Roche has been arrested-under the Crimes Act.

Tna FOG.—MoRE FATALITIES.—The fog was still dense at Sunderland on Friday. At Liverpool there was in- tense darkness. The fog still prevailed in North Eng- land. Some of Lord Durham's collieries are stopped. Andrew Allan, relies ing officer, walked into the Wear at Spennymoor, and was drowned. A young lady named James was drowned near Wol,verhampton on Thursday evening through her father's trap falling into the canal during the fog. The Channel mail service has now been resumed. Two fatalities have been reported in Worcestershire, the victim in each case walking into the water, which he was unable to see owing to the fog. SHOCKING MURDER OF AN OLD MAN.—Some commo- tion was caused in the neighbourhood of Addlestone, Surrey, on Friday morning, on its becoming known that during the r;ght an old•retired carpenter named Chav- ter, who lived in a small cottage, had been brutally murdered. It appears that the deceased lived with his son, who, however, was absent on Thursday night. It is supposed that this fact becoming known, combined with the belief that the deceased had in his possession a con- siderable sum of money that he had saved, some person or persons broke into the house during the night, and battered in the skull of the only occupant. The old man, who was between 60 and 70 years of age, must have been most savagely illtreated, his features, when he was found, being almost unrecognizable. No arrests have yet been made.
ALLEGED PLOT AGAINST THE CROWN PRINCE'S LIFE.

The "Daily Chronicle" Paris correspondent says :—A plot against the Crown Prince's life is announced from San Rev°. One of the Socialists in the conspiracy tamed Informer, and the Italian and the German police have taken every precaution. PANIC IN A CHURCH.—EIGHT PERSONS KILLED.

The " Daily Chronicle" Vienna correspondent tele- raplisl—A terrible disaster occurred at Lavis, in the Southern Tyrol, on Wednesday evening. While the priest was preaching a member of the congregation was t4,4zed 3sith an epileptic tit, and in the confusion which followed someone raised an alarm of fire. • The congre- gation became panic-stricken, and made a sudden rush for the doors. Eight persons were crushed to death and many injured.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

TRH FIRE IN ORPOED•LA.NIL—We understand that the fire that occurred last evening week on the premises of Mr. Joseph Ashbrook, farmer. of Orford- lane, resulted in damage to the amount of over £lOO being done to the farm buildings and stock The loss is covered by insurance. THE LAI% MR. JAIIES MONICS.—The mortal re- mains of the late Mr. James Monks, rope and twine manufacturer, Bridge-foot, who died last week after a lingering illness, were on Saturday interred at the cemetery, the funeral service being conducted by the Rev. J. Warnock, pastor of St. John's Presbyte- rian Church, Wi n wick-street.

CADISIIEAD.—The Post o,lXee : Recently the Post Office has been removed from the Central-place to Sunnyside, Liverpool-road.= Wes/cyan chapel : A sacred cantata, entitled "The night of glory." was Oven by the choir in this chapel, on Monday even- ing. An efficient band was conducted by Mr. Thomas L. Browne. The following ladies and gen- tlemen contributed :—Misses Mary Johnson, Ada Browne, Mary liampson, Margaret Iresford, Mary Toft, Elizabeth Taylor; and Messrs. Lot Broqlcs, John Wright, Robinson, Davies, Shaw, J. H. Gatenby, and T. Hanipson. SUDDEN DEATH OP A WINWICIC LABOURER.— Michael Mulligan (59). a labourer in the employ of Mr. Cooper, farmer. Wi nwick, died "suddenly on Tuesday atthe Warrington Union Workhouse. It appears that deceased had been suffering from a severe cold for some time, and he was taken to the Workhouse in a cab by order of the Newton re- lieving officer. When he arrived there he walked to the house of the Master, in the direction of the hos- pital, but seemed very weak. He was placed on a chair in the Master's house, and brandy was admin- istered, but he died in a few minutes. before medi- cal assistance could be obtained.—lt was not deemed necessary that a coroner's inquiry should be held.

CHRIST CHURCH SUNDAY ScrrooL, CROFT.—On Sunday morning, the Rev. T. P. Kirkman, rector of Croft, presented the annual prizes, consisting of choice and useful books, to the scholars attending the above Sunday 00l for good attendance during the past year. The following were the recinients : —Leah Monks, Sarah Ann Wild. Bessie Whiston, Annie Maines, Elizabeth Waywell. Alice Moines, Jane Hatton, Annie Beckett, Gertrude Mary Owen, Margaret Hatton, Mary Monks, and Elizabeth Shaw; William Green, Arthur Monks, Samuel Street, John Maines, John Monks. Albert Beckett, Reginald Owen, and Archie James Owen. FUNERAL OF Mn. JOHN GRACE.—The interment of the remains of the late Mr. John Grace, of St. Helens, and formerly of Penketh, took place at St. Mary's Chapel, -Sankey, on Sunday. The &ceased was an old and valued servant of the Royal London Friendly Society, and in the first few years of its introduction into Lancashire he displayed con- siderable energy on its behalf in travelling through Warrington. St. Helens, Widnes, Earlestown, Ash- ton, rfarlock, Golborne, Newton, Wigan, ke. He had for 25 years been connected wi,h the Society and his death. occasioned a feeling of sorrow among his brother officials, a large number of whom atten- ded the funeral as a last mark of respect. He died at St. Helens On Wednesday week, and his body was interred at Sankey, as stated. The mourning coaches contained the deceased's sons, Mr. Thomas Grace, Mr. William Graco, Mr Ed. Grace, Mr Richard Grace. and Miss Grace : Mr. T. Fyans (district superintendent Wigan and St. Helens), of the Royal London Friendly Society: Mr. David Owen (superintendent, Liverpool), Mr. T. H. Ashcroft (superintendent, Warrington), Mr. J. P. Callaghan (Assistant superintendent, Bolton), Mr. Richard Higharri (assistant superintendent, St. H4lens). and Mr. John Houghton. the oldest agent in• St. Helens. The next four oldest agents were carriers, viz. :—Messrs, Henry Anderton, J. Garner, William Cox, and Thomas Cowen, of St. Helens. Amongst those present were Messrs. W, Crick, Wil- liam Wallace. Anthony Rigby. and James ; Messrs. B. Hobson, Penketh ; Thomas Groves, Jacob Holey, Andrew Jennings. John Cotterhill, and T. Booth, of Warrington. The funeral service was conducted by the vicar, the Rev, Edwin Sandys Jackson.

MARRIAGE OF THE Rim I'. L. GOOD.—OR Mon day morning the Rev. F. Lake Good, curatt.in- charge of the Emmanuel Reformed Church of Eng- land, Bold-street, was married at the Reformed Church to Miss Sutton, third daughter of the late Mr. Samuel Sutton. The ceremony wa§ of a private character, only intimate friends being present,. The newly-married couple afterwards left for South- port, where the honeymoon will be spent. The Rev. W. Mules, of Eccles, was the officiating clergyman at the.marriage. HALL - STREET WESLEYAN MISSION SUNDAY SCHOOL. --The annual free tea in connection with the above school was given on Tuesday evening, in the Buttermarket-street school. About 130 scholars sat down to tea, after which they enjoyed several games. At nine o'clock, prizes were given to the scholars who had made the best attendance. An orange was given to all present and the enjoyable meeting was brought to a close. Mr. W. Isaac gave a subscription of 10s, and Mr. Kneen gave prizes to the value of ss. Several subscriptions were also given by the teachers. PEASLEY CROSS CONGREGATIONAL CHAzzi—A. meeting of the members of the Congregational Churches in St. Helens was held in the Lecture Hall, Brook-street, on Wednesday night, when it was unanimously decided to ins ite the Rev. W. R. Parry, of Warrington, to take charge of the Peasley Cross Church district. A deputation from the church has since waited upon Mr. Parry, and urged his acceptance of the post, but the reverend gentle- man has taken time to consider the matter. Mr. Parry has been very successful at Cockhedge Mis- sion, which is an off-shoot of the Wycliffe Congrega- tional Church. Warrington. He is a zealous and active worker, and his loss will be much felt if he should decide to leave the town. The chapel at Peasley Cross will, we learn, seat about 700 people.
